senses.d: A thin cake made of flour and other ingredients.
q: Wafers piping hot out of the gleed.
The curious work in pastry, the fine cakes, wafers, and marchpanes.
A woman's oaths are wafers — break with making

senses.d: A thin cake or piece of bread (commonly unleavened, circular, and stamped with a crucifix or with the sacred monogram) used in the Eucharist, as in the Roman Catholic Church.
An adhesive disk of dried paste, made of flour, gelatin, isinglass, or the like, and coloring matter, — used in sealing letters and other documents.

Wafer.etym: [OE. wafre, OF. waufre, qaufre, F. qaufre; of Teutonic origin; cf. LG. & D. wafel, G. waffel, Dan. vaffel, Sw. våffla; all akin to G. wabe a honeycomb, OHG. waba, being named from the resemblance to a honeycomb. G. wabe is probably akin to E. weave. See Weave, and cf. Waffle, Gauffer.]

senses.d: To seal or close with a wafer.
To move one way and the other with quick turns; to shake to and fro; to move vibratingly; to cause to vibrate, as a part of the body; as, to wag the head.
q: No discerner durst wag his tongue in censure.
Every one that passeth thereby shall be astonished, and wag his head.

Wag.etym: [OE. waggen; probably of Scand. origin; cf. Sw. vagga to rock a cradle, vagga cradle, Icel. vagga, Dan. vugge; akin to AS. wagian to move, wag, wegan to bear, carry, G. & D. bewegen to move, and E. weigh. √136. See Weigh.]

senses.d: To move one way and the other; to be shaken to and fro; to vibrate.
q: The resty sieve wagged ne'er the more.

senses.d: To be in action or motion; to move; to get along; to progress; to stir.
q: “Thus we may see,” quoth he, “how the world wags.”

senses.d: To go; to depart; to pack oft.
q: I will provoke him to 't, or let him wag.

senses.d: The act of wagging; a shake; as, a wag of the head.
A man full of sport and humor; a ludicrous fellow; a humorist; a wit; a joker.
q: We wink at wags when they offend.
A counselor never pleaded without a piece of pack thread in his hand, which he used to twist about a finger all the while he was speaking; the wags used to call it the thread of his discourse.

senses.d: To pledge; to hazard on the event of a contest; to stake; to bet, to lay; to wager; as, to wage a dollar.
q: My life I never but as a pawn To wage against thy enemies.

senses.d: To expose one's self to, as a risk; to incur, as a danger; to venture; to hazard.
q: To wake and wage a danger profitless.

senses.d: To engage in, as a contest, as if by previous gage or pledge; to carry on, as a war.
q: which of all his sons was fit To reign and wage immortal war with wit.
The two are waging war, and the one triumphs by the destruction of the other.

senses.d: To adventure, or lay out, for hire or reward; to hire out.
To put upon wages; to hire; to employ; to pay wages to.
q: Abundance of treasure which he had in store, wherewith he might wage soldiers.
I would have them waged for their labor.

senses.d: To give security for the performance of.

Wage.etym: [OE. wagen, OF. wagier, gagier, to pledge, promise, F. gager to wager, lay, bet, fr. LL. wadium a pledge; of Teutonic origin; cf. Goth. wadi a pledge, gawadjōn to pledge, akin to E. wed, G. wette a wager. See Wed, and cf. Gage.]

senses.d: To bind one's self; to engage.
That which is staked or ventured; that for which one incurs risk or danger; prize; gage.
That for which one labors; meed; reward; stipulated payment for service performed; hire; pay; compensation; — at present generally used in the plural. See Wages.
q: By Tom Thumb, a fairy page, He sent it, and doth him engage, By promise of a mighty wage, It secretly to carry.
Our praises are our wages.
Existing legislation on the subject of wages.

Wage.syn: Hire; reward; stipend; salary; allowance; pay; compensation; remuneration; fruit.
Wage.etym: [OF. wage, gage, guarantee, engagement. See Wage, v. t. ]

senses.d: A compensation given to a hired person for services; price paid for labor; recompense; hire. See Wage, n., 2.
q: The wages of sin is death.

Wages.etym: [Plural of wage; cf. F. gages, pl., wages, hire. See Wage, n.]

senses.d: The share of the annual product or national dividend which goes as a reward to labor, as distinct from the remuneration received by capital in its various forms. This economic or technical sense of the word wages is broader than the current sense, and includes not only amounts actually paid to laborers, but the remuneration obtained by those who sell the products of their own work, and the wages of superintendence or management, which are earned by skill in directing the work of others.
A wheeled carriage; a vehicle on four wheels, and usually drawn by horses; especially, one used for carrying freight or merchandise.
A freight car on a railway.
A chariot
The Dipper, or Charles's Wain.
To transport in a wagon or wagons; as, goods are wagoned from city to city.
To wagon goods as a business; as, the man wagons between Philadelphia and its suburbs.
To choose; to select.

Wail.etym: [Cf. Icel. val choice, velja to choose, akin to Goth. waljan, G. wählen.]

senses.d: To lament; to bewail; to grieve over; as, to wail one's death.

Wail.etym: [OE. wailen, weilen, probably fr. Icel. væla; cf. Icel. væ, vei, woe, and E. wayment, also OE. wai, wei, woe. Cf. Woe.]

senses.d: To express sorrow audibly; to make mournful outcry; to weep.
q: Therefore I will wail and howl.

senses.d: Loud weeping; violent lamentation; wailing.
To watch; to observe; to take notice.
q: “But ye wait well and be privy, I wot right well, I am but dead,” quoth she.

senses.d: To stay or rest in expectation; to stop or remain stationary till the arrival of some person or event; to rest in patience; to stay; not to depart.
q: All the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come.
They also serve who only stand and wait.
Haste, my dear father; 't is no time to wait.

Wait.etym: [OE. waiten, OF. waitier, gaitier, to watch, attend, F. guetter to watch, to wait for, fr. OHG. wahta a guard, watch, G. wacht, from OHG. wahhēn to watch, be awake. √134. See Wake, v. i.]

senses.d: To stay for; to rest or remain stationary in expectation of; to await; as, to wait orders.
q: Awed with these words, in camps they still abide, And wait with longing looks their promised guide.

senses.d: To attend as a consequence; to follow upon; to accompany; to await.
To attend on; to accompany; especially, to attend with ceremony or respect.
q: He chose a thousand horse, the flower of all His warlike troops, to wait the funeral.
Remorse and heaviness of heart shall wait thee, And everlasting anguish be thy portion.

senses.d: To cause to wait; to defer; to postpone; — said of a meal; as, to wait dinner.
The act of waiting; a delay; a halt.
q: There is a wait of three hours at the border Mexican town of El Paso.

senses.d: Ambush.
One who watches; a watchman.
Hautboys, or oboes, played by town musicians; not used in the singular.
Musicians who sing or play at night or in the early morning, especially at Christmas time; serenaders; musical watchmen.
q: Hark! are the waits abroad?
The sound of the waits, rude as may be their minstrelsy, breaks upon the mild watches of a winter night with the effect of perfect harmony.

Wait.etym: [OF. waite, guaite, gaite, F. guet watch, watching, guard, from OHG. wahta. See Wait, v. i.]

senses.d: The track left by a vessel in the water; by extension, any track; as, the wake of an army.
q: This effect followed immediately in the wake of his earliest exertions.
Several humbler persons . . . formed quite a procession in the dusty wake of his chariot wheels.

Wake.etym: [Originally, an open space of water s�rrounded by ice, and then, the passage cut through ice for a vessel, probably of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. vök a hole, opening in ice, Sw. vak, Dan. vaage, perhaps akin to E. humid.]

senses.d: To be or to continue awake; to watch; not to sleep.
q: The father waketh for the daughter.
Though wisdom wake, suspicion sleeps.
I can not think any time, waking or sleeping, without being sensible of it.

senses.d: To sit up late festive purposes; to hold a night revel.
q: The king doth wake to-night, and takes his rouse, Keeps wassail, and the swaggering upspring reels.

senses.d: To be excited or roused from sleep; to awake; to be awakened; to cease to sleep; — often with up.
q: He infallibly woke up at the sound of the concluding doxology.

senses.d: To be exited or roused up; to be stirred up from a dormant, torpid, or inactive state; to be active.
q: Gentle airs due at their hour To fan the earth now waked.
Then wake, my soul, to high desires.

Wake.etym: [AS. wacan, wacian; akin to OFries. waka, OS. wak�n, D. waken, G. wachen, OHG. wahh�n, Icel. vaka, Sw. vaken, Dan. vaage, Goth. wakan, v. i., uswakjan, v. t., Skr. vājay to rouse, to impel. ����. Cf. Vigil, Wait, v. i., Watch, v. i.]

senses.d: To rouse from sleep; to awake.
q: The angel . . . came again and waked me.

senses.d: To put in motion or action; to arouse; to excite.
q: Lest fierce remembrance wake my sudden rage.
Even Richard's crusade woke little interest in his island realm.

senses.d: To bring to life again, as if from the sleep of death; to reanimate; to revive.
q: To second life Waked in the renovation of the just.

senses.d: To watch, or sit up with, at night, as a dead body.
The act of waking, or being awaked; also, the state of being awake.
q: Making such difference 'twixt wake and sleep.
Singing her flatteries to my morning wake.

senses.d: The state of forbearing sleep, especially for solemn or festive purposes; a vigil.
q: The warlike wakes continued all the night, And funeral games played at new returning light.
The wood nymphs, decked with daises trim, Their merry wakes and pastimes keep.

senses.d: An annual parish festival formerly held in commemoration of the dedication of a church. Originally, prayers were said on the evening preceding, and hymns were sung during the night, in the church; subsequently, these vigils were discontinued, and the day itself, often with succeeding days, was occupied in rural pastimes and exercises, attended by eating and drinking, often to excess.
q: Great solemnities were made in all churches, and great fairs and wakes throughout all England.
And every village smokes at wakes with lusty cheer.

senses.d: The sitting up of persons with a dead body, often attended with a degree of festivity, chiefly among the Irish.
To wake; to cease to sleep; to be awakened.
q: Early, Turnus wakening with the light.

Waken.etym: [OE. waknen, AS. wæcnan; akin to Goth. gawaknan. See Wake, v. i.]

senses.d: To excite or rouse from sleep; to wake; to awake; to awaken.
To excite; to rouse; to move to action; to awaken.
q: Then Homer's and Tyrtæus' martial muse Wakened the world.
Venus now wakes, and wakens love.
They introduce Their sacred song, and waken raptures high.

senses.d: The act of waking, or the state or period of being awake.
A watch; a watching.
q: In the fourth waking of the night.

senses.d: To move along on foot; to advance by steps; to go on at a moderate pace; specifically, of two-legged creatures, to proceed at a slower or faster rate, but without running, or lifting one foot entirely before the other touches the ground.
q: At the end of twelve months, he walked in the palace of the kingdom of Babylon.
When Peter was come down out of the ship, he walked on the water, to go to Jesus.

senses.d: To move or go on the feet for exercise or amusement; to take one's exercise; to ramble.

To be stirring; to be abroad; to go restlessly about; — said of things or persons expected to remain quiet, as a sleeping person, or the spirit of a dead person; to go about as a somnambulist or a specter.
q: I have heard, but not believed, the spirits of the dead May walk again.
When was it she last walked?

senses.d: To be in motion; to act; to move; to wag.
q: Do you think I'd walk in any plot?
I heard a pen walking in the chimney behind the cloth.

senses.d: To behave; to pursue a course of life; to conduct one's self.
q: We walk perversely with God, and he will walk crookedly toward us.

senses.d: To move off; to depart.
q: He will make their cows and garrans to walk.

Walk.etym: [OE. walken, probably from AS. wealcan to roll, turn, revolve, akin to D. walken to felt hats, to work a hat, G. walken to full, OHG. walchan to beat, to full, Icel. vālka to roll, to stamp, Sw. valka to full, to roll, Dan. valke to full; cf. Skr. valg to spring; but cf. also AS. weallian to roam, r

senses.d: To pass through, over, or upon; to traverse; to perambulate; as, to walk the streets.
q: As we walk our earthly round.

senses.d: To cause to walk; to lead, drive, or ride with a slow pace; as to walk one's horses.
To subject, as cloth or yarn, to the fulling process; to full.
The act of walking, or moving on the feet with a slow pace; advance without running or leaping.
The act of walking for recreation or exercise; as, a morning walk; an evening walk.
Manner of walking; gait; step; as, we often know a person at a distance by his walk.

That in or through which one walks; place or distance walked over; a place for walking; a path or avenue prepared for foot passengers, or for taking air and exercise; way; road; hence, a place or region in which animals may graze; place of wandering; range; as, a sheep walk.
q: A woody mountain . . . with goodliest trees Planted, with walks and bowers.
He had walk for a hundred sheep.
Amid the sound of steps that beat The murmuring walks like rain.

senses.d: A frequented track; habitual place of action; sphere; as, the walk of the historian.
q: The mountains are his walks.
He opened a boundless walk for his imagination.

senses.d: Conduct; course of action; behavior.
The route or district regularly served by a vender; as, a milkman's walk.
In coffee, coconut, and other plantations, the space between them.
A place for keeping and training puppies.
To put or keep (a puppy) in a walk; to train (puppies) in a walk.
To move in a manner likened to walking.
q: She walked a spinning wheel into the house, making it use first one and then the other of its own spindling legs to achieve progression rather than lifting it by main force.

senses.d: A kind of knot often used at the end of a rope; a wall knot; a wale.

A work or structure of stone, brick, or other materials, raised to some height, and intended for defense or security, solid and permanent inclosing fence, as around a field, a park, a town, etc., also, one of the upright inclosing parts of a building or a room.
q: The plaster of the wall of the King's palace.

senses.d: A defense; a rampart; a means of protection; in the plural, fortifications, in general; works for defense.
q: The waters were a wall unto them on their right hand, and on their left.
In such a night, Troilus, methinks, mounted the Troyan walls.
To rush undaunted to defend the walls.

senses.d: An inclosing part of a receptacle or vessel; as, the walls of a steam-engine cylinder.
The side of a level or drift.

Wall.etym: [AS. weall, from L. vallum a wall, vallus a stake, pale, palisade; akin to Gr. � a nail. Cf. Interval.]

senses.d: To inclose with a wall, or as with a wall.
q: The king of Thebes, Amphion, That with his singing walled that city.

senses.d: To defend by walls, or as if by walls; to fortify.
q: The terror of his name that walls us in.

senses.d: To close or fill with a wall, as a doorway.
To roll one's self about, as in mire; to tumble and roll about; to move lazily or heavily in any medium; to flounder; as, swine wallow in the mire.
q: I may wallow in the lily beds.

senses.d: To live in filth or gross vice; to disport one's self in a beastly and unworthy manner.
q: God sees a man wallowing in his native impurity.

senses.d: To wither; to fade.

Wallow.etym: [OE. walwen, AS. wealwian; akin to Goth. walwjan (in comp.) to roll, L. volvere; cf. Skr. val to turn. √147. Cf. Voluble Well, n.]

senses.d: To roll; esp., to roll in anything defiling or unclean.
A kind of rolling walk.
q: One taught the toss, and one the new French wallow.

senses.d: Act of wallowing.
A place to which an animal comes to wallow; also, the depression in the ground made by its wallowing; as, a buffalo wallow.
A small stick; a rod; a verge.
q: With good smart blows of a wand on his back.

senses.d: A staff of authority.
q: Though he had both spurs and wand, they seemed rather marks of sovereignty than instruments of punishment.

senses.d: A rod used by conjurers, diviners, magicians, etc.
q: Picus bore a buckler in his hand; His other waved a long divining wand.

Wand.etym: [Of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. vöndr, akin to Dan. vaand, Goth. wandus; perhaps originally, a pliant twig, and akin to E. wind to turn.]

senses.d: To ramble here and there without any certain course or with no definite object in view; to range about; to stroll; to rove; as, to wander over the fields.
q: They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins.
He wandereth abroad for bread.

senses.d: To go away; to depart; to stray off; to deviate; to go astray; as, a writer wanders from his subject.
q: When God caused me to wander from my father's house.
O, let me not wander from thy commandments.

senses.d: To be delirious; not to be under the guidance of reason; to rave; as, the mind wanders.

Wander.syn: To roam; rove; range; stroll; gad; stray; straggly; err; swerve; deviate; depart.
Wander.etym: [OE. wandren, wandrien, AS. wandrian; akin to G. wandern to wander; fr. AS. windan to turn. See Wind to turn.]

senses.d: To travel over without a certain course; to traverse; to stroll through.
One who wanders; a rambler; one who roves; hence, one who deviates from duty.

The state of not having; the condition of being without anything; absence or scarcity of what is needed or desired; deficiency; lack; as, a want of power or knowledge for any purpose; want of food and clothing.
q: And me, his parent, would full soon devour For want of other prey.
From having wishes in consequence of our wants, we often feel wants in consequence of our wishes.
Pride is as loud a beggar as want, and more saucy.

senses.d: Specifically, absence or lack of necessaries; destitution; poverty; penury; indigence; need.
q: Nothing is so hard for those who abound in riches, as to conceive how others can be in want.

senses.d: That which is needed or desired; a thing of which the loss is felt; what is not possessed, and is necessary for use or pleasure.
q: Habitual superfluities become actual wants.

senses.d: A depression in coal strata, hollowed out before the subsequent deposition took place.

Want.syn: Indigence; deficiency; defect; destitution; lack; failure; dearth; scarceness.
Want.etym: [Originally an adj., from Icel. vant, neuter of vanr lacking, deficient. √139. See Wane, v. i.]

senses.d: To be without; to be destitute of, or deficient in; not to have; to lack; as, to want knowledge; to want judgment; to want learning; to want food and clothing.
q: They that want honesty, want anything.
Nor think, though men were none, That heaven would want spectators, God want praise.
The unhappy never want enemies.

senses.d: To have occasion for, as useful, proper, or requisite; to require; to need; as, in winter we want a fire; in summer we want cooling breezes.
To feel need of; to wish or long for; to desire; to crave.
q: I want to speak to you about something.

senses.d: To be absent; to be deficient or lacking; to fail; not to be sufficient; to fall or come short; to lack; — often used impersonally with of; as, it wants ten minutes of four.
q: The disposition, the manners, and the thoughts are all before it; where any of those are wanting or imperfect, so much wants or is imperfect in the imitation of human life.

senses.d: To be in a state of destitution; to be needy; to lack.
q: You have a gift, sir (thank your education), Will never let you want.
For as in bodies, thus in souls, we find What wants in blood and spirits, swelled with wind.

Want.etym: [Icel. vanta to be wanting. See Want to lack.]

senses.d: Absent; lacking; missing; also, deficient; destitute; needy; as, one of the twelve is wanting; I shall not be wanting in exertion.
Untrained; undisciplined; unrestrained; hence, loose; free; luxuriant; roving; sportive.
q: A wanton and a merry .
her unadorned golden tresses wore Disheveled, but in wanton ringlets waved.
How does your tongue grow wanton in her praise!

senses.d: Wandering from moral rectitude; perverse; dissolute.
Specifically: Deviating from the rules of chastity; lewd; lustful; lascivious; libidinous; lecherous.
q: Not with wanton looking of folly.
froward by nature, enemy to peace, Lascivious, wanton.

senses.d: Reckless; heedless; as, wanton mischief.

Wanton.etym: [OE. wantoun, contr. from wantowen; pref. wan- wanting (see Wane, v. i.), hence expressing negation + towen, p. p., AS. togen, p. p. of teón to draw, to educate, bring up; hence, properly, ill bred. See Tug, v. t.]

senses.d: A roving, frolicsome thing; a trifler; — used rarely as a term of endearment.
q: I am afeard you make a wanton of me.
Peace, my wantons; he will do More than you can aim unto.

senses.d: One brought up without restraint; a pampered pet.
q: Anything, sir, That's dry and wholesome; I am no bred wanton.

senses.d: A lewd person; a lascivious man or woman.
To rove and ramble without restraint, rule, or limit; to revel; to play loosely; to frolic.
q: Nature here wantoned as in her prime.
How merrily we would sally into the fields, and strip under the first warmth of the sun, and wanton like young dace in the streams!

senses.d: To sport in lewdness; to play the wanton; to play lasciviously.
To cause to become wanton; also, to waste in wantonness.
The quality or state of being wanton; negligence of restraint; sportiveness; recklessness; lasciviousness.
q: The tumults threatened to abuse all acts of grace, and turn them into wantonness.
Young gentlemen would be as sad as night Only for wantonness.

senses.d: Ware; aware.

A contest between nations or states, carried on by force, whether for defence, for revenging insults and redressing wrongs, for the extension of commerce, for the acquisition of territory, for obtaining and establishing the superiority and dominion of one over the other, or for any other purpose; armed conflict of sovereign powers; declared and open hostilities.
q: Men will ever distinguish war from mere bloodshed.

senses.d: A condition of belligerency to be maintained by physical force. In this sense, levying war against the sovereign authority is treason.
Instruments of war.
q: His complement of stores, and total war.

senses.d: Forces; army.
q: On their embattled ranks the waves return, And overwhelm their war.

senses.d: The profession of arms; the art of war.
q: Thou art but a youth, and he is a man of war from his youth.

senses.d: a state of opposition or contest; an act of opposition; an inimical contest, act, or action; enmity; hostility.
q: The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart.

War.etym: [OE. & AS. werre; akin to OHG. werra scandal, quarrel, sedition, werran to confound, mix, D. warren, G. wirren, verwirren, to embroil, confound, disturb, and perhaps to E. worse; cf. OF. werre war, F. querre, of Teutonic origin. Cf. Guerrilla, Warrior.]

senses.d: To make war; to invade or attack a state or nation with force of arms; to carry on hostilities; to be in a state by violence.
q: Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up toward Jerusalem to war against it.
Why should I war without the walls of Troy?
Our countrymen were warring on that day!

senses.d: To contend; to strive violently; to fight.
To make war upon; to fight.
q: To war the Scot, and borders to defend.

senses.d: To carry on, as a contest; to wage.
q: That thou . . . mightest war a good warfare.

senses.d: The act of guarding; watch; guard; guardianship; specifically, a guarding during the day. See the Note under Watch, n., 1.
q: Still, when she slept, he kept both watch and ward.

senses.d: One who, or that which, guards; garrison; defender; protector; means of guarding; defense; protection.
q: For the best ward of mine honor.
The assieged castle's ward Their steadfast stands did mightily maintain.
For want of other ward, He lifted up his hand, his front to guard.

senses.d: The state of being under guard or guardianship; confinement under guard; the condition of a child under a guardian; custody.
q: And he put them in ward in the house of the captain of the guard.
I must attend his majesty's command, to whom I am now in ward.
It is also inconvenient, in Ireland, that the wards and marriages of gentlemen's children should be in the disposal of any of those lords.

senses.d: A guarding or defensive motion or position, as in fencing; guard.
One who, or that which, is guarded.
A minor or person under the care of a guardian; as, a ward in chancery.
A division of a county.
A division, district, or quarter of a town or city.
q: Throughout the trembling city placed a guard, Dealing an equal share to every ward.

senses.d: A division of a forest.
A division of a hospital; as, a fever ward.
A projecting ridge of metal in the interior of a lock, to prevent the use of any key which has not a corresponding notch for passing it.
q: The lock is made . . . more secure by attaching wards to the front, as well as to the back, plate of the lock, in which case the key must be furnished with corresponding notches.

Ward.etym: [AS. weard, fem., guard, weard, masc., keeper, guard; akin to OS. ward a watcher, warden, G. wart, OHG. wart, Icel. vörðr a warden, a watch, Goth. -wards in daúrawards a doorkeeper, and E. wary; cf. OF. warde guard, from the German. See Ware, a., Wary, and cf. Guard, Wraith.]

senses.d: To keep in safety; to watch; to guard; formerly, in a specific sense, to guard during the day time.
q: Whose gates he found fast shut, no living wight To ward the same.

senses.d: To defend; to protect.
q: Tell him it was a hand that warded him From thousand dangers.

senses.d: To defend by walls, fortifications, etc.
To fend off; to repel; to turn aside, as anything mischievous that approaches; — usually followed by off.
q: Now wards a felling blow, now strikes again.
The pointed javelin warded off his rage.
It instructs the scholar in the various methods of warding off the force of objections.

Ward.etym: [OE. wardien, AS. weardian to keep, protect; akin to OS. ward�n to watch, take care, OFries. wardia, OHG. wart�n, G. warten to wait, wait on, attend to, Icel. var�a to guarantee defend, Sw. vårda to guard, to watch; cf. OF. warder, of German origin. See Ward, n., and cf. Award, Guard, Reward.]

senses.d: To be vigilant; to keep guard.
To act on the defensive with a weapon.
q: She redoubling her blows drove the stranger to no other shift than to ward and go back.

senses.d: A room or apartment where clothes are kept, or wearing apparel is stored; a portable closet for hanging up clothes.
Wearing apparel, in general; articles of dress or personal decoration.
q: Flowers that their gay wardrobe wear.
With a pair of saddlebags containing his wardrobe.

senses.d: A privy.

Wardrobe.etym: [OE. warderobe, OF. warderobe, F. garderobe; of German origin. See Ward, v. t., and Robe.]

senses.d: Wore.
To wear, or veer. See Wear.
Seaweed.
Articles of merchandise; the sum of articles of a particular kind or class; style or class of manufactures; especially, in the plural, goods; commodities; merchandise.
q: It the people of the land bring ware or any victuals on the Sabbath day to sell, that we would not buy it of them on the Sabbath, or on the holy day.

Ware.etym: [OE. ware, AS. waru; akin to D. waar, G. waare, Icel. & Sw. vara, Dan. vare; and probably to E. worth, a. See Worth, a.]

senses.d: A ware; taking notice; hence, wary; cautious; on one's guard. See Beware.
q: She was ware and knew it bet than he.
Of whom be thou ware also.
He is ware enough; he is wily and circumspect for stirring up any sedition.
The only good that grows of passed fear Is to be wise, and ware of like again.

senses.d: The state of being ware or aware; heed.
To make ware; to warn; to take heed of; to beware of; to guard against.
q: God . . . ware you for the sin of avarice.
Then ware a rising tempest on the main.

senses.d: Military service; military life; contest carried on by enemies; hostilities; war.
q: The Philistines gathered their armies together for warfare, to fight with Israel.
This day from battle rest; Faithful hath been your warfare.

senses.d: Contest; struggle.
q: The weapons of our warfare are not carnal.

Warfare.etym: [War + OE. fare a journey, a passage, course, AS. faru. See Fare, n.]

senses.d: To lead a military life; to carry on continual wars.
Having heat in a moderate degree; not cold as, warm milk.
q: Warm and still is the summer night.

senses.d: Having a sensation of heat, esp. of gentle heat; glowing.
Subject to heat; having prevalence of heat, or little or no cold weather; as, the warm climate of Egypt.
Fig.: Not cool, indifferent, lukewarm, or the like, in spirit or temper; zealous; ardent; fervent; excited; sprightly; irritable; excitable.
q: Mirth, and youth, and warm desire!
Each warm wish springs mutual from the heart.
They say he's warm man and does not care to be mad� mouths at.
I had been none of the warmest of partisans.

senses.d: Violent; vehement; furious; excited; passionate; as, a warm contest; a warm debate.
q: Welcome, daylight; we shall have warm work on't.

senses.d: Being well off as to property, or in good circumstances; forehanded; rich.
q: Warm householders, every one of them.
You shall have a draft upon him, payable at sight: and let me tell you he as warm a man as any within five miles round him.

senses.d: In children's games, being near the object sought for; hence, being close to the discovery of some person, thing, or fact concealed.
q: Here, indeed, young Mr. Dowse was getting “warm,” �� children say at blindman's buff.

senses.d: Having yellow or red for a basis, or in their composition; — said of colors, and opposed to cold which is of blue and its compounds.

Warm.syn: Ardent; zealous; fervent; glowing; enthusiastic; cordial; keen; violent; furious; hot.
Warm.etym: [AS. wearm; akin to OS., OFries., D., & G. warm, Icel. varmr, Sw. & Dan. varm, Goth. warmjan to warm; probably akin to Lith. virti to cook, boil; or perhaps to Skr. gharma heat, OL. formus warm. ���, ���.]

senses.d: To communicate a moderate degree of heat to; to render warm; to supply or furnish heat to; as, a stove warms an apartment.
q: Then shall it be for a man to burn; for he will take thereof and warm himself.
Enough to warm, but not enough to burn.

senses.d: To make engaged or earnest; to interest; to engage; to excite ardor or zeal; to enliven.
q: I formerly warmed my head with reading controversial writings.
Bright hopes, that erst bosom warmed.

senses.d: To become warm, or moderately heated; as, the earth soon warms in a clear day summer.
q: There shall not be a coal to warm at.

senses.d: To become ardent or animated; as, the speake� warms as he proceeds.
The act of warming, or the state of being warmed; a warming; a heating.
To refuse.

Warn.etym: [OE. wernen, AS. weornan, wyrnan. Cf. Warn to admonish.]

senses.d: To make ware or aware; to give previous information to; to give notice to; to notify; to admonish; hence, to notify or summon by authority; as, to warn a town meeting; to warn a tenant to quit a house.
q: Cornelius the centurion . . . was warned from God by an holy angel to send for thee.
Who is it that hath warned us to the walls?

senses.d: To give notice to, of approaching or probable danger or evil; to caution against anything that may prove injurious.
To ward off.

Warn.etym: [OE. warnen, warnien, AS. warnian, wearnian, to take heed, to warn; akin to AS. wearn denial, refusal, OS. warning, wernian, to refuse, OHG. warnen, G. warnen to warn, OFries. warna, werna, Icel. varna to refuse; and probably to E. wary. ����.]

senses.d: Giving previous notice; cautioning; admonishing; as, a warning voice.
q: That warning timepiece never ceased.

senses.d: Previous notice.
q: A great journey to take upon so short a warning.

senses.d: Caution against danger, or against faults or evil practices which incur danger; admonition; monition.
q: Could warning make the world more just or wise.

senses.d: To throw; hence, to send forth, or throw out, as words; to utter.
To turn or twist out of shape; esp., to twist or bend out of a flat plane by contraction or otherwise.
q: The planks looked warped.
Walter warped his mouth at this To something so mock solemn, that I laughed.

senses.d: To turn aside from the true direction; to cause to bend or incline; to pervert.
q: This first avowed, nor folly warped my mind.
I have no private considerations to warp me in this controversy.
We are divested of all those passions which cloud the intellects, and warp the understandings, of men.

senses.d: To weave; to fabricate.
q: While doth he mischief warp.

senses.d: To tow or move, as a vessel, with a line, or warp, attached to a buoy, anchor, or other fixed object.
To cast prematurely, as young; — said of cattle, sheep, etc.
To let the tide or other water in upon (lowlying land), for the purpose of fertilization, by a deposit of warp, or slimy substance.
To run off the reel into hauls to be tarred, as yarns.
To arrange (yarns) on a warp beam.

Warp.etym: [OE. warpen; fr. Icel. varpa to throw, cast, varp a casting, fr. verpa to throw; akin to Dan. varpe to warp a ship, Sw. varpa, AS. weorpan to cast, OS. werpan, OFries. werpa, D. & LG. werpen, G. werfen, Goth. waírpan; cf. Skr. vrj to twist. ����. Cf. Wrap.]

senses.d: To turn, twist, or be twisted out of shape; esp., to be twisted or bent out of a flat plane; as, a board warps in seasoning or shrinking.
q: One of you will prove a shrunk panel, and, like green timber, warp, warp.
They clamp one piece of wood to the end of another, to keep it from casting, or warping.

senses.d: to turn or incline from a straight, true, or proper course; to deviate; to swerve.
q: There is our commission, From which we would not have you warp.

senses.d: To fly with a bending or waving motion; to turn and wave, like a flock of birds or insects.
q: A pitchy cloud Of locusts, warping on the eastern wind.

senses.d: To cast the young prematurely; to slink; — said of cattle, sheep, etc.
To wind yarn off bobbins for forming the warp of a web; to wind a warp on a warp beam.
The threads which are extended lengthwise in the loom, and crossed by the woof.
A rope used in hauling or moving a vessel, usually with one end attached to an anchor, a post, or other fixed object; a towing line; a warping hawser.
A slimy substance deposited on land by tides, etc., by which a rich alluvial soil is formed.
A premature casting of young; — said of cattle, sheep, etc.
Four; esp., four herrings; a cast. See Cast, n., 17.
The state of being warped or twisted; as, the warp of a board.

Warp.etym: [AS. wearp; akin to Icel. varp a casting, throwing, Sw. varp the draught of a net, Dan. varp a towline, OHG. warf warp, G. werft. See Warp, v.]

senses.d: To twist the end surfaces of (an aërocurve in an aëroplane) in order to restore or maintain equilibrium.
Worse.
q: They say the world is much warre than it wont.

Warre.etym: [OE. werre; of Scand. origin. See Worse.]

senses.d: A man engaged or experienced in war, or in the military life; a soldier; a champion.
q: Warriors old with ordered spear and shield.

Warrior.etym: [OE. werreour, OF. werreour, guerreor, from guerre, werre, war. See War, and Warray.]

senses.d: The first and third persons singular of the verb be, in the indicative mood, preterit (imperfect) tense; as, I was; he was.

Was.etym: [AS. wæs, 2d pers. wǣre, 3d pers. wæs, pl. wǣron, with the inf. wesan to be; akin to D. wezen, imp. was, OHG. wesan, imp. was, G. wesen, n., a being, essence, war was, Icel. vera to be, imp. var, Goth. wisan to be, to dwell, to remain, imp. was, Skr. vas to remain, to dwell. √148. Cf. Vernacular, Wa

senses.d: To cleanse by ablution, or dipping or rubbing in water; to apply water or other liquid to for the purpose of cleansing; to scrub with water, etc., or as with water; as, to wash the hands or body; to wash garments; to wash sheep or wool; to wash the pavement or floor; to wash the bark of trees.
q: When Pilate saw that he could prevail nothing, . . . he took water and washed his hands before the multitude, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this just person.

senses.d: To cover with water or any liquid; to wet; to fall on and moisten; hence, to overflow or dash against; as, waves wash the shore.
q: Fresh-blown roses washed with dew.
washed with a cold, gray mist.

senses.d: To waste or abrade by the force of water in motion; as, heavy rains wash a road or an embankment.
To remove by washing to take away by, or as by, the action of water; to drag or draw off as by the tide; — often with away, off, out, etc.; as, to wash dirt from the hands.
q: Arise, and be baptized, and wash away thy sins.
The tide will wash you off.

senses.d: To cover with a thin or watery coat of color; to tint lightly and thinly.
To overlay with a thin coat of metal; as, steel washed with silver.

Wash.etym: [OE. waschen, AS. wascan; akin to D. wasschen, G. waschen, OHG. wascan, Icel. & Sw. vaska, Dan. vaske, and perhaps to E. water. √150.]

senses.d: To perform the act of ablution.
q: Wash in Jordan seven times.

senses.d: To clean anything by rubbing or dipping it in water; to perform the business of cleansing clothes, ore, etc., in water.
To bear without injury the operation of being washed; as, some calicoes do not wash.
To be wasted or worn away by the action of water, as by a running or overflowing stream, or by the dashing of the sea; — said of road, a beach, etc.
The act of washing; an ablution; a cleansing, wetting, or dashing with water; hence, a quantity, as of clothes, washed at once.

A piece of ground washed by the action of a sea or river, or sometimes covered and sometimes left dry; the shallowest part of a river, or arm of the sea; also, a bog; a marsh; a fen; as, the washes in Lincolnshire.
q: These Lincoln washes have devoured them.

senses.d: Substances collected and deposited by the action of water; as, the wash of a sewer, of a river, etc.
q: The wash of pastures, fields, commons, and roads, where rain water hath a long time settled.

senses.d: Waste liquid, the refuse of food, the collection from washed dishes, etc., from a kitchen, often used as food for pigs.
The fermented wort before the spirit is extracted.
That with which anything is washed, or wetted, smeared, tinted, etc., upon the surface.
A liquid cosmetic for the complexion.
A liquid dentifrice.
A liquid preparation for the hair; as, a hair wash.
A medical preparation in a liquid form for external application; a lotion.
A thin coat of color, esp. water color.
A thin coat of metal laid on anything for beauty or preservation.
Washy; weak.
q: Their bodies of so weak and wash a temper.

senses.d: Capable of being washed without injury; washable; as, wash goods.
To cause dephosphorisation of (molten pig iron) by adding substances containing iron oxide, and sometimes manganese oxide.
To pass (a gas or gaseous mixture) through or over a liquid for the purpose of purifying it, esp. by removing soluble constituents.
To use washes, as for the face or hair.
To move with a lapping or swashing sound, or the like; to lap; splash; as, to hear the water washing.
Gravel and other rock débris transported and deposited by running water; coarse alluvium.
The dry bed of an intermittent stream, sometimes at the bottom of a cañon; as, the Amargosa wash, Diamond wash; — called also dry wash.
The upper surface of a member or material when given a slope to shed water. Hence, a structure or receptacle shaped so as to receive and carry off water, as a carriage wash in a stable.
Appearing as if overlaid with a thin layer of different color; — said of the colors of certain birds and insects.
The act of one who washes; the act of cleansing with water; ablution.
The clothes washed, esp. at one time; a wash.
Gold dust procured by washing; also, a place where this is done; a washery.
A thin covering or coat; as, a washing of silver.
The operation of simultaneously buying and selling the same stock for the purpose of manipulating the market. The transaction is fictitious, and is prohibited by stock-exchange rules.
The covering of a piece with an infusible powder, which prevents it from sticking to its supports, while receiving the glaze.
A pot or vessel in which anything is washed.
A pot containing melted tin into which the plates are dipped to be coated.
The second person singular of the verb be, in the indicative mood, imperfect tense; — now used only in solemn or poetical style. See Was.
Desolate; devastated; stripped; bare; hence, dreary; dismal; gloomy; cheerless.
q: The dismal situation waste and wild.
His heart became appalled as he gazed forward into the waste darkness of futurity.

senses.d: Lying unused; unproductive; worthless; valueless; refuse; rejected; as, waste land; waste paper.
q: But his waste words returned to him in vain.
Not a waste or needless sound, Till we come to holier ground.
Ill day which made this beauty waste.

senses.d: Lost for want of occupiers or use; superfluous.
q: And strangled with her waste fertility.

Waste.etym: [OE. wast, OF. wast, from L. vastus, influenced by the kindred German word; cf. OHG. wuosti, G. wüst, OS. w�sti, D. woest, AS. wēste. Cf. Vast.]

senses.d: To bring to ruin; to devastate; to desolate; to destroy.
q: Thou barren ground, whom winter's wrath hath wasted, Art made a mirror to behold my plight.
The Tiber Insults our walls, and wastes our fruitful grounds.

senses.d: To wear away by degrees; to impair gradually; to diminish by constant loss; to use up; to consume; to spend; to wear out.
q: Until your carcasses be wasted in the wilderness.
O, were I able To waste it all myself, and leave ye none!
Here condemned To waste eternal days in woe and pain.
Wasted by such a course of life, the infirmities of age daily grew on him.

senses.d: To spend unnecessarily or carelessly; to employ prodigally; to expend without valuable result; to apply to useless purposes; to lavish vainly; to squander; to cause to be lost; to destroy by scattering or injury.
q: The younger son gathered all together, and . . . wasted his substance with riotous living.
Full many a flower is born to blush unseen, And waste its sweetness on the desert air.

senses.d: To damage, impair, or injure, as an estate, voluntarily, or by suffering the buildings, fences, etc., to go to decay.

Waste.etym: [OE. wasten, OF. waster, guaster, gaster, F. gâter to spoil, L. vastare to devastate, to lay waste, fr. vastus waste, desert, uncultivated, ravaged, vast, but influenced by a kindred German word; cf. OHG. wuosten, G. wüsten, AS. wēstan. See Waste, a.]

senses.d: To be diminished; to lose bulk, substance, strength, value, or the like, gradually; to be consumed; to dwindle; to grow less.
q: The time wasteth night and day.
The barrel of meal shall not waste.
But man dieth, and wasteth away.

senses.d: To procure or sustain a reduction of flesh; — said of a jockey in preparation for a race, etc.

The act of wasting, or the state of being wasted; a squandering; needless destruction; useless consumption or expenditure; devastation; loss without equivalent gain; gradual loss or decrease, by use, wear, or decay; as, a waste of property, time, labor, words, etc.
q: For all this waste of wealth loss of blood.
He will never . . . in the way of waste, attempt us again.
Little wastes in great establishments, constantly occurring, may defeat the energies of a mighty capital.

senses.d: That which is wasted or desolate; a devastated, uncultivated, or wild country; a deserted region; an unoccupied or unemployed space; a dreary void; a desert; a wilderness.
q: All the leafy nation sinks at last, And Vulcan rides in triumph o'er the waste.
The gloomy waste of waters which bears his name is his tomb and his monument.

senses.d: That which is of no value; worthless remnants; refuse. Specifically: Remnants of cops, or other refuse resulting from the working of cotton, wool, hemp, and the like, used for wiping machinery, absorbing oil in the axle boxes of railway cars, etc.
Spoil, destruction, or injury, done to houses, woods, fences, lands, etc., by a tenant for life or for years, to the prejudice of the heir, or of him in reversion or remainder.
Old or abandoned workings, whether left as vacant space or filled with refuse.

Waste.syn: Prodigality; diminution; loss; dissipation; destruction; devastation; havoc; desolation; ravage.
Waste.etym: [OE. waste; cf. the kindred AS. w�sten, OHG. w�stī, wuostī, G. wüste. See Waste, a. & v.]

senses.d: Material derived by mechanical and chemical erosion from the land, carried by streams to the sea.
The quality or state of being waste; a desolate state or condition; desolation.
q: A day of trouble and distress, a day of wasteness.

senses.d: That which is waste; a desert; a waste.
q: Through woods and wasteness wide him daily sought.

senses.d: One who, or that which, wastes; one who squanders; one who consumes or expends extravagantly; a spendthrift; a prodigal.
q: He also that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster.
Sconces are great wasters of candles.

senses.d: An imperfection in the wick of a candle, causing it to waste; — called also a thief.
A kind of cudgel; also, a blunt-edged sword used as a foil.
q: Half a dozen of veneys at wasters with a good fellow for a broken head.
Being unable to wield the intellectual arms of reason, they are fain to betake them unto wasters.

Waster.etym: [OE. wastour, OF. wasteor, gasteor. See Waste, v. t.]

senses.d: Causing waste; also, undergoing waste; diminishing; as, a wasting disease; a wasting fortune.

The act of watching; forbearance of sleep; vigil; wakeful, vigilant, or constantly observant attention; close observation; guard; preservative or preventive vigilance; formerly, a watching or guarding by night.
q: Shepherds keeping watch by night.
All the long night their mournful watch they keep.
Still, when she slept, he kept both watch and ward.

Ward, guard, or custodia, is chiefly applied to the daytime, in order to apprehend rioters, and robbers on the highway . . . Watch, is properly applicable to the night only, . . . and it begins when ward ends, and ends when that begins.

senses.d: One who watches, or those who watch; a watchman, or a body of watchmen; a sentry; a guard.
q: Pilate said unto them, Ye have a watch; go your way, make it as sure as ye can.

senses.d: The post or office of a watchman; also, the place where a watchman is posted, or where a guard is kept.
q: He upbraids Iago, that he made him Brave me upon the watch.

senses.d: The period of the night during which a person does duty as a sentinel, or guard; the time from the placing of a sentinel till his relief; hence, a division of the night.
q: I did stand my watch upon the hill.
Might we but hear . . . Or whistle from the lodge, or village cock Count the night watches to his feathery dames.

senses.d: A small timepiece, or chronometer, to be carried about the person, the machinery of which is moved by a spring.
An allotted portion of time, usually four hour for standing watch, or being on deck ready for duty. Cf. Dogwatch.

Watch.etym: [OE. wacche, AS. wæcce, fr. wacian to wake; akin to D. wacht, waak, G. wacht, wache. √134. See Wake, v. i. ]

senses.d: To be awake; to be or continue without sleep; to wake; to keep vigil.
q: I have two nights watched with you.
Couldest thou not watch one hour ?

senses.d: To be attentive or vigilant; to give heed; to be on the lookout; to keep guard; to act as sentinel.
q: Take ye heed, watch and pray.
The Son gave signal high To the bright minister that watched.

senses.d: To be expectant; to look with expectation; to wait; to seek opportunity.
q: My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning.

senses.d: To remain awake with any one as nurse or attendant; to attend on the sick during the night; as, to watch with a man in a fever.
To serve the purpose of a watchman by floating properly in its place; — said of a buoy.

Watch.etym: [Cf. AS. wœccan, wacian. √134. See Watch, n., Wake, v. i. ]

senses.d: To give heed to; to observe the actions or motions of, for any purpose; to keep in view; not to lose from sight and observation; as, to watch the progress of a bill in the legislature.
q: Saul also sent messengers unto David's house to watch him, and to slay him.
I must cool a little, and watch my opportunity.
In lazy mood I watched the little circles die.

senses.d: To tend; to guard; to have in keeping.
q: And flaming ministers, to watch and tend Their earthy charge.
Paris watched the flocks in the groves of Ida.

senses.d: One who watches; one who sits up or continues; a diligent observer; specifically, one who attends upon the sick during the night.
The leaves of Saracenia flava. See Trumpets.

Full of watch; vigilant; attentive; careful to observe closely; observant; cautious; — with of before the thing to be regulated or guarded; as, to be watchful of one's behavior; and with against before the thing to be avoided; as, to be watchful against the growth of vicious habits.
q: 'Twixt prayer and watchful love his heart dividing.

Watchful.syn: Vigilant; attentive; cautious; observant; circumspect; wakeful; heedful.

senses.d: One set to watch; a person who keeps guard; a guard; a sentinel.
Specifically, one who guards a building, or the streets of a city, by night.
A tower in which a sentinel is placed to watch for enemies, the approach of danger, or the like.
The fluid which descends from the clouds in rain, and which forms rivers, lakes, seas, etc.
A body of water, standing or flowing; a lake, river, or other collection of water.
q: Remembering he had passed over a small water a poor scholar when first coming to the university, he kneeled.

senses.d: Any liquid secretion, humor, or the like, resembling water; esp., the urine.
A solution in water of a gaseous or readily volatile substance; as, ammonia water.

The limpidity and luster of a precious stone, especially a diamond; as, a diamond of the first water, that is, perfectly pure and transparent. Hence, of the first water, that is, of the first excellence.
A wavy, lustrous pattern or decoration such as is imparted to linen, silk, metals, etc. See Water, v. t., 3, Damask, v. t., and Damaskeen.
An addition to the shares representing the capital of a stock company so that the aggregate par value of the shares is increased while their value for investment is diminished, or “diluted.”

Water.etym: [AS. wæter; akin to OS. watar, OFries. wetir, weter, LG. & D. water, G. wasser, OHG. wazzar, Icel. vatn, Sw. vatten, Dan. vand, Goth. watō, O. Slav. & Russ. voda, Gr. ὔδωρ, Skr. udan water, ud to wet, and perhaps to L. unda wave. √137. Cf. Dropsy, Hydra, Otter, Wet, Whisky.]

senses.d: To wet or supply with water; to moisten; to overflow with water; to irrigate; as, to water land; to water flowers.
q: With tears watering the ground.
Men whose lives gilded on like rivers that water the woodlands.

senses.d: To supply with water for drink; to cause or allow to drink; as, to water cattle and horses.
To wet and calender, as cloth, so as to impart to it a lustrous appearance in wavy lines; to diversify with wavelike lines; as, to water silk. Cf. Water, n., 6.
To add water to (anything), thereby extending the quantity or bulk while reducing the strength or quality; to extend; to dilute; to weaken.
To shed, secrete, or fill with, water or liquid matter; as, his eyes began to water.
q: If thine eyes can water for his death.

senses.d: To get or take in water; as, the ship put into port to water.
A stream of water; a river or brook.
A natural channel for water; also, a canal for the conveyance of water, especially in draining lands.
A running stream of water having a bed and banks; the easement one may have in the flowing of such a stream in its accustomed course. A water course may be sometimes dry.
One of the holes in floor or other plates to permit water to flow through.
A flood of water; an inundation.
A vessel for holding or conveying water, or for sprinkling water on cloth, plants, etc.
A remarkable meteorological phenomenon, of the nature of a tornado or whirlwind, usually observed over the sea, but sometimes over the land.
To play loosely; to move like a wave, one way and the other; to float; to flutter; to undulate.
q: His purple robes waved careless to the winds.
Where the flags of three nations has successively waved.

senses.d: To be moved to and fro as a signal.
To fluctuate; to waver; to be in an unsettled state; to vacillate.
q: He waved indifferently 'twixt doing them neither good nor harm.

Wave.etym: [OE. waven, AS. wafian to waver, to hesitate, to wonder; akin to wæfre wavering, restless, MHG. wabern to be in motion, Icel. vafra to hover about; cf. Icel. vāfa to vibrate. Cf. Waft, Waver.]

senses.d: To move one way and the other; to brandish.
To raise into inequalities of surface; to give an undulating form a surface to.
q: Horns whelked and waved like the enridged sea.

senses.d: To move like a wave, or by floating; to waft.
To call attention to, or give a direction or command to, by a waving motion, as of the hand; to signify by waving; to beckon; to signal; to indicate.
q: Look, with what courteous action It waves you to a more removed ground.
She spoke, and bowing waved Dismissal.

senses.d: An advancing ridge or swell on the surface of a liquid, as of the sea, resulting from the oscillatory motion of the particles composing it when disturbed by any force their position of rest; an undulation.
q: The wave behind impels the wave before.

senses.d: A vibration propagated from particle to particle through a body or elastic medium, as in the transmission of sound; an assemblage of vibrating molecules in all phases of a vibration, with no phase repeated; a wave of vibration; an undulation. See Undulation.
Water; a body of water.
q: Build a ship to save thee from the flood, I 'll furnish thee with fresh wave, bread, and wine.

senses.d: Unevenness; inequality of surface.
A waving or undulating motion; a signal made with the hand, a flag, etc.
The undulating line or streak of luster on cloth watered, or calendered, or on damask steel.
Fig.: A swelling or excitement of thought, feeling, or energy; a tide; as, waves of enthusiasm.

Wave.etym: [From Wave, v.; not the same word as OE. wawe, waghe, a wave, which is akin to E. wag to move. ����. See Wave, v. i.]

senses.d: Woe.

Something resembling or likened to a water wave, as in rising unusually high, in being of unusual extent, or in progressive motion; a swelling or excitement, as of feeling or energy; a tide; flood; period of intensity, usual activity, or the like; as, a wave of enthusiasm.
Exhibiting a wavelike form or outline; undulating; intended; wavy; as, waved edge.
Having a wavelike appearance; marked with wavelike lines of color; as, waved, or watered, silk.
Having undulations like waves; — said of one of the lines in heraldry which serve as outlines to the ordinaries, etc.
To play or move to and fro; to move one way and the other; hence, to totter; to reel; to swing; to flutter.
q: With banners and pennons wavering with the wind.
Thou wouldst waver on one of these trees as a terror to all evil speakers against dignities.

senses.d: To be unsettled in opinion; to vacillate; to be undetermined; to fluctuate; as, to water in judgment.
q: Let us hold fast . . . without wavering.
In feeble hearts, propense enough before To waver, or fall off and join with idols.

Waver.syn: To reel; totter; vacillate. See Fluctuate.
Waver.etym: [OE. waveren, from AS. wæfre wavering, restless. See Wave, v. i.]

senses.d: A sapling left standing in a fallen wood.
To increase in size; to grow bigger; to become larger or fuller; — opposed to wane.
q: The waxing and the waning of the moon.
Truth's treasures . . . never shall wax ne wane.

senses.d: To pass from one state to another; to become; to grow; as, to wax strong; to wax warmer or colder; to wax feeble; to wax old; to wax worse and worse.
q: Your clothes are not waxen old upon you.
Where young Adonis oft reposes, Waxing well of his deep wound.

Wax.etym: [AS. weaxan; akin to OFries. waxa, D. wassen, OS. & OHG. wahsan, G. wachsen, Icel. vaxa, Sw. växa, Dan. voxe, Goth. wahsjan, Gr. � to increase, Skr. waksh, uksh, to grow. ���. Cf. Waist.]

senses.d: A fatty, solid substance, produced by bees, and employed by them in the construction of their comb; — usually called beeswax. It is first excreted, from a row of pouches along their sides, in the form of scales, which, being masticated and mixed with saliva, become whitened and tenacious. Its natural color is pale or dull yellow.
Hence, any substance resembling beeswax in consistency or appearance.
Cerumen, or earwax.
A waxlike composition used for uniting surfaces, for excluding air, and for other purposes; as, sealing wax, grafting wax, etching wax, etc.
A waxlike composition used by shoemakers for rubbing their thread.
A substance similar to beeswax, secreted by several species of scale insects, as the Chinese wax. See Wax insect, below.
A waxlike product secreted by certain plants. See Vegetable wax, under Vegetable.
A substance, somewhat resembling wax, found in connection with certain deposits of rock salt and coal; — called also mineral wax, and ozocerite.
Thick sirup made by boiling down the sap of the sugar maple, and then cooling.

Wax.etym: [AS. weax; akin to OFries. wax, D. was, G. wachs, OHG. wahs, Icel. & Sw. vax, Dan. vox, Lith. vaszkas, Russ. vosk'.]

senses.d: To smear or rub with wax; to treat with wax; as, to wax a thread or a table.
Made of wax.
Covered with wax; waxed; as, a waxen tablet.
Resembling wax; waxy; hence, soft; yielding.
q: Men have marble, women waxen, minds.

senses.d: Away.
That by, upon, or along, which one passes or processes; opportunity or room to pass; place of passing; passage; road, street, track, or path of any kind; as, they built a way to the mine.
q: I shall him seek by way and eke by street.
The way seems difficult, and steep to scale.
The season and ways were very improper for his majesty's forces to march so great a distance.

senses.d: Length of space; distance; interval; as, a great way; a long way.
q: And whenever the way seemed long, Or his heart began to fail.

senses.d: A moving; passage; procession; journey.
q: I prythee, now, lead the way.

senses.d: Course or direction of motion or process; tendency of action; advance.
q: If that way be your walk, you have not far.
And let eternal justice take the way.

senses.d: The means by which anything is reached, or anything is accomplished; scheme; device; plan.
q: My best way is to creep under his gaberdine.
By noble ways we conquest will prepare.
What impious ways my wishes took!

senses.d: Manner; method; mode; fashion; style; as, the way of expressing one's ideas.
Regular course; habitual method of life or action; plan of conduct; mode of dealing.
q: Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace.
When men lived in a grander way.

senses.d: Sphere or scope of observation.
q: The public ministers that fell in my way.

senses.d: Determined course; resolved mode of action or conduct; as, to have one's way.
Progress; as, a ship has way.
The longitudinal guides, or guiding surfaces, on the bed of a planer, lathe, or the like, along which a table or carriage moves.
Right of way. See below.
q: All keep the broad highway, and take delight With many rather for to go astray.
There is but one road by which to climb up.
When night Darkens the streets, then wander forth the sons Of Belial, flown with insolence and wine.

Way.etym: [OE. wey, way, AS. weg; akin to OS., D., OHG., & G. weg, Icel. vegr, Sw. väg, Dan. vei, Goth. wigs, L. via, and AS. wegan to move, L. vehere to carry, Skr. vah. √136. Cf. Convex, Inveigh, Vehicle, Vex, Via, Voyage, Wag, Wagon, Wee, Weigh.]

senses.d: To go or travel to; to go in, as a way or path.
To move; to progress; to go.
q: On a time as they together wayed.

senses.d: To journey; to travel; to go to and fro.
q: A certain Laconian, as he wayfared, came unto a place where there dwelt an old friend of his.

senses.d: The act of journeying; travel; passage.
Traveling; passing; being on a journey.
A mark to guide in traveling.
The side of the way; the edge or border of a road or path.
Of or pertaining to the wayside; as, wayside flowers.

The plural nominative case of the pronoun of the first person; the word with which a person in speaking or writing denotes a number or company of which he is one, as the subject of an action expressed by a verb.

We.etym: [As. wē; akin to OS. wī, OFries. & LG. wi, D. wij, G. wir, Icel. vēr, Sw. & Dan. vi, Goth. weis, Skr. vayam. √190.]

senses.d: Wanting physical strength.
Deficient in strength of body; feeble; infirm; sickly; debilitated; enfeebled; exhausted.
q: A poor, infirm, weak, and despised old man.
Weak with hunger, mad with love.

senses.d: Not able to sustain a great weight, pressure, or strain; as, a weak timber; a weak rope.
Not firmly united or adhesive; easily broken or separated into pieces; not compact; as, a weak ship.
Not stiff; pliant; frail; soft; as, the weak stalk of a plant.
Not able to resist external force or onset; easily subdued or overcome; as, a weak barrier; as, a weak fortress.
Lacking force of utterance or sound; not sonorous; low; small; feeble; faint.
q: A voice not soft, weak, piping, and womanish.

senses.d: Not thoroughly or abundantly impregnated with the usual or required ingredients, or with stimulating and nourishing substances; of less than the usual strength; as, weak tea, broth, or liquor; a weak decoction or solution; a weak dose of medicine.
Lacking ability for an appropriate function or office; as, weak eyes; a weak stomach; a weak magistrate; a weak regiment, or army.
Not possessing or manifesting intellectual, logical, moral, or political strength, vigor, etc.
Feeble of mind; wanting discernment; lacking vigor; spiritless; as, a weak king or magistrate.
q: To think every thing disputable is a proof of a weak mind and captious temper.
Origen was never weak enough to imagine that there were two Gods.

senses.d: Resulting from, or indicating, lack of judgment, discernment, or firmness; unwise; hence, foolish.
q: If evil thence ensue, She first his weak indulgence will accuse.

Weak.etym: [OE. weik, Icel. veikr; akin to Sw. vek, Dan. veg soft, flexible, pliant, AS. wāc weak, soft, pliant, D. week, G. weich, OHG. weih; all from the verb seen in Icel. vīkja to turn, veer, recede, AS. wīcan to yield, give way, G. weichen, OHG. wīhhan, akin to Skr. vij, and probably to E. week, L. vicis

senses.d: To make or become weak; to weaken.
q: Never to seek weaking variety.

Weak.etym: [Cf. AS. w�can. wācian. See Weak, a.]

senses.d: Tending toward a lower price or lower prices; as, wheat is weak; a weak market.
Lacking in good cards; deficient as to number or strength; as, a hand weak in trumps.
Lacking contrast; as, a weak negative.

To make weak; to lessen the strength of; to deprive of strength; to debilitate; to enfeeble; to enervate; as, to weaken the body or the mind; to weaken the hands of a magistrate; to weaken the force of an objection or an argument.
q: Their hands shall be weakened from the work, that it be not done.

senses.d: To reduce in quality, strength, or spirit; as, to weaken tea; to weaken any solution or decoction.
To become weak or weaker; to lose strength, spirit, or determination; to become less positive or resolute; as, the patient weakened; the witness weakened on cross-examination.
The quality or state of being weak; want of strength or firmness; lack of vigor; want of resolution or of moral strength; feebleness.
That which is a mark of lack of strength or resolution; a fault; a defect.
q: Many take pleasure in spreading abroad the weakness of an exalted character.

Weakness.syn: Feebleness; debility; languor; imbecility; infirmness; infirmity; decrepitude; frailty; faintness.

senses.d: The mark of a stripe. See Wale.
To mark with stripes. See Wale.
A sound, healthy, or prosperous state of a person or thing; prosperity; happiness; welfare.
q: God . . . grant you wele and prosperity.
As we love the weal of our souls and bodies.
To him linked in weal or woe.
Never was there a time when it more concerned the public weal that the character of the Parliament should stand high.

senses.d: The body politic; the state; common wealth.
q: The special watchmen of our English weal.

Weal.etym: [OE. wele, AS. wela, weola, wealth, from wel well. See Well, adv., and cf. Wealth.]

senses.d: To promote the weal of; to cause to be prosperous.
Weal; welfare; prosperity; good.
Large possessions; a comparative abundance of things which are objects of human desire; esp., abundance of worldly estate; affluence; opulence; riches.
q: I have little wealth to lose.
Each day new wealth, without their care, provides.
Wealth comprises all articles of value and nothing else.

Wealth.etym: [OE. welthe, from wele; cf. D. weelde luxury. See Weal prosperity.]

senses.d: In the private sense, all pooperty which has a money value.
In the public sense, all objects, esp. material objects, which have economic utility.
Those energies, faculties, and habits directly contributing to make people industrially efficient.
Having wealth; having large possessions, or larger than most men, as lands, goods, money, or securities; opulent; affluent; rich.
q: A wealthy Hebrew of my tribe.
Thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place.

senses.d: Hence, ample; full; satisfactory; abundant.
q: The wealthy witness of my pen.

senses.d: To accustom and reconcile, as a child or other young animal, to a want or deprivation of mother's milk; to take from the breast or udder; to cause to cease to depend on the mother nourishment.
q: And the child grew, and was weaned; and Abraham made a great feast the same day that Isaac was weaned.

senses.d: Hence, to detach or alienate the affections of, from any object of desire; to reconcile to the want or loss of anything.
q: The troubles of age were intended . . . to wean us gradually from our fondness of life.

Wean.etym: [OE. wenen, AS. wenian, wennan, to accustom; akin to D. wennen, G. gewöhnen, OHG. giwennan, Icel. venja, Sw. vänja, Dan. vænne, Icel. vanr accustomed, wont; cf. AS. āwenian to wean, G. entwöhnen. See Wont, a.]

senses.d: A weanling; a young child.
q: I, being but a yearling wean.

senses.d: An instrument of offensive of defensive combat; something to fight with; anything used, or designed to be used, in destroying, defeating, or injuring an enemy, as a gun, a sword, etc.
q: The weapons of our warfare are not carnal.
They, astonished, all resistance lost, All courage; down their idle weapons dropped.

senses.d: Fig.: The means or instrument with which one contends against another; as, argument was his only weapon.
A thorn, prickle, or sting with which many plants are furnished.

Weapon.etym: [OE. wepen, AS. w�pen; akin to OS. w�pan, OFries. w�pin, w�pen, D. wapen, G. waffe, OHG. waffan, wāfan, Icel. vāpn, Dan. vaaben, Sw. vapen, Goth. w�pna, pl.; of uncertain origin. Cf. Wapentake.]

senses.d: Same as Weir.

To cause to go about, as a vessel, by putting the helm up, instead of alee as in tacking, so that the vessel's bow is turned away from, and her stern is presented to, the wind, and, as she turns still farther, her sails fill on the other side; to veer.

To carry or bear upon the person; to bear upon one's self, as an article of clothing, decoration, warfare, bondage, etc.; to have appendant to one's body; to have on; as, to wear a coat; to wear a shackle.
q: What compass will you wear your farthingale?
On her white breast a sparkling cross s�� wore, Which Jews might kiss, and infidels adore.

senses.d: To have or exhibit an appearance of, as an aspect or manner; to bear; as, she wears a smile on her countenance.
q: His innocent gestures wear A meaning half divine.

senses.d: To use up by carrying or having upon one's self; hence, to consume by use; to waste; to use up; as, to wear clothes rapidly.
To impair, waste, or diminish, by continual attrition, scraping, percussion, on the like; to consume gradually; to cause to lower or disappear; to spend.
q: That wicked wight his days doth wear.
The waters wear the stones.

senses.d: To cause or make by friction or wasting; as, to wear a channel; to wear a hole.
To form or shape by, or as by, attrition.
q: Trials wear us into a liking of what, possibly, in the first essay, displeased us.

Wear.etym: [OE. weren, werien, AS. werian to carry, to wear, as arms or clothes; akin to OHG. werien, weren, to clothe, Goth. wasjan, L. vestis clothing, vestire to clothe, Gr. �, Skr. vas. Cf. Vest.]

senses.d: To endure or suffer use; to last under employment; to bear the consequences of use, as waste, consumption, or attrition; as, a coat wears well or ill; — hence, sometimes applied to character, qualifications, etc.; as, a man wears well as an acquaintance.
To be wasted, consumed, or diminished, by being used; to suffer injury, loss, or extinction by use or time; to decay, or be spent, gradually.
q: Away, I say; time wears.
Thou wilt surely wear away, both thou and this people that is with thee.
His stock of money began to wear very low.
The family . . . wore out in the earlier part of the century.

senses.d: The act of wearing, or the state of being worn; consumption by use; diminution by friction; as, the wear of a garment.
The thing worn; style of dress; the fashion.
q: Motley 's the only wear.

senses.d: The result of wearing or use; consumption, diminution, or impairment due to use, friction, or the like; as, the wear of this coat has been good.
The quality or state of being weary or tried; lassitude; exhaustion of strength; fatigue.
q: With weariness and wine oppressed.
A man would die, though he were neither valiant nor miserable, only upon a weariness to do the same thing so oft over and over.

senses.d: The act of one who wears; the manner in which a thing wears; use; conduct; consumption.
q: Belike he meant to ward, and there to see his wearing.

senses.d: That which is worn; clothes; garments.
q: Give me my nightly wearing and adieu.

senses.d: Pertaining to, or designed for, wear; as, wearing apparel.
Causing weariness; tiresome; tedious; weariful; as, a wearisome march; a wearisome day's work; a wearisome book.
q: These high wild hills and rough uneven ways Draws out our miles, and makes them wearisome.

Wearisome.syn: Irksome; tiresome; tedious; fatiguing; annoying; vexatious. See Irksome.

senses.d: Having the strength exhausted by toil or exertion; worn out in respect to strength, endurance, etc.; tired; fatigued.
q: I care not for my spirits if my legs were not weary.
am weary, thinking of your task.

senses.d: Causing weariness; tiresome.
Having one's patience, relish, or contentment exhausted; tired; sick; — with of before the cause; as, weary of marching, or of confinement; weary of study.

Weary.etym: [OE. weri, AS. w�rig; akin to OS. w�rig, OHG. wu�rag; of uncertain origin; cf. AS. w�rian to ramble.]

senses.d: To reduce or exhaust the physical strength or endurance of; to tire; to fatigue; as, to weary one's self with labor or traveling.
q: So shall he waste his means, weary his soldiers.

senses.d: To make weary of anything; to exhaust the patience of, as by continuance.
q: I stay too long by thee; I weary thee.

senses.d: To harass by anything irksome.
q: I would not cease To weary him with my assiduous cries.

Weary.syn: To jade; tire; fatigue; fag. See Jade.

senses.d: To grow tired; to become exhausted or impatient; as, to weary of an undertaking.

Any one of various species of small carnivores belonging to the genus Putorius, as the ermine and ferret. They have a slender, elongated body, and are noted for the quickness of their movements and for their bloodthirsty habit in destroying poultry, rats, etc. The ermine and some other species are brown in summer, and turn white in winter; others are brown at all seasons.

Weasel.etym: [OE. wesele, AS. wesle; akin to D. wezel, G. wiesel, OHG. wisala, Icel. hreyivīsla, Dan. väsel, Sw. vessla; of uncertain origin; cf. Gr. �, �, cat, weasel.]

senses.d: The state of the air or atmosphere with respect to heat or cold, wetness or dryness, calm or storm, clearness or cloudiness, or any other meteorological phenomena; meteorological condition of the atmosphere; as, warm weather; cold weather; wet weather; dry weather, etc.
q: Not amiss to cool a man's stomach this hot weather.
Fair weather cometh out of the north.

senses.d: Vicissitude of season; meteorological change; alternation of the state of the air.
Storm; tempest.
q: What gusts of weather from that gathering cloud My thoughts presage!

senses.d: A light rain; a shower.

Weather.etym: [OE. weder, AS. weder; akin to OS. wedar, OFries. weder, D. weder, weêr, G. wetter, OHG. wetar, Icel. veðr, Dan. veir, Sw. väder wind, air, weather, and perhaps to OSlav. vedro fair weather; or perhaps to Lith. vetra storm, Russ. vieter', vietr', wind, and E. wind. Cf. Wither.]

senses.d: To expose to the air; to air; to season by exposure to air.
q: soaring through his wide empire of the air To weather his broad sails.
This gear lacks weathering.

senses.d: Hence, to sustain the trying effect of; to bear up against and overcome; to sustain; to endure; to resist; as, to weather the storm.
q: For I can weather the roughest gale.
You will weather the difficulties yet.

senses.d: To sail or pass to the windward of; as, to weather a cape; to weather another ship.
To place (a hawk) unhooded in the open air.
To undergo or endure the action of the atmosphere; to suffer meteorological influences; sometimes, to wear away, or alter, under atmospheric influences; to suffer waste by weather.
q: The organisms . . . seem indestructible, while the hard matrix in which they are imbedded has weathered from around them.

senses.d: Being toward the wind, or windward — opposed to lee; as, weather bow, weather braces, weather gauge, weather lifts, weather quarter, weather shrouds, etc.

To unite, as threads of any kind, in such a manner as to form a texture; to entwine or interlace into a fabric; as, to weave wool, silk, etc.; hence, to unite by close connection or intermixture; to unite intimately.
q: This weaves itself, perforce, into my business.
That in their green shops weave the smooth-haired silk To deck her sons.
And for these words, thus woven into song.

senses.d: To form, as cloth, by interlacing threads; to compose, as a texture of any kind, by putting together textile materials; as, to weave broadcloth; to weave a carpet; hence, to form into a fabric; to compose; to fabricate; as, to weave the plot of a story.
q: When she weaved the sleided silk.
Her starry wreaths the virgin jasmin weaves.

Weave.etym: [OE. weven, AS. wefan; akin to D. weven, G. weben, OHG. weban, Icel. vefa, Sw. väfva, Dan. væve, Gr. �, v., � web, Skr. �r�avābhi spider, lit., wool weaver. Cf. Waper, Waffle, Web, Weevil, Weft, Woof.]

senses.d: To practice weaving; to work with a loom.
To become woven or interwoven.
A particular method or pattern of weaving; as, the cassimere weave.
One who weaves, or whose occupation is to weave.
A weaver bird.
An aquatic beetle of the genus Gyrinus. See Whirling.
A weaver.
That which is woven; a texture; textile fabric; esp., something woven in a loom.
q: Penelope, for her Ulysses' sake, Devised a web her wooers to deceive.
Not web might be woven, not a shuttle thrown, or penalty of exile.

senses.d: A whole piece of linen cloth as woven.
The texture of very fine thread spun by a spider for catching insects at its prey; a cobweb.
Fig.: Tissue; texture; complicated fabrication.
q: The somber spirit of our forefathers, who wove their web of life with hardly a . . . thread of rose-color or gold.
Such has been the perplexing ingenuity of commentators that it is difficult to extricate the truth from the web of conjectures.

senses.d: A band of webbing used to regulate the extension of the hood.
A thin metal sheet, plate, or strip, as of lead.
q: And Christians slain roll up in webs of lead.

senses.d: The blade of a sword.
q: The sword, whereof the web was steel, Pommel rich stone, hilt gold.

senses.d: The blade of a saw.
The thin, sharp part of a colter.
The bit of a key.
A plate or thin portion, continuous or perforated, connecting stiffening ribs or flanges, or other parts of an object.
The thin vertical plate or portion connecting the upper and lower flanges of an lower flanges of an iron girder, rolled beam, or railroad rail.

Web.etym: [OE. web, AS. webb; akin to D. web, webbe, OHG. weppi, G. gewebe, Icel. vefr, Sw. väf, Dan. væv. See Weave.]

senses.d: To unite or surround with a web, or as if with a web; to envelop; to entangle.
A pledge; a pawn.
q: Let him be ware, his neck lieth to wed [i.e., for a security].

Wed.etym: [AS. wedd; akin to OFries. wed, OD. wedde, OHG, wetti, G. wette a wager, Icel. veð a pledge, Sw. vad a wager, an appeal, Goth. wadi a pledge, Lith. vadůti to redeem (a pledge), LL. vadium, L. vas, vadis, bail, security, vadimonium security, and Gr. �, � a prize. Cf. Athlete, Gage a pledge, Wage.]

senses.d: To take for husband or for wife by a formal ceremony; to marry; to espouse.
q: With this ring I thee wed.
I saw thee first, and wedded thee.

senses.d: To join in marriage; to give in wedlock.
q: And Adam, wedded to another Eve, Shall live with her.

senses.d: Fig.: To unite as if by the affections or the bond of marriage; to attach firmly or indissolubly.
q: Thou art wedded to calamity.
Men are wedded to their lusts.
are wedded thus, like beauty to old age.

senses.d: To take to one's self and support; to espouse.
q: They positively and concernedly wedded his cause.

Wed.etym: [OE. wedden, AS. weddian to covenant, promise, to wed, marry; akin to OFries. weddia to promise, D. wedden to wager, to bet, G. wetten, Icel. veðja, Dan. vedde, Sw. vädja to appeal, Goth. gawadjōn to betroth. See Wed, n.]

senses.d: To contact matrimony; to marry.
Nuptial ceremony; nuptial festivities; marriage; nuptials.
q: Simple and brief was the wedding, as that of Ruth and of Boaz.
Let her beauty be her wedding dower.

senses.d: A piece of metal, or other hard material, thick at one end, and tapering to a thin edge at the other, used in splitting wood, rocks, etc., in raising heavy bodies, and the like. It is one of the six elementary machines called the mechanical powers. See Illust. of Mechanical powers, under Mechanical.
A solid of five sides, having a rectangular base, two rectangular or trapezoidal sides meeting in an edge, and two triangular ends.
A mass of metal, especially when of a wedgelike form.
Anything in the form of a wedge, as a body of troops drawn up in such a form.
q: In warlike muster they appear, In rhombs, and wedges, and half-moons, and wings.

senses.d: The person whose name stands lowest on the list of the classical tripos; — so called after a person (Wedgewood) who occupied this position on the first list of 1828.

Wedge.etym: [OE. wegge, AS. wecg; akin to D. wig, wigge, OHG. wecki, G. weck a (wedge-shaped) loaf, Icel. veggr, Dan. vægge, Sw. vigg, and probably to Lith. vagis a peg. Cf. Wigg.]

senses.d: To cleave or separate with a wedge or wedges, or as with a wedge; to rive.
To force or drive as a wedge is driven.
q: Among the crowd in the abbey where a finger Could not be wedged in more.
He 's just the sort of man to wedge himself into a snug berth.
