senses.d: To force by crowding and pushing as a wedge does; as, to wedge one's way.
To press closely; to fix, or make fast, in the manner of a wedge that is driven into something.
q: Wedged in the rocky shoals, and sticking fast.

senses.d: To fasten with a wedge, or with wedges; as, to wedge a scythe on the snath; to wedge a rail or a piece of timber in its place.
To cut, as clay, into wedgelike masses, and work by dashing together, in order to expel air bubbles, etc.
The ceremony, or the state, of marriage; matrimony.
q: For what is wedlock forced but a hell, An age of discord or continual strife?

senses.d: A wife; a married woman.

Wedlock.etym: [AS. wedlāc a pledge, be trothal; wedd a pledge + lāc a gift, an offering. See Wed, n., and cf. Lake, v. i., Knowledge.]

senses.d: To marry; to unite in marriage; to wed.
A garment; clothing; especially, an upper or outer garment.
q: He on his bed sat, the soft weeds he wore Put off.

senses.d: An article of dress worn in token of grief; a mourning garment or badge; as, he wore a weed on his hat; especially, in the plural, mourning garb, as of a woman; as, a widow's weeds.
q: In a mourning weed, with ashes upon her head, and tears abundantly flowing.

Weed.etym: [OE. wede, AS. w�de, w�d; akin to OS. wādi, giwādi, OFries, w�de, w�d, OD. wade, OHG. wāt, Icel. vā�, Zend vadh to clothe.]

senses.d: A sudden illness or relapse, often attended with fever, which attacks women in childbed.
Underbrush; low shrubs.
q: One rushing forth out of the thickest weed.
A wild and wanton pard . . . Crouched fawning in the weed.

senses.d: Any plant growing in cultivated ground to the injury of the crop or desired vegetation, or to the disfigurement of the place; an unsightly, useless, or injurious plant.
q: Too much manuring filled that field with weeds.

senses.d: Fig.: Something unprofitable or troublesome; anything useless.
An animal unfit to breed from.
Tobacco, or a cigar.

Weed.etym: [OE. weed, weod, AS. weód, wiód, akin to OS. wiod, LG. woden the stalks and leaves of vegetables D. wieden to weed, OS. wiodōn.]

senses.d: To free from noxious plants; to clear of weeds; as, to weed corn or onions; to weed a garden.
To take away, as noxious plants; to remove, as something hurtful; to extirpate.
q: Wise fathers . . . weeding from their children ill things.
Revenge is a kind of wild justice, which the more man's nature runs to, the more ought law to weed it out.

senses.d: To free from anything hurtful or offensive.
q: He weeded the kingdom of such as were devoted to Elaiana.

senses.d: To reject as unfit for breeding purposes.
A period of seven days, usually that reckoned from one Sabbath or Sunday to the next.
q: I fast twice in the week.

Week.etym: [OE. weke, wike, woke, wuke AS. weocu, wicu, wucu; akin to OS. wika, OFries. wike, D. week, G. woche, OHG. wohha, wehha, Icel. vika, Sw. vecka, Dan. uge, Goth. wik�, probably originally meaning, a succession or change, and akin to G. wechsel change, L. vicis turn, alternation, and E. weak. Cf. Weak.

senses.d: The lapwing; the wipe; — so called from its cry.
Formerly, to express sorrow, grief, or anguish, by outcry, or by other manifest signs; in modern use, to show grief or other passions by shedding tears; to shed tears; to cry.
q: And they all wept sore, and fell on Paul's neck.
Phocion was rarely seen to weep or to laugh.
And eyes that wake to weep.
And they wept together in silence.

senses.d: To lament; to complain.
To flow in drops; to run in drops.
q: The blood weeps from my heart.

senses.d: To drop water, or the like; to drip; to be soaked.
To hang the branches, as if in sorrow; to be pendent; to droop; — said of a plant or its branches.

Weep.etym: [OE. wepen, AS. w�pan, from w�p lamentation; akin to OFries. w�pa to lament, OS. w�p lamentation, OHG. wuof, Icel. �p a shouting, crying, OS. w�pian to lament, OHG. wuoffan, wuoffen, Icel. �pa, Goth. w�pjan. ����.]

senses.d: To lament; to bewail; to bemoan.
q: We wandering go Through dreary wastes, and weep each other's woe.

senses.d: To shed, or pour forth, as tears; to shed drop by drop, as if tears; as, to weep tears of joy.
q: Tears, such as angels weep, burst forth.
Groves whose rich trees wept odorous gums and balm.

senses.d: The act of one who weeps; lamentation with tears; shedding of tears.
Grieving; lamenting; shedding tears.
Discharging water, or other liquid, in drops or very slowly; surcharged with water.
Having slender, pendent branches; — said of trees; as, weeping willow; a weeping ash.
Pertaining to lamentation, or those who weep.
A corruption of Way, used only in the phrase under weigh.
q: An expedition was got under weigh from New York.
The Athenians . . . hurried on board and with considerable difficulty got under weigh.

senses.d: To bear up; to raise; to lift into the air; to swing up; as, to weigh anchor.

To examine by the balance; to ascertain the weight of, that is, the force with which a thing tends to the center of the earth; to determine the heaviness, or quantity of matter of; as, to weigh sugar; to weigh gold.
q: Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting.

senses.d: To be equivalent to in weight; to counterbalance; to have the heaviness of.
To pay, allot, take, or give by weight.
q: They weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver.

senses.d: To examine or test as if by the balance; to ponder in the mind; to consider or examine for the purpose of forming an opinion or coming to a conclusion; to estimate deliberately and maturely; to balance.
q: A young man not weighed in state affairs.
Had no better weighed The strength he was to cope with, or his own.
Regard not who it is which speaketh, but weigh only what is spoken.
In nice balance, truth with gold she weighs.
Without sufficiently weighing his expressions.

senses.d: To consider as worthy of notice; to regard.
q: All that she so dear did weigh.

Weigh.etym: [OE. weien, weyen, weghen, AS. wegan to bear, move; akin to D. wegen to weigh, G. wägen, wiegen, to weigh, bewegen to move, OHG. wegan, Icel. vega to move, carry, lift, weigh, Sw. väga to weigh, Dan. veie, Goth. gawigan to shake, L. vehere to carry, Skr. vah. ����. See Way, and cf. Wey.]

senses.d: To have weight; to be heavy.
To be considered as important; to have weight in the intellectual balance.
q: Your vows to her and me . . . will even weigh.
This objection ought to weigh with those whose reading is designed for much talk and little knowledge.

senses.d: To bear heavily; to press hard.
q: Cleanse the stuffed bosom of that perilous stuff Which weighs upon the heart.

senses.d: To judge; to estimate.
q: Could not weigh of worthiness aright.

senses.d: A certain quantity estimated by weight; an English measure of weight. See Wey.

The quality of being heavy; that property of bodies by which they tend toward the center of the earth; the effect of gravitative force, especially when expressed in certain units or standards, as pounds, grams, etc.

The quantity of heaviness; comparative tendency to the center of the earth; the quantity of matter as estimated by the balance, or expressed numerically with reference to some standard unit; as, a mass of stone having the weight of five hundred pounds.
q: For sorrow, like a heavy-hanging bell, Once set on ringing, with his own weight goes.

senses.d: Hence, pressure; burden; as, the weight of care or business.
q: For the public all this weight he bears.
who singly bore the world's sad weight.

senses.d: Importance; power; influence; efficacy; consequence; moment; impressiveness; as, a consideration of vast weight.
q: In such a point of weight, so near mine honor.

senses.d: A scale, or graduated standard, of heaviness; a mode of estimating weight; as, avoirdupois weight; troy weight; apothecaries' weight.
A ponderous mass; something heavy; as, a clock weight; a paper weight.
q: A man leapeth better with weights in his hands.

senses.d: A definite mass of iron, lead, brass, or other metal, to be used for ascertaining the weight of other bodies; as, an ounce weight.
The resistance against which a machine acts, as opposed to the power which moves it.

Weight.syn: Ponderousness; gravity; heaviness; pressure; burden; load; importance; power; influence; efficacy; consequence; moment; impressiveness.
Weight.etym: [OE. weght, wight, AS. gewiht; akin to D. gewigt, G. gewicht, Icel. vætt, Sw. vigt, Dan. vægt. See Weigh, v. t.]

senses.d: To load with a weight or weights; to load down; to make heavy; to attach weights to; as, to weight a horse or a jockey at a race; to weight a whip handle.
q: The arrows of satire, . . . weighted with sense.

senses.d: To assign a weight to; to express by a number the probable accuracy of, as an observation. See Weight of observations, under Weight.
To load (fabrics) as with barite, to increase the weight, etc.
Having weight; heavy; ponderous; as, a weighty body.
Adapted to turn the balance in the mind, or to convince; important; forcible; serious; momentous.
q: Let me have your advice in a weighty affair.

senses.d: Rigorous; severe; afflictive.

Weighty.syn: Heavy; ponderous; burdensome; onerous; forcible; momentous; efficacious; impressive; cogent.

senses.d: Well-doing or well-being in any respect; the enjoyment of health and the common blessings of life; exemption from any evil or calamity; prosperity; happiness.
q: How to study for the people's welfare.
In whose deep eyes Men read the welfare of the times to come.

Welfare.etym: [Well + fare to go, to proceed, to happen.]

senses.d: An issue of water from the earth; a spring; a fountain.
q: Begin, then, sisters of the sacred well.

senses.d: A pit or hole sunk into the earth to such a depth as to reach a supply of water, generally of a cylindrical form, and often walled with stone or bricks to prevent the earth from caving in.
q: The woman said unto him, Sir, thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep.

senses.d: A shaft made in the earth to obtain oil or brine.
Fig.: A source of supply; fountain; wellspring.
q: Dan Chaucer, well of English undefiled.
A well of serious thought and pure.

senses.d: An inclosure in the middle of a vessel's hold, around the pumps, from the bottom to the lower deck, to preserve the pumps from damage and facilitate their inspection.
A hole or excavation in the earth, in mining, from which run branches or galleries.
An opening through the floors of a building, as for a staircase or an elevator; a wellhole.
The lower part of a furnace, into which the metal falls.

Well.etym: [OE. welle, AS. wella, wylla, from weallan to well up, surge, boil; akin to D. wel a spring or fountain. ����. See Well, v. i.]

senses.d: To issue forth, as water from the earth; to flow; to spring.
q: From his two springs in Gojam's sunny realm, Pure welling out, he through the lucid lake Of fair Dambea rolls his infant streams.

Well.etym: [OE. wellen, AS. wyllan, wellan, fr. weallan; akin to OFries. walla, OS. & OHG. wallan, G. wallen, Icel. vella, G. welle, wave, OHG. wella, walm, AS. wylm; cf. L. volvere to roll, Gr. � to inwrap, � to roll. Cf. Voluble, Wallop to boil, Wallow, Weld of metal.]

senses.d: To pour forth, as from a well.
In a good or proper manner; justly; rightly; not ill or wickedly.
q: If thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door.

senses.d: Suitably to one's condition, to the occasion, or to a proposed end or use; suitably; abundantly; fully; adequately; thoroughly.
q: Lot . . . beheld all the plain of Jordan, that it was well watered everywhere.
WE are wellable to overcome it.
She looketh well to the ways of her household.
Servant of God, well done! well hast thou fought The better fight.

senses.d: Fully or about; — used with numbers.
q: Well nine and twenty in a company.

senses.d: In such manner as is desirable; so as one could wish; satisfactorily; favorably; advantageously; conveniently.
q: Know In measure what the mind may well contain.
All the world speaks well of you.

senses.d: Considerably; not a little; far.
q: Abraham and Sarah were old and well stricken in age.

Well.etym: [OE. wel, AS. wel; akin to OS., OFries., & D. wel, G. wohl, OHG. wola, wela, Icel. & Dan. vel, Sw. väl, Goth. waíla; originally meaning, according to one's will or wish. See Will, v. t., and cf. Wealth.]

senses.d: Good in condition or circumstances; desirable, either in a natural or moral sense; fortunate; convenient; advantageous; happy; as, it is well for the country that the crops did not fail; it is well that the mistake was discovered.
q: It was well with us in Egypt.

senses.d: Being in health; sound in body; not ailing, diseased, or sick; healthy; as, a well man; the patient is perfectly well.
q: Is your father well, the old man of whom ye spake?

senses.d: Being in favor; favored; fortunate.
q: He followed the fortunes of that family, and was well with Henry the Fourth.

senses.d: Safe; as, a chip warranted well at a certain day and place.
A fountain; a spring; a source of continual supply.
q: Understanding is a wellspring of life unto him that hath it; but the instruction of fools is folly.

senses.d: A young woman; a girl; a maiden.
q: Lord and lady, groom and wench.
That they may send again My most sweet wench, and gifts to boot.
He was received by the daughter of the house, a pretty, buxom, blue-eyed little wench.

senses.d: A low, vicious young woman; a drab; a strumpet.
q: She shall be called his wench or his leman.
It is not a digression to talk of bawds in a discourse upon wenches.

senses.d: A colored woman; a negress.

Wench.etym: [OE. wenche, for older wenchel a child, originally, weak, tottering; cf. AS. wencle a maid, a daughter, wencel a pupil, orphan, wincel, winclu, children, offspring, wencel weak, wancol unstable, OHG. wanchol; perhaps akin to E. wink. See Wink.]

senses.d: To frequent the company of wenches, or women of ill fame.
Course; way; path; journey; direction.
q: But here my weary team, nigh overspent, Shall breathe itself awhile after so long a went.
He knew the diverse went of mortal ways.

senses.d: To wear. See 3d Wear.
A weir. See Weir.
To guard; to protect.
The imperfect indicative plural, and imperfect subjunctive singular and plural, of the verb be. See Be.

Were.etym: [AS. wǣre (thou) wast, wǣron (we, you, they) were, wǣre imp. subj. See Was.]

senses.d: A man.
A fine for slaying a man; the money value set upon a man's life; weregild.
q: Every man was valued at a certain sum, which was called his were.

Were.etym: [AS. wer; akin to OS. & OHG. wer, Goth. waír, L. vir, Skr. vīra. Cf. Weregild, and Werewolf.]

senses.d: The second person singular, indicative and subjunctive moods, imperfect tense, of the verb be. It is formed from were, with the ending -t, after the analogy of wast. Now used only in solemn or poetic style.
A wart.

The point in the heavens where the sun is seen to set at the equinox; or, the corresponding point on the earth; that one of the four cardinal points of the compass which is in a direction at right angles to that of north and south, and on the left hand of a person facing north; the point directly opposite to east.
q: And fresh from the west is the free wind's breath.

senses.d: A country, or region of country, which, with regard to some other country or region, is situated in the direction toward the west.
The Westen hemisphere, or the New World so called, it having been discovered by sailing westward from Europe; the Occident.

West.etym: [AS. west, adv.; akin to D. west, G. west, westen, OHG. westan, Icel. vestr, Sw. vest, vester, vestan, Dan. vest, vesten, and perhaps to L. vesper evening, Gr. �. ����. Cf. Vesper, Visigoth.]

senses.d: Lying toward the west; situated at the west, or in a western direction from the point of observation or reckoning; proceeding toward the west, or coming from the west; as, a west course is one toward the west; an east and west line; a west wind blows from the west.
q: This shall be your west border.

senses.d: Westward.
To pass to the west; to set, as the sun.
To turn or move toward the west; to veer from the north or south toward the west.
Designating, or situated in, that part of a church which is opposite to, and farthest from, the east, or the part containing the chancel and choir.
Of or pertaining to the west; situated in the west, or in the region nearly in the direction of west; being in that quarter where the sun sets; as, the western shore of France; the western ocean.
q: Far o'er the glowing western main.

senses.d: Moving toward the west; as, a ship makes a western course; coming from the west; as, a western breeze.
Toward the west; as, to ride or sail westward.
q: Westward the course of empire takes its way.

senses.d: Lying toward the west.
q: Yond same star that's westward from the pole.

senses.d: The western region or countries; the west.
Containing, or consisting of, water or other liquid; moist; soaked with a liquid; having water or other liquid upon the surface; as, wet land; a wet cloth; a wet table.
Very damp; rainy; as, wet weather; a wet season.
Employing, or done by means of, water or some other liquid; as, the wet extraction of copper, in distinction from dry extraction in which dry heat or fusion is employed.
Refreshed with liquor; drunk.

Wet.syn: Nasty; humid; damp; moist. See Nasty.
Wet.etym: [OE. wet, weet, AS. wǣt; akin to OFries. wēt, Icel. vātr, Sw. våt, Dan. vaad, and E. water. √137. See Water.]

senses.d: Water or wetness; moisture or humidity in considerable degree.
q: Have here a cloth and wipe away the wet.
Now the sun, with more effectual beams, Had cheered the face of earth, and dried the wet From drooping plant.

senses.d: Rainy weather; foggy or misty weather.
A dram; a drink.

To fill or moisten with water or other liquid; to sprinkle; to cause to have water or other fluid adherent to the surface; to dip or soak in a liquid; as, to wet a sponge; to wet the hands; to wet cloth.
q: Ye mists and exhalations, that now rise . . . Whether to deck with clouds the uncolored sky, Or wet the thirsty earth with falling showers.
Let us drink the other cup to wet our whistles.

senses.d: Any aquatic mammal of the order Cetacea, especially any one of the large species, some of which become nearly one hundred feet long. Whales are hunted chiefly for their oil and baleen, or whalebone.

Whale.etym: [OE. whal, AS. hwæl; akin to D. walvisch, G. wal, walfisch, OHG. wal, Icel. hvalr, Dan. & Sw. hval, hvalfisk. Cf. Narwhal, Walrus.]

senses.d: As an interrogative pronoun, used in asking questions regarding either persons or things; as, what is this? what did you say? what poem is this? what child is lost?
q: What see'st thou in the ground?
What is man, that thou art mindful of him?
What manner of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him!

senses.d: As an exclamatory word: — (a) Used absolutely or independently; — often with a question following.
q: What, could ye not watch with me one hour?

senses.d: Used adjectively, meaning how remarkable, or how great; as, what folly! what eloquence! what courage!
q: What a piece of work is man!
O what a riddle of absurdity!

senses.d: Sometimes prefixed to adjectives in an adverbial sense, as nearly equivalent to how; as, what happy boys!
q: What partial judges are our love and hate!

senses.d: As a relative pronoun
Used substantively with the antecedent suppressed, equivalent to that which, or those who, or those which; — called a compound relative.
q: With joy beyond what victory bestows.
I'm thinking Captain Lawton will count the noses of what are left before they see their whaleboats.
What followed was in perfect harmony with this beginning.
I know well . . . how little you will be disposed to criticise what comes to you from me.

senses.d: Used adjectively, equivalent to the . . . which; the sort or kind of . . . which; rarely, the . . . on, or at, which.
q: See what natures accompany what colors.
To restrain what power either the devil or any earthly enemy hath to work us woe.
We know what master laid thy keel, What workmen wrought thy ribs of steel.

senses.d: Used adverbially in a sense corresponding to the adjectival use; as, he picked what good fruit he saw.
Whatever; whatsoever; what thing soever; — used indefinitely.
q: Whether it were the shortness of his foresight, the strength of his will, . . . or what it was.

senses.d: Used adverbially, in part; partly; somewhat; — with a following preposition, especially, with, and commonly with repetition.
q: What for lust and what for lore.
Thus, what with the war, what with the sweat, what with the gallows, and what with poverty, I am custom shrunk.
The year before he had so used the matter that what by force, what by policy, he had taken from the Christians above thirty small castles.

What.etym: [AS. hwæt, neuter of hwā who; akin to OS. hwat what, OFries. hwet, D. & LG. wat, G. was, OHG. waz, hwaz, Icel. hvat, Sw. & Dan. hvad, Goth. hwa. √182. See Who.]

senses.d: Something; thing; stuff.
q: And gave him for to feed, Such homely what as serves the simple clown.

senses.d: Why? For what purpose? On what account?
q: What should I tell the answer of the knight.
But what do I stand reckoning upon advantages and gains lost by the misrule and turbulency of the prelates? What do I pick up so thriftily their scatterings and diminishings of the meaner subject?

senses.d: Whatever.
q: Whatsoever God hath said unto thee, do.

senses.d: A cereal grass (Triticum vulgare) and its grain, which furnishes a white flour for bread, and, next to rice, is the grain most largely used by the human race.

Wheat.etym: [OE. whete, AS. hw�te; akin to OS. hw�ti, D. weit, G. weizen, OHG. weizzi, Icel. hveiti, Sw. hvete, Dan. hvede, Goth. hwaiteis, and E. while. See White.]

senses.d: Made of wheat; as, wheaten bread.

A circular frame turning about an axis; a rotating disk, whether solid, or a frame composed of an outer rim, spokes or radii, and a central hub or nave, in which is inserted the axle, — used for supporting and conveying vehicles, in machinery, and for various purposes; as, the wheel of a wagon, of a locomotive, of a mill, of a watch, etc.
q: The gasping charioteer beneath the wheel Of his own car.

senses.d: Any instrument having the form of, or chiefly consisting of, a wheel.
A spinning wheel. See under Spinning.
An instrument of torture formerly used.
q: His examination is like that which is made by the rack and wheel.

senses.d: A circular frame having handles on the periphery, and an axle which is so connected with the tiller as to form a means of controlling the rudder for the purpose of steering.
A potter's wheel. See under Potter.
q: Then I went down to the potter's house, and, behold, he wrought a work on the wheels.
Turn, turn, my wheel! This earthen jar A touch can make, a touch can mar.

senses.d: A firework which, while burning, is caused to revolve on an axis by the reaction of the escaping gases.
The burden or refrain of a song.
q: You must sing a-down a-down, An you call him a-down-a. O, how the wheel becomes it!

senses.d: A bicycle or a tricycle; a velocipede.
A rolling or revolving body; anything of a circular form; a disk; an orb.
A turn revolution; rotation; compass.
q: According to the common vicissitude and wheel of things, the proud and the insolent, after long trampling upon others, come at length to be trampled upon themselves.
throws his steep flight in many an aëry wheel.

Wheel.etym: [OE. wheel, hweol, AS. hweól, hweogul, hweowol; akin to D. wiel, Icel. hvēl, Gr. κύκλοσ, Skr. cakra; cf. Icel. hjōl, Dan. hiul, Sw. hjul. √218. Cf. Cycle, Cyclopedia.]

senses.d: To convey on wheels, or in a wheeled vehicle; as, to wheel a load of hay or wood.
To put into a rotatory motion; to cause to turn or revolve; to cause to gyrate; to make or perform in a circle.
q: Now heaven, in all her glory, shone, and rolled Her motions, as the great first mover's hand First wheeled their course.

senses.d: To turn on an axis, or as on an axis; to revolve; to more about; to rotate; to gyrate.
q: The moon carried about the earth always shows the same face to us, not once wheeling upon her own center.

senses.d: To change direction, as if revolving upon an axis or pivot; to turn; as, the troops wheeled to the right.
q: Being able to advance no further, they are in a fair way to wheel about to the other extreme.

senses.d: To go round in a circuit; to fetch a compass.
q: Then wheeling down the steep of heaven he flies.

senses.d: To roll forward.
q: Thunder mixed with hail, Hail mixed with fire, must rend the Egyptian sky, And wheel on the earth, devouring where it rolls.

senses.d: One of the young of a dog or a beast of prey; a puppy; a cub; as, a lion's whelps.
A child; a youth; — jocosely or in contempt.
q: That awkward whelp with his money bags would have made his entrance.

senses.d: One of the longitudinal ribs or ridges on the barrel of a capstan or a windless; — usually in the plural; as, the whelps of a windlass.
One of the teeth of a sprocket wheel.

Whelp.etym: [AS. hwelp; akin to D. welp, G. & OHG. welf, Icel. hvelpr, Dan. hvalp, Sw. valp.]

senses.d: To bring forth young; — said of the female of the dog and some beasts of prey.
To bring forth, as cubs or young; to give birth to.
q: Unless she had whelped it herself, she could not have loved a thing better.
Did thy foul fancy whelp so black a scheme?

senses.d: At what time; — used interrogatively.
q: When shall these things be?

senses.d: At what time; at, during, or after the time that; at or just after, the moment that; — used relatively.
q: Kings may Take their advantage when and how they list.
Book lore ne'er served, when trial came, Nor gifts, when faith was dead.

senses.d: While; whereas; although; — used in the manner of a conjunction to introduce a dependent adverbial sentence or clause, having a causal, conditional, or adversative relation to the principal proposition; as, he chose to turn highwayman when he might have continued an honest man; he removed the tree when it was the best in the grounds.
Which time; then; — used elliptically as a noun.
q: I was adopted heir by his consent; Since when, his oath is broke.
Come hither; mend my ruff: Here, when! thou art such a tedious lady!
When as sacred light began to dawn.
When that mine eye is famished for a look.

When.etym: [OE. when, whan, whenne, whanne, AS. hwænne, hwanne, hwonne; akin to OS. hwan, OD. wan, OHG. wanne, G. wann when, wenn if, when, Goth. hwan when, and to E. who. ����. See Who.]

senses.d: From what place; hence, from what or which source, origin, antecedent, premise, or the like; how; — used interrogatively.
q: Whence hath this man this wisdom?
Whence and what art thou?

senses.d: From what or which place, source, material, cause, etc.; the place, source, etc., from which; — used relatively.
q: Grateful to acknowledge whence his good Descends.

Whence.etym: [OE. whennes, whens (with adverbial s, properly a genitive ending; — see -wards), also whenne, whanene, AS. hwanan, hwanon, hwonan, hwanone; akin to D. when. See When, and cf. Hence, Thence.]

senses.d: At what time soever; at whatever time; whenever.
At or in what place; hence, in what situation, position, or circumstances; — used interrogatively.
q: God called unto Adam, . . . Where art thou?

senses.d: At or in which place; at the place in which; hence, in the case or instance in which; — used relatively.
q: She visited that place where first she was so happy.
Where I thought the remnant of mine age Should have been cherished by her childlike duty.
Where one on his side fights, thousands will fly.
But where he rode one mile, the dwarf ran four.

senses.d: To what or which place; hence, to what goal, result, or issue; whither; — used interrogatively and relatively; as, where are you going?

The star . . . stood over where the young child was.
The Son of man hath not where to lay his head.
Within about twenty paces of where we were.
Where did the minstrels come from?

Where.etym: [OE. wher, whar, AS. hw�r; akin to D. waar, OS. hw�r, OHG. hwār, wār, wā, G. wo, Icel. and Sw. hvar, Dan. hvor, Goth. hwar, and E. who; cf. Skr. karhi when. √182. See Who, and cf. There.]

senses.d: Whereas.
q: And flight and die is death destroying death; Where fearing dying pays death servile breath.

senses.d: Place; situation.

Concerning which; about which.
The place where a person or thing is; as, they did not know his whereabouts.

senses.d: At which place; where.

When in fact; while on the contrary; the case being in truth that; although; — implying opposition to something that precedes; or implying recognition of facts, sometimes followed by a different statement, and sometimes by inferences or something consequent.

senses.d: By which; — used relatively.
By what; how; — used interrogatively.
q: Whereby shall I know this?

senses.d: For which reason; so; — used relatively.
q: Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.

senses.d: For what reason; why; — used interrogatively.
q: But wherefore that I tell my tale.
Wherefore didst thou doubt?

senses.d: the reason why.
In which; in which place, thing, time, respect, or the like; — used relatively.

There are times wherein a man ought to be cautious as well as innocent.

senses.d: In what; — used interrogatively.

senses.d: Into which; — used relatively.

The brook, whereinto he loved to look.

senses.d: Into what; — used interrogatively.
Of which; of whom; formerly, also, with which; — used relatively.

senses.d: Of what; — used interrogatively.

senses.d: On what; — used interrogatively; as, whereon do we stand?
In what place soever; in whatever place; wherever.
To which; — used relatively.

senses.d: To what; to what end; — used interrogatively.
Same as Whereto.
Upon which; in consequence of which; after which.
q: The townsmen mutinied and sent to Essex; whereupon he came thither.

senses.d: With which; — used relatively.
q: The love wherewith thou hast loved me.

senses.d: With what; — used interrogatively.
q: Wherewith shall I save Israel?

senses.d: The necessary means or instrument.
q: So shall I have wherewith to answer him.
The wherewith to meet excessive loss by radiation.

senses.d: Wherewith.

senses.d: To rub or on with some substance, as a piece of stone, for the purpose of sharpening; to sharpen by attrition; as, to whet a knife.

Here roams the wolf, the eagle whets his beak.

senses.d: To make sharp, keen, or eager; to excite; to stimulate; as, to whet the appetite or the courage.

Whet.etym: [AS. hwettan; akin to D. wetten, G. wetzen, OHG. wezzen, Icel. hvetja, Sw. vättja, and AS. hwæt vigorous, brave, OS. hwat, OHG. waz, was, sharp, Icel. hvatr, bold, active, Sw. hvass sharp, Dan. hvas, Goth. hwassaba sharply, and probably to Skr. cud to impel, urge on.]

senses.d: The act of whetting.
That which whets or sharpens; esp., an appetizer.
Which (of two); which one (of two); — used interrogatively and relatively.

Whether of them twain did the will of his father?

Whether.etym: [OE. whether, AS. hwæ�er; akin to OS. hwe�ar, OFries. hweder, OHG. hwedar, wedar, G. weder, conj., neither, Icel. hvārr whether, Goth. hwa�ar, Lith. katras, L. uter, Gr. �, �, Skr. katara, from the interrogatively pronoun, in AS. hwā who. ����. senses.d: In case; if; — used to introduce the first or two or more alternative clauses, the other or others being connected by or, or by or whether. You have said; but whether wisely or no, let the forest judge.
For whether we live, we live unto the Lord; and whether we die, we die unto the Lord; whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's.
But whether thus these things, or whether not; Whether the sun, predominant in heaven, Rise on the earth, or earth rise on the sun, . . . Solicit not thy thoughts with matters hid.

senses.d: Of what sort or kind; what; what a; who.
q: And which they weren and of what degree.

senses.d: A interrogative pronoun, used both substantively and adjectively, and in direct and indirect questions, to ask for, or refer to, an individual person or thing among several of a class; as, which man is it? which woman was it? which is the house? he asked which route he should take; which is best, to live or to die? See the Note under What, pron., 1.
q: Which of you convinceth me of sin?

senses.d: A relative pronoun, used esp. in referring to an antecedent noun or clause, but sometimes with reference to what is specified or implied in a sentence, or to a following noun or clause (generally involving a reference, however, to something which has preceded). q: And when thou fail'st — as God forbid the hour! — Must Edward fall, which peril heaven forfend!
God . . . rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made.
Our Father, which art in heaven.
The temple of God is holy, which temple ye are.

senses.d: A compound relative or indefinite pronoun, standing for any one which, whichever, that which, those which, the . . . which, and the like; as, take which you will.
q: Do not they blaspheme that worthy name by the which ye are called?

senses.d: To cause to pass away pleasantly or without irksomeness or disgust; to spend or pass; — usually followed by away.

senses.d: To loiter.
During the time that; as long as; whilst; at the same time that; as, while I write, you sleep.

senses.d: Hence, under which circumstances; in which case; though; whereas.
Until; till.

senses.d: Meanwhile; meantime.

senses.d: sometimes; at times.
During the time that; while.

senses.d: While.

senses.d: To strike with a lash, a cord, a rod, or anything slender and lithe; to lash; to beat; as, to whip a horse, or a carpet.
To drive with lashes or strokes of a whip; to cause to rotate by lashing with a cord; as, to whip a top.
To punish with a whip, scourge, or rod; to flog; to beat; as, to whip a vagrant; to whip one with thirty nine lashes; to whip a perverse boy.
q: Who, for false quantities, was whipped at school.

senses.d: To apply that which hurts keenly to; to lash, as with sarcasm, abuse, or the like; to apply cutting language to.
q: They would whip me with their fine wits.

senses.d: To thrash; to beat out, as grain, by striking; as, to whip wheat.
To beat (eggs, cream, or the like) into a froth, as with a whisk, fork, or the like.
To conquer; to defeat, as in a contest or game; to beat; to surpass.
To overlay (a cord, rope, or the like) with other cords going round and round it; to overcast, as the edge of a seam; to wrap; — often with about, around, or over.

senses.d: To sew lightly; specifically, to form (a fabric) into gathers by loosely overcasting the rolled edge and drawing up the thread; as, to whip a ruffle.

senses.d: To take or move by a sudden motion; to jerk; to snatch; — with into, out, up, off, and the like.

He whips out his pocketbook every moment, and writes descriptions of everything he sees.

senses.d: To hoist or purchase by means of a whip.
To fish (a body of water) with a rod and artificial fly, the motion being that employed in using a whip.
q: Whipping their rough surface for a trout.

Whip.etym: [OE. whippen to overlay, as a cord, with other cords, probably akin to G. & D. wippen to shake, to move up and down, Sw. vippa, Dan. vippe to swing to and fro, to shake, to toss up, and L. vibrare to shake. Cf. Vibrate.]

senses.d: To move nimbly; to start or turn suddenly and do something; to whisk; as, he whipped around the corner.

senses.d: An instrument or driving horses or other animals, or for correction, consisting usually of a lash attached to a handle, or of a handle and lash so combined as to form a flexible rod.

A huntsman who whips in the hounds; whipper-in.

A person (as a member of Parliament) appointed to enforce party discipline, and secure the attendance of the members of a Parliament party at any important session, especially when their votes are needed.

A whipping motion; a thrashing about; as, the whip of a tense rope or wire which has suddenly parted; also, the quality of being whiplike or flexible; flexibility; suppleness, as of the shaft of a golf club.
Any of various pieces that operate with a quick vibratory motion, as a spring in certain electrical devices for making a circuit, or a rocking certain piano actions.
To turn round rapidly; to cause to rotate with velocity; to make to revolve.
q: He whirls his sword around without delay.

senses.d: To remove or carry quickly with, or as with, a revolving motion; to snatch; to harry.

The passionate heart of the poet is whirl'd into folly.

Whirl.etym: [OE. whirlen, probably from the Scand.; cf. Icel. & Sw. hvirfla, Dan. hvirvle; akin to D. wervelen, G. wirbeln, freq. of the verb seen in Icel. hverfa to turn. √16. See Wharf, and cf. Warble, Whorl.]

senses.d: To be turned round rapidly; to move round with velocity; to revolve or rotate with great speed; to gyrate.

senses.d: A turning with rapidity or velocity; rapid rotation or circumvolution; quick gyration; rapid or confusing motion; as, the whirl of a top; the whirl of a wheel.

senses.d: Anything that moves with a whirling motion.

senses.d: A revolving hook used in twisting, as the hooked spindle of a rope machine, to which the threads to be twisted are attached.
A whorl. See Whorl.

Whirl.etym: [Cf. Dan. hvirvel, Sw. hvirfvel, Icel. hvirfill the crown of the head, G. wirbel whirl, crown of the head, D. wervel. See Whirl, v. t.]

senses.d: Fig.: A body of objects sweeping violently onward.

Whirlwind.etym: [Cf. Icel. hvirfilvindr, Sw. hvirfvelvind, Dan. hvirvelvind, G. wirbelwind. See Whirl, and Wind, n.]

senses.d: A flock of snipe.

To speak softly, or under the breath, so as to be heard only by one near at hand; to utter words without sonant breath; to talk without that vibration in the larynx which gives sonorous, or vocal, sound. See Whisper, n.
To make a low, sibilant sound or noise.
q: The hollow, whispering breeze.

senses.d: To speak with suspicion, or timorous caution; to converse in whispers, as in secret plotting.
q: All that hate me whisper together against me.

senses.d: To prompt secretly or cautiously; to inform privately.

A low, soft, sibilant voice or utterance, which can be heard only by those near at hand; voice or utterance that employs only breath sound without tone, friction against the edges of the vocal cords and arytenoid cartilages taking the place of the vibration of the cords that produces tone; sometimes, in a limited sense, the sound produced by such friction as distinguished from breath sound made by friction against parts of the mouth. See Voice, n., 2, and Guide to Pronunciation, §§ 5, 153, 154.

Soft whispers through the assembly went.

Something communicated in secret or by whispering; a suggestion or insinuation.
A low, sibilant sound.
One who whispers.
A tattler; one who tells secrets; a conveyer of intelligence secretly; hence; a backbiter; one who slanders secretly.
The smallest part or particle imaginable; a bit; a jot; an iota; — generally used in an adverbial phrase in a negative sentence.
q: So shall I no whit be behind in duty.
It does not me a whit displease.

Whit.etym: [OE. wight, wiht, AS. wiht a creature, a thing. See Wight, and cf. Aught, Naught.]

senses.d: Reflecting to the eye all the rays of the spectrum combined; not tinted with any of the proper colors or their mixtures; having the color of pure snow; snowy; — the opposite of black or dark; as, white paper; a white skin.
q: White as the whitest lily on a stream.

senses.d: Destitute of color, as in the cheeks, or of the tinge of blood color; pale; pallid; as, white with fear.
q: Or whispering with white lips, “The foe! They come! they come!”

senses.d: Having the color of purity; free from spot or blemish, or from guilt or pollution; innocent; pure.

No whiter page than Addison's remains.

senses.d: Gray, as from age; having silvery hair; hoary.

senses.d: Characterized by freedom from that which disturbs, and the like; fortunate; happy; favorable.

senses.d: Regarded with especial favor; favorite; darling.

I am his white boy, and will not be gullet.

White.etym: [OE. whit, AS. hw�t; akin to OFries. and OS. hwīt, D. wit, G. weiss, OHG. wīz, hwīz, Icel. hvītr, Sw. hvit, Dan. hvid, Goth. hweits, Lith. szveisti, to make bright, Russ. sviet' light, Skr. �v�ta white, �vit to be bright. ���. Cf. Wheat, Whitsunday.]

q: Finely attired in a of white.

senses.d: Something having the color of snow; something white, or nearly so; as, the white of the eye.
Specifically, the central part of the butt in archery, which was formerly painted white; the center of a mark at which a missile is shot.
q: 'T was I won the wager, though you hit the white.

senses.d: A person with a white skin; a member of the white, or Caucasian, races of men.
A white pigment; as, Venice white.
Any one of numerous species of butterflies belonging to Pieris, and allied genera in which the color is usually white. See Cabbage butterfly, under Cabbage.
To make white; to whiten; to whitewash; to bleach.
q: Whited sepulchers, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of . . . uncleanness.
So as no fuller on earth can white them.

Who and whom, as relative pronouns (in the sense of that), are properly used of persons (corresponding to which, as applied to things), but are sometimes, less properly and now rarely, used of animals, plants, etc. Who and whom, as compound relatives, are also used especially of persons, meaning the person that; the persons that; the one that; whosoever.
q: should not tell whose children they were.

Adders who with cloven tongues Do hiss into madness.

Who cheapens life, abates the fear of death.
The brace of large greyhounds, who were the companions of his sports.

senses.d: One; any; one.

Whole.syn: All; total; complete; entire; integral; undivided; uninjured; unimpaired; unbroken; healthy.

q: “This not the whole of life to live, Nor all of death to die.

senses.d: A regular combination of parts; a system.
q: Parts answering parts shall slide into a whole.

senses.d: Tending to promote health; favoring health; salubrious; salutary.
q: Wholesome thirst and appetite.
From which the industrious poor derive an agreeable and wholesome variety of food.

senses.d: Contributing to the health of the mind; favorable to morals, religion, or prosperity; conducive to good; salutary; sound; as, wholesome advice; wholesome doctrines; wholesome truths; wholesome laws.
q: A wholesome tongue is a tree of life.
I can not . . . make you a wholesome answer; my wit's diseased.
A wholesome suspicion began to be entertained.

senses.d: Sound; healthy.

Wholesome.etym: [Whole + some; cf. Icel. heilsamr, G. heilsam, D. heilzaam.]

senses.d: In a whole or complete manner; entirely; completely; perfectly.
q: Nor wholly overcome, nor wholly yield.

senses.d: To the exclusion of other things; totally; fully.

q: And every grass that groweth upon root She shall eke know, and whom it will do boot.

The practice of unlawful intercourse with the other sex; fornication; lewdness.
The sin of worshiping idols; idolatry.
q: O Ephraim, thou committest whoredom, and Israel is defiled; they will not . . . turn unto their God.

senses.d: A whoremaster; a lecher; a man who frequents the society of whores.
Resembling a whore in character or conduct; addicted to unlawful pleasures; incontinent; lewd; unchaste.

The question whose solution I require.

Whose.etym: [OE. whos, whas, AS. hwæs, gen. of hwā. See Who.]

senses.d: Whosoever.

senses.d: Whatsoever person; any person whatever that; whoever.

Wick.etym: [AS. wīc village, fr. L. vicus. In some names of places, perhaps fr. Icel. vīk an inlet, creek, bay. See Vicinity, and cf. Villa.]

senses.d: A bundle of fibers, or a loosely twisted or braided cord, tape, or tube, usually made of soft spun cotton threads, which by capillary attraction draws up a steady supply of the oil in lamps, the melted tallow or wax in candles, or other material used for illumination, in small successive portions, to be burned.
q: But true it is, that when the oil is spent The light goes out, and wick is thrown away.

Wick.etym: [OE. wicke, weyke, weke, AS. weoca or wecca; cf. D. wiek a roll of lint, Prov. G. wicke, and wieche, OHG. wiohha, Sw. veke, Dan. væge; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: To strike a stone in an oblique direction.
Wicked.
Having a wick; — used chiefly in composition; as, a two-wicked lamp.

Evil in principle or practice; deviating from morality; contrary to the moral or divine law; addicted to vice or sin; sinful; immoral; profligate; — said of persons and things; as, a wicked king; a wicked woman; a wicked deed; wicked designs.
q: Hence, then, and evil go with thee along, Thy offspring, to the place of evil, hell, Thou and thy wicked crew!
Never, never, wicked man was wise.

senses.d: Cursed; baneful; hurtful; bad; pernicious; dangerous.
q: This were a wicked way, but whoso had a guide.

senses.d: Ludicrously or sportively mischievous; disposed to mischief; roguish.
q: Pen looked uncommonly wicked.

Wicked.syn: Iniquitous; sinful; criminal; guilty; immoral; unjust; unrighteous; unholy; irreligious; ungodly; profane; vicious; pernicious; atrocious; nefarious; heinous; flagrant; flagitious; abandoned. See Iniquitous.
Wicked.etym: [OE. wicked, fr. wicke wicked; probably originally the same word as wicche wizard, witch. See Witch.]

senses.d: In a wicked manner; in a manner, or with motives and designs, contrary to the divine law or the law of morality; viciously; corruptly; immorally.
q: I have sinned, and I have done wickedly.

senses.d: The quality or state of being wicked; departure from the rules of the divine or the moral law; evil disposition or practices; immorality; depravity; sinfulness.
q: God saw that the wickedness of man was great.
Their inward part is very wickedness.

senses.d: A wicked thing or act; crime; sin; iniquity.
q: I'll never care what wickedness I do, If this man comes to good.

senses.d: Having considerable distance or extent between the sides; spacious across; much extended in a direction at right angles to that of length; not narrow; broad; as, wide cloth; a wide table; a wide highway; a wide bed; a wide hall or entry.
q: The chambers and the stables weren wyde.
Wide is the gate . . . that leadeth to destruction.

senses.d: Having a great extent every way; extended; spacious; broad; vast; extensive; as, a wide plain; the wide ocean; a wide difference.
q: For sceptered cynics earth were far too wide a den.
When the wide bloom, on earth that lies, Seems of a brighter world than ours.

senses.d: Of large scope; comprehensive; liberal; broad; as, wide views; a wide understanding.
q: Men of strongest head and widest culture.

senses.d: Of a certain measure between the sides; measuring in a direction at right angles to that of length; as, a table three feet wide.
Remote; distant; far.
q: The contrary being so wide from the truth of Scripture and the attributes of God.

senses.d: Far from truth, from propriety, from necessity, or the like.
q: It is far wide that the people have such judgments.
How wide is all this long pretense !

senses.d: On one side or the other of the mark; too far side-wise from the mark, the wicket, the batsman, etc.
q: Surely he shoots wide on the bow hand.
I was but two bows wide.

senses.d: Made, as a vowel, with a less tense, and more open and relaxed, condition of the mouth organs; — opposed to primary as used by Mr. Bell, and to narrow as used by Mr. Sweet. The effect, as explained by Mr. Bell, is due to the relaxation or tension of the pharynx; as explained by Mr. Sweet and others, it is due to the action of the tongue. The wide of ē (ēve) is ĭ (ĭll); of ā (āte) is ĕ (ĕnd), etc. See Guide to Pronunciation, § 13-15.

Wide.etym: [OE. wid, wyde, AS. wīd; akin to OFries. & OS. wīd, D. wijd, G. weit, OHG. wīt, Icel. vīðr, Sw. & Dan. vid; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: To a distance; far; widely; to a great distance or extent; as, his fame was spread wide.
q: went wyde in this world, wonders to hear.

senses.d: So as to leave or have a great space between the sides; so as to form a large opening.
So as to be or strike far from, or on one side of, an object or purpose; aside; astray.
That which is wide; wide space; width; extent.
That which goes wide, or to one side of the mark.
Having or showing a wide difference between the highest and lowest price, amount of supply, etc.; as, a wide opening; wide prices, where the prices bid and asked differ by several points.
The quality or state of being wide; breadth; width; great extent from side to side; as, the wideness of a room.
Large extent in all directions; broadness; greatness; as, the wideness of the sea or ocean.
A woman who has lost her husband by death, and has not married again; one living bereaved of a husband.

Widow.etym: [OE. widewe, widwe, AS. weoduwe, widuwe, wuduwe; akin to OFries. widwe, OS. widowa, D. weduwe, G. wittwe, witwe, OHG. wituwa, witawa, Goth. widuw�, Russ. udova, OIr. fedb, W. gweddw, L. vidua, Skr. vidhavā; and probably to Skr. vidh to be empty, to lack; cf. Gr. � a bachelor. ����. Cf. Vidual.]

senses.d: Widowed.
To reduce to the condition of a widow; to bereave of a husband; — rarely used except in the past participle.
q: Though in thus city he Hath widowed and unchilded many a one, Which to this hour bewail the injury.

senses.d: To deprive of one who is loved; to strip of anything beloved or highly esteemed; to make desolate or bare; to bereave.
q: The widowed isle, in mourning, Dries up her tears.
Tress of their shriveled fruits Are widowed, dreary storms o'er all prevail.
Mourn, widowed queen; forgotten Sion, mourn.

senses.d: To endow with a widow's right.
To become, or survive as, the widow of.
q: Let me be married to three kings in a forenoon, and widow them all.

senses.d: In various games, any extra hand or part of a hand, as one dealt to the table.
The state of being a widow; the time during which a woman is widow; also, rarely, the state of being a widower.
q: Johnson clung to her memory during a widowhood of more than thirty years.

senses.d: Estate settled on a widow.
A woman; an adult female; — now used in literature only in certain compounds and phrases, as alewife, fishwife, goodwife, and the like.
q: On the green he saw sitting a wife.

senses.d: The lawful consort of a man; a woman who is united to a man in wedlock; a woman who has a husband; a married woman; — correlative of husband.
q: Let every one you . . . so love his wife even as himself, and the wife see that she reverence her husband.

Wife.etym: [OE. wif, AS. wif; akin to OFries. & OS. wif, D. wijf, G. weib, OHG. wīb, Icel. vīf, Dan. viv; and perhaps to Skr. vip excited, agitated, inspired, vip to tremble, L. vibrare to vibrate, E. vibrate. Cf. Tacitus, : Inesse quin etiam sanctum aliquid et providum putant, nec aut consilia earum aspernant

senses.d: Living in a state of nature; inhabiting natural haunts, as the forest or open field; not familiar with, or not easily approached by, man; not tamed or domesticated; as, a wild boar; a wild ox; a wild cat.
q: Winter's not gone yet, if the wild geese fly that way.

senses.d: Growing or produced without culture; growing or prepared without the aid and care of man; native; not cultivated; brought forth by unassisted nature or by animals not domesticated; as, wild parsnip, wild camomile, wild strawberry, wild honey.
q: The woods and desert caves, With wild thyme and gadding vine o'ergrown.

senses.d: Desert; not inhabited or cultivated; as, wild land.
Savage; uncivilized; not refined by culture; ferocious; rude; as, wild natives of Africa or America.
Not submitted to restraint, training, or regulation; turbulent; tempestuous; violent; ungoverned; licentious; inordinate; disorderly; irregular; fanciful; imaginary; visionary; crazy.
q: What are these So withered and so wild in their attire ?
With mountains, as with weapons, armed; which makes Wild work in heaven.
The wild winds howl.
Search then the ruling passion, there, alone The wild are constant, and the cunning known.

senses.d: Exposed to the wind and sea; unsheltered; as, a wild roadstead.
Indicating strong emotion, intense excitement, or �ewilderment; as, a wild look.
Hard to steer; — said of a vessel.

Wild.etym: [OE. wilde, AS. wilde; akin to OFries. wilde, D. wild, OS. & OHG. wildi, G. wild, Sw. & Dan. vild, Icel. villr wild, bewildered, astray, Goth. wilpeis wild, and G. & OHG. wild game, deer; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: An uninhabited and uncultivated tract or region; a forest or desert; a wilderness; a waste; as, the wilds of America; the wilds of Africa.
q: then Libya first, of all her moisture drained, Became a barren waste, a wild of sand.

senses.d: Wildly; as, to talk wild.
To bewilder; to perplex.
q: Long lost and wildered in the maze of fate.
Again the wildered fancy dreams Of spouting fountains, frozen as they rose.

Wilder.etym: [Akin to E. wild, Dan. forvilde to bewilder, Icel. villr bewildered, villa to bewilder; cf. AS. wildor a wild animal. See Wild, a., and cf. Wilderness.]

senses.d: A tract of land, or a region, uncultivated and uninhabited by human beings, whether a forest or a wide, barren plain; a wild; a waste; a desert; a pathless waste of any kind.
q: The wat'ry wilderness yields no supply.

senses.d: A disorderly or neglected place.
Quality or state of being wild; wildness.
q: These paths and bowers doubt not but our joint hands. Will keep from wilderness with ease.

Wilderness.etym: [OE. wildernesse, wilderne,probably from AS. wildor a wild beast; cf. D. wildernis wilderness. See Wilder, v. t.]

senses.d: A trick or stratagem practiced for insnaring or deception; a sly, insidious; artifice; a beguilement; an allurement.
q: Put on the whole armor of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.
Not more almighty to resist our might, Than wise to frustrate all our plots and wiles.

Wile.etym: [OE. wile, AS. wīl; cf. Icel. v�l, væl. Cf. Guile.]

senses.d: To practice artifice upon; to deceive; to beguile; to allure.
To draw or turn away, as by diversion; to while or while away; to cause to pass pleasantly.

The power of choosing; the faculty or endowment of the soul by which it is capable of choosing; the faculty or power of the mind by which we decide to do or not to do; the power or faculty of preferring or selecting one of two or more objects.
q: It is necessary to form a distinct notion of what is meant by the word “volition” in order to understand the import of the word will, for this last word expresses the power of mind of which “volition” is the act.

Will is an ambiguous word, being sometimes put for the faculty of willing; sometimes for the act of that faculty, besides other meanings. But “volition” always signifies the act of willing, and nothing else.
Appetite is the will's solicitor, and the will is appetite's controller; what we covet according to the one, by the other we often reject.
The will is plainly that by which the mind chooses anything.

senses.d: The choice which is made; a determination or preference which results from the act or exercise of the power of choice; a volition.
q: The word “will,” however, is not always used in this its proper acceptation, but is frequently substituted for “volition”, as when I say that my hand mover in obedience to my will.

senses.d: The choice or determination of one who has authority; a decree; a command; discretionary pleasure.
q: Thy will be done.
Our prayers should be according to the will of God.

senses.d: Strong wish or inclination; desire; purpose.
That which is strongly wished or desired.
q: What's your will, good friar?
The mariner hath his will.

senses.d: Arbitrary disposal; power to control, dispose, or determine.
q: Deliver me not over unto the will of mine enemies.

senses.d: The legal declaration of a person's mind as to the manner in which he would have his property or estate disposed of after his death; the written instrument, legally executed, by which a man makes disposition of his estate, to take effect after his death; testament; devise. See the Note under Testament, 1.

Will.etym: [OE. wille, AS. willa; akin to OFries. willa, OS. willeo, willio, D. wil, G. wille, Icel. vili, Dan. villie, Sw. vilja, Goth wilja. See Will, v.]

senses.d: To wish; to desire; to incline to have.
q: A wife as of herself no thing ne sholde Wille in effect, but as her husband wolde .
Caleb said unto her, What will thou ?
They would none of my counsel.

senses.d: As an auxiliary, will is used to denote futurity dependent on the verb. Thus, in first person, “I will” denotes willingness, consent, promise; and when “will” is emphasized, it denotes determination or fixed purpose; as, I will go if you wish; I will go at all hazards. In the second and third persons, the idea of distinct volition, wish, or purpose is evanescent, and simple certainty is appropriately expressed; as, “You will go,” or “He will go,” describes a future event as a fact only. To emphasize will denotes (according to the tone or context) certain futurity or fixed determination.

Will.etym: [OE. willen, imp. wolde; akin to OS. willan, OFries. willa, D. willen, G. wollen, OHG. wollan, wellan, Icel. & Sw. vilja, Dan. ville, Goth. wiljan, OSlav. voliti, L. velle to wish, volo I wish; cf. Skr. vṛ to choose, to prefer. Cf. Voluntary, Welcome, Well, adv.]

senses.d: To be willing; to be inclined or disposed; to be pleased; to wish; to desire.
q: And behold, there came a leper and worshiped him, saying, Lord if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean. And Jesus . . . touched him, saying, I will; be thou clean.

senses.d: To form a distinct volition of; to determine by an act of choice; to ordain; to decree.
q: By all law and reason, that which the Parliament will not, is no more established in this kingdom.
Two things he willeth, that we should be good, and that we should be happy.

senses.d: To enjoin or command, as that which is determined by an act of volition; to direct; to order.
q: They willed me say so, madam.
Send for music, And will the cooks to use their best of cunning To please the palate.
As you go, will the lord mayor . . . To attend our further pleasure presently.

senses.d: To give or direct the disposal of by testament; to bequeath; to devise; as, to will one's estate to a child; also, to order or direct by testament; as, he willed that his nephew should have his watch.
To exercise an act of volition; to choose; to decide; to determine; to decree.
q: At Winchester he lies, so himself willed.
He that shall turn his thoughts inward upon what passes in his own mind when he wills.
I contend for liberty as it signifies a power in man to do as he wills or pleases.

senses.d: Free to do or to grant; having the mind inclined; not opposed in mind; not choosing to refuse; disposed; not averse; desirous; consenting; complying; ready.
q: Felix, willing to show the Jews a pleasure, left Paul bound.
With wearied wings and willing feet.
shaken in August from the willing boughs.

senses.d: Received of choice, or without reluctance; submitted to voluntarily; chosen; desired.
q: are held, with his melodious harmony, In willing chains and sweet captivity.

senses.d: Spontaneous; self-moved.
q: No spouts of blood run willing from a tree.

senses.d: In a willing manner; with free will; without reluctance; cheerfully.
q: The condition of that people is not so much to be envied as some would willingly represent it.

senses.d: Any tree or shrub of the genus Salix, including many species, most of which are characterized often used as an emblem of sorrow, desolation, or desertion. “A wreath of willow to show my forsaken plight.” Sir W. Scott. Hence, a lover forsaken by, or having lost, the person beloved, is said to wear the willow.
q: And I must wear the willow garland For him that's dead or false to me.

senses.d: A machine in which cotton or wool is opened and cleansed by the action of long spikes projecting from a drum which revolves within a box studded with similar spikes; — probably so called from having been originally a cylindrical cage made of willow rods, though some derive the term from winnow, as denoting the winnowing, or cleansing, action of the machine. Called also willy, twilly, twilly devil, and devil.

Willow.etym: [OE. wilowe, wilwe, AS. wilig, welig; akin to OD. wilge, D. wilg, LG. wilge. Cf. Willy.]

senses.d: To open and cleanse, as cotton, flax, or wool, by means of a willow. See Willow, n., 2.
To begin to wither; to lose freshness and become flaccid, as a plant when exposed when exposed to drought, or to great heat in a dry day, or when separated from its root; to droop;. to wither.

Wilt.etym: [Written also welt, a modification of welk.]

senses.d: To cause to begin to wither; to make flaccid, as a green plant.
Hence, to cause to languish; to depress or destroy the vigor and energy of.
q: Despots have wilted the human race into sloth and imbecility.

senses.d: Full of wiles, tricks, or stratagems; using craft or stratagem to accomplish a purpose; mischievously artful; subtle.
q: This false, wily, doubling disposition of mind.

Wily.syn: Cunning; artful; sly; crafty. See Cunning.

senses.d: A covering of silk, linen, or other material, for the neck and chin, formerly worn by women as an outdoor protection, and still retained in the dress of nuns.
q: Full seemly her wympel ipinched is.
For she had laid her mournful stole aside, And widowlike sad wimple thrown away.
Then Vivian rose, And from her brown-locked head the wimple throws.

senses.d: A flag or streamer.

Wimple.etym: [OE. wimpel, AS. winpel; akin to D. & G. wimpel a pennant, streamer, OHG. wimpal a veil, Icel. vimpill, Dan. & Sw. vimpel a pennant, streamer; of uncertain origin. Cf. Gimp.]

senses.d: To clothe with a wimple; to cover, as with a veil; hence, to hoodwink.
q: This wimpled, whining, purblind, wayward boy.

senses.d: To draw down, as a veil; to lay in folds or plaits, as a veil.
To cause to appear as if laid in folds or plaits; to cause to ripple or undulate; as, the wind wimples the surface of water.
To lie in folds; also, to appear as if laid in folds or plaits; to ripple; to undulate.
q: For with a veil, that wimpled everywhere, Her head and face was hid.
With me through . . . meadows stray, Where wimpling waters make their way.

senses.d: To gain by superiority in competition or contest; to obtain by victory over competitors or rivals; as, to win the prize in a gate; to win money; to win a battle, or to win a country.
q: Thy well-breathed horse Impels the flying car, and wins the course.

senses.d: To allure to kindness; to bring to compliance; to gain or obtain, as by solicitation or courtship.
q: Thy virtue wan me; with virtue preserve me.
She is a woman; therefore to be won.

senses.d: To gain over to one's side or party; to obtain the favor, friendship, or support of; to render friendly or approving; as, to win an enemy; to win a jury.
To come to by toil or effort; to reach; to overtake.
q: Even in the porch he him did win.
And when the stony path began, By which the naked peak they wan, Up flew the snowy ptarmigan.

senses.d: To extract, as ore or coal.

Win.syn: To gain; get; procure; earn. See Gain.
Win.etym: [OE. winnen, AS. winnan to strive, labor, fight, endure; akin to OFries. winna, OS. winnan, D. winnen to win, gain, G. gewinnen, OHG. winnan to strive, struggle, Icel. vinna to labor, suffer, win, Dan. vinde to win, Sw. vinna, Goth. winnan to suffer, Skr. van to wish, get, gain, conquer. √138. Cf. V

senses.d: To gain the victory; to be successful; to triumph; to prevail.
q: Nor is it aught but just That he, who in debate of truth hath won, should win in arms.

senses.d: To turn completely, or with repeated turns; especially, to turn about something fixed; to cause to form convolutions about anything; to coil; to twine; to twist; to wreathe; as, to wind thread on a spool or into a ball.
q: Whether to wind The woodbine round this arbor.

senses.d: To entwist; to infold; to encircle.
q: Sleep, and I will wind thee in arms.

senses.d: To have complete control over; to turn and bend at one's pleasure; to vary or alter or will; to regulate; to govern.
q: In his terms so he would him wind.
Gifts blind the wise, and bribes do please And wind all other witnesses.
Were our legislature vested in the prince, he might wind and turn our constitution at his pleasure.

senses.d: To introduce by insinuation; to insinuate.
q: You have contrived . . . to wind Yourself into a power tyrannical.
Little arts and dexterities they have to wind in such things into discourse.

senses.d: To cover or surround with something coiled about; as, to wind a rope with twine.

Wind.etym: [OE. winden, AS. windan; akin to OS. windan, D. & G. winden, OHG. wintan, Icel. & Sw. vinda, Dan. vinde, Goth. windan (in comp.). Cf. Wander, Wend.]

senses.d: To turn completely or repeatedly; to become coiled about anything; to assume a convolved or spiral form; as, vines wind round a pole.
q: So swift your judgments turn and wind.

senses.d: To have a circular course or direction; to crook; to bend; to meander; as, to wind in and out among trees.
q: And where the valley winded out below, The murmuring main was heard, and scarcely heard, to flow.
He therefore turned him to the steep and rocky path which . . . winded through the thickets of wild boxwood and other low aromatic shrubs.

senses.d: To go to the one side or the other; to move this way and that; to double on one's course; as, a hare pursued turns and winds.
q: The lowing herd wind �lowly o'er the lea.
To wind out, to extricate one's self; to escape. Long struggling underneath are they could wind Out of such prison.

senses.d: The act of winding or turning; a turn; a bend; a twist; a winding.
Air naturally in motion with any degree of velocity; a current of air.
q: Except wind stands as never it stood, It is an ill wind that turns none to good.
Winds were soft, and woods were green.

senses.d: Air artificially put in motion by any force or action; as, the wind of a cannon ball; the wind of a bellows.
Breath modulated by the respiratory and vocal organs, or by an instrument.
q: Their instruments were various in their kind, Some for the bow, and some for breathing wind.

senses.d: Power of respiration; breath.
q: If my wind were but long enough to say my prayers, I would repent.

senses.d: Air or gas generated in the stomach or bowels; flatulence; as, to be troubled with wind.
Air impregnated with an odor or scent.
q: A pack of dogfish had him in the wind.

senses.d: A direction from which the wind may blow; a point of the compass; especially, one of the cardinal points, which are often called the four winds.
q: Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain.

senses.d: A disease of sheep, in which the intestines are distended with air, or rather affected with a violent inflammation. It occurs immediately after shearing.
Mere breath or talk; empty effort; idle words.
q: Nor think thou with wind Of airy threats to awe.

senses.d: The dotterel.

Wind.etym: [AS. wind; akin to OS., OFries., D., & G. wind, OHG. wint, Dan. & Sw. vind, Icel. vindr, Goth winds, W. gwynt, L. ventus, Skr. vāta (cf. Gr. αἤτησ a blast, gale, αἠ̑ναι to breathe hard, to blow, as the wind); originally a p. pr. from the verb seen in Skr. vā to blow, akin to AS. wāwan, D. waaijen, G

senses.d: To expose to the wind; to winnow; to ventilate.
To perceive or follow by the scent; to scent; to nose; as, the hounds winded the game.
To drive hard, or force to violent exertion, as a horse, so as to render scant of wind; to put out of breath.
To blow; to sound by blowing; esp., to sound with prolonged and mutually involved notes.
q: Ye vigorous swains, while youth ferments your blood, . . . Wind the shrill horn.
That blast was winded by the king.

Wind.etym: [From Wind, moving air, but confused in sense and in conjugation with wind to turn.]

senses.d: The region of the pit of the stomach, where a blow may paralyze the diaphragm and cause temporary loss of breath or other injury; the mark.
A call by the boatswain's whistle.
Twisting from a direct line or an even surface; circuitous.
A turn or turning; a bend; a curve; flexure; meander; as, the windings of a road or stream.
q: To nurse the saplings tall, and curl the grove With ringlets quaint, and wanton windings wove.

senses.d: The material, as wire or rope, wound or coiled about anything, or a single round or turn of the material;

a series winding, or one in which the armature coil, the field-magnet coil, and the external circuit form a continuous conductor; a shunt winding, or one of such a character that the armature current is divided, a portion of the current being led around the field-magnet coils.

An opening in the wall of a building for the admission of light and air, usually closed by casements or sashes containing some transparent material, as glass, and capable of being opened and shut at pleasure.
q: I leaped from the window of the citadel.
Then to come, in spite of sorrow, And at my window bid good morrow.

senses.d: The shutter, casement, sash with its fittings, or other framework, which closes a window opening.
A figure formed of lines crossing each other.
q: Till he has windows on his bread and butter.

Window.etym: [OE. windowe, windoge, Icel. vindauga window, properly, wind eye; akin to Dan. vindue. ����. See Wind, n., and Eye.]

senses.d: To furnish with windows.
To place at or in a window.
q: Wouldst thou be windowed in great Rome and see Thy master thus with pleach'd arms, bending down His corrigible neck?

senses.d: Consisting of wind; accompanied or characterized by wind; exposed to wind.
q: Blown with the windy tempest of my heart.

senses.d: Next the wind; windward.
q: It keeps on the windy side of care.

senses.d: Tempestuous; boisterous; as, windy weather.
Serving to occasion wind or gas in the intestines; flatulent; as, windy food.
Attended or caused by wind, or gas, in the intestines.
Fig.: Empty; airy.
q: Here's that windy applause, that poor, transitory pleasure, for which I was dishonored.

senses.d: The expressed juice of grapes, esp. when fermented; a beverage or liquor prepared from grapes by squeezing out their juice, and (usually) allowing it to ferment.
q: Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging, and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise.
Bacchus, that first from out the purple grape Crushed the sweet poison of misused wine.

senses.d: A liquor or beverage prepared from the juice of any fruit or plant by a process similar to that for grape wine; as, currant wine; gooseberry wine; palm wine.
The effect of drinking wine in excess; intoxication.
q: Noah awoke from his wine.

Wine.etym: [OE. win, AS. win, fr. L. vinum (cf. Icel. vīn; all from the Latin); akin to Gr. οἰ̑νοσ, �, and E. withy. Cf. Vine, Vineyard, Vinous, Withy.]

senses.d: One who drinks much wine.

One of the two anterior limbs of a bird, pterodactyl, or bat. They correspond to the arms of man, and are usually modified for flight, but in the case of a few species of birds, as the ostrich, auk, etc., the wings are used only as an assistance in running or swimming.
q: As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings.

senses.d: Any similar member or instrument used for the purpose of flying.
Passage by flying; flight; as, to take wing.
q: Light thickens; and the crow Makes wing to the rooky wood.

senses.d: Motive or instrument of flight; means of flight or of rapid motion.
q: Fiery expedition be my wing.

senses.d: Anything which agitates the air as a wing does, or which is put in winglike motion by the action of the air, as a fan or vane for winnowing grain, the vane or sail of a windmill, etc.
An ornament worn on the shoulder; a small epaulet or shoulder knot.
Any appendage resembling the wing of a bird or insect in shape or appearance.
One of two corresponding appendages attached; a sidepiece.

Wing.etym: [OE. winge, wenge; probably of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. & Sw. vinge, Icel. vængr.]

senses.d: To furnish with wings; to enable to fly, or to move with celerity.
q: Who heaves old ocean, and whowings the storms.
Living, to wing with mirth the weary hours.

senses.d: To supply with wings or sidepieces.
q: The main battle, whose puissance on either side Shall be well winged with our chiefest horse.

senses.d: To transport by flight; to cause to fly.
q: I, an old turtle, Will wing me to some withered bough.

senses.d: To move through in flight; to fly through.
q: There's not an arrow wings the sky But fancy turns its point to him.

senses.d: To cut off the wings of; to wound in the wing; to disable a wing of; as, to wing a bird.
Any surface used primarily for supporting a flying machine in flight, whether by edge-on motion, or flapping, or rotation; specif., either of a pair of supporting planes of a flying machine.
Furnished with wings; transported by flying; having winglike expansions.
Soaring with wings, or as if with wings; hence, elevated; lofty; sublime.
q: How winged the sentiment that virtue is to be followed for its own sake.

senses.d: Swift; rapid.
Wounded or hurt in the wing.
Furnished with a leaflike appendage, as the fruit of the elm and the ash, or the stem in certain plants; alate.
Represented with wings, or having wings, of a different tincture from the body.
Fanned with wings; swarming with birds.
To nod; to sleep; to nap.
To shut the eyes quickly; to close the eyelids with a quick motion.
q: He must wink, so loud he would cry.
And I will wink, so shall the day seem night.
They are not blind, but they wink.

senses.d: To close and open the eyelids quickly; to nictitate; to blink.
q: A baby of some three months old, who winked, and turned aside its little face from the too vivid light of day.

senses.d: To give a hint by a motion of the eyelids, often those of one eye only.
q: Wink at the footman to leave him without a plate.

senses.d: To avoid taking notice, as if by shutting the eyes; to connive at anything; to be tolerant; — generally with at.
q: The times of this ignorance God winked at.
And yet, as though he knew it not, His knowledge winks, and lets his humors reign.
Obstinacy can not be winked at, but must be subdued.

senses.d: To be dim and flicker; as, the light winks.

Wink.etym: [OE. winken, AS. wincian; akin to D. wenken, G. winken to wink, nod, beckon, OHG. winchan, Sw. vinka, Dan. vinke, AS. wancol wavering, OHG. wanchal wavering, wanch�n to waver, G. wanken, and perhaps to E. weak; cf. AS. wincel a corner. Cf. Wench, Wince, v. i.]

senses.d: To cause (the eyes) to wink.
The act of closing, or closing and opening, the eyelids quickly; hence, the time necessary for such an act; a moment.
q: I have not slept one wink.
I could eclipse and cloud them with a wink.

senses.d: A hint given by shutting the eye with a significant cast.
q: The stockjobber thus from Change Alley goes down, And tips you, the freeman, a wink.

senses.d: To separate chaff from grain.
q: Winnow not with every wind.

senses.d: The season of the year in which the sun shines most obliquely upon any region; the coldest season of the year.
q: And after summer evermore succeeds Barren winter, with his wrathful nipping cold.
Winter lingering chills the lap of May.

senses.d: The period of decay, old age, death, or the like.
q: Life's autumn past, I stand on winter's verge.

Winter.etym: [AS. winter; akin to OFries. & D. winter, OS. & OHG. wintar, G. winter, D. & Sw. vinter, Icel. vetr, Goth. wintrus; of uncertain origin; cf. Old Gallic vindo- white (in comp.), OIr. find white. ����.]

senses.d: To pass the winter; to hibernate; as, to winter in Florida.
q: Because the haven was not commodious to winter in, the more part advised to depart thence.

senses.d: To keep, feed or manage, during the winter; as, to winter young cattle on straw.
The lapwing.

Wipe.etym: [Cf. Sw. vipa, Dan. vibe, the lapwing.]

senses.d: To rub with something soft for cleaning; to clean or dry by rubbing; as, to wipe the hands or face with a towel.
q: Let me wipe thy face.
I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down.

senses.d: To remove by rubbing; to rub off; to obliterate; — usually followed by away, off or out. Also used figuratively.
q: Some natural tears they dropped, but wiped them soon.

senses.d: To cheat; to defraud; to trick; — usually followed by out.
q: If they by coveyne or gile be wiped beside their goods.

Wipe.etym: [OE. vipen, AS. wīpian; cf. LG. wiep a wisp of straw, Sw. vepa to wrap up, to cuddle one's self up, vepa a blanket; perhaps akin to E. whip.]

senses.d: Act of rubbing, esp. in order to clean.
A blow; a stroke; a hit; a swipe.
A gibe; a jeer; a severe sarcasm.
A handkerchief.
Stain; brand.
A thread or slender rod of metal; a metallic substance formed to an even thread by being passed between grooved rollers, or drawn through holes in a plate of steel.
A telegraph wire or cable; hence, an electric telegraph; as, to send a message by wire.

Wire.etym: [OE. wir, AS. wir; akin to Icel. vīrr, Dan. vire, LG. wir, wire; cf. OHG. wiara fine gold; perhaps akin to E. withy. ����.]

senses.d: To bind with wire; to attach with wires; to apply wire to; as, to wire corks in bottling liquors.
To put upon a wire; as, to wire beads.
To snare by means of a wire or wires.
To send (a message) by telegraph.
To pass like a wire; to flow in a wirelike form, or in a tenuous stream.
To send a telegraphic message.
The system of wires used to operate the puppets in a puppet show;
One who picks women's pockets.
A knitting needle.
A wire stretching across over a race track at the judges' stand, to mark the line at which the races end.
To place (a ball) so that the wire of a wicket prevents a successful shot.
Certainly; really; indeed.

Wis.etym: [Aphetic form of iwis, ywis; or fr. Icel. viss certain. See Ywis.]

senses.d: To think; to suppose; to imagine; — used chiefly in the first person sing. present tense, I wis. See the Note under Ywis.
q: Nor do I know how long it is (For I have lain entranced, I wis).

Wis.etym: [Due to mistaking OE. iwis certain, AS. gewiss, for I wis. See Ywis.]

senses.d: The quality of being wise; knowledge, and the capacity to make due use of it; knowledge of the best ends and the best means; discernment and judgment; discretion; sagacity; skill; dexterity.
q: We speak also not in wise words of man's wisdom, but in the doctrine of the spirit.
Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding.
It is hoped that our rulers will act with dignity and wisdom that they will yield everything to reason, and refuse everything to force.
Common sense in an uncommon degree is what the world calls wisdom.

senses.d: The results of wise judgments; scientific or practical truth; acquired knowledge; erudition.
q: Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and was mighty in words and in deeds.

Knowledge and wisdom, far from being one, Have ofttimes no connection. Knowledge dwells In heads replete with thoughts of other men; Wisdom, in minds attentive to their own. Knowledge, a rude, unprofitable mass, The mere materials with which wisdom builds, Till smoothed, and squared, and fitted to its place, Does but encumber whom it seems to enrich. Knowledge is proud that he has learned so much; Wisdom is humble that he knows no more.

senses.d: Having knowledge; knowing; enlightened; of extensive information; erudite; learned.
q: They are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge.

senses.d: Hence, especially, making due use of knowledge; discerning and judging soundly concerning what is true or false, proper or improper; choosing the best ends and the best means for accomplishing them; sagacious.
q: When clouds appear, wise men put their cloaks.
From a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation.

senses.d: Versed in art or science; skillful; dexterous; specifically, skilled in divination.
