q: Fal. There was, mine host, an old fat woman even now with me; but she's gone. Sim. Pray you, sir, was't not the wise woman of Brentford?

senses.d: Hence, prudent; calculating; shrewd; wary; subtle; crafty.
q: Nor, on the other side, Will I be penuriously wise As to make money, that's my slave, my idol.
Lords do not care for me: I am too wise to die yet.

senses.d: Dictated or guided by wisdom; containing or exhibiting wisdom; well adapted to produce good effects; judicious; discreet; as, a wise saying; a wise scheme or plan; wise conduct or management; a wise determination.
q: A very grave, state bachelor, my dainty one; He's wise in years, and of a temperate warmth.
You are too wise in years, too full of counsel, For my green experience.

Wise.etym: [OE. wis, AS. wīs; akin to OS. & OFries. wīs, D. wijs, G. weise, OHG. wīs, wīsi, Icel. vīss, Sw. vis, Dan. viis, Goth. weis; akin to wit, v. i. See Wit, v., and cf. Righteous, Wisdom.]

senses.d: Way of being or acting; manner; mode; fashion.
q: To love her in my beste wyse.
This song she sings in most commanding wise.
Let not these blessings then, sent from above, Abused be, or spilt in profane wise.

Wise.etym: [OE. wise, AS. wīse; akin to OS. wīsa, OFries. wīs, D. wijs, wijze, OHG. wīsa, G. weise, Sw. vis, Dan. viis, Icel. ö�ruvīs otherwise; from the root of E. wit; hence, originally, knowledge, skill. See Wit, v., and cf. Guise.]

senses.d: In a wise manner; prudently; judiciously; discreetly; with wisdom.
q: And wisely learn to curb thy sorrows wild.

senses.d: To have a desire or yearning; to long; to hanker.
q: They cast four anchors out of the stern, and wished for the day.
This is as good an argument as an antiquary could wish for.

Wish.etym: [OE. wischen, weschen, wuschen, AS. w�scan; akin to D. wenschen, G. wünschen, Icel. æeskja, Dan. önske, Sw. önska; from AS. w�sc a wish; akin to OD. & G. wunsch, OHG. wunsc, Icel. �sk, Skr. vā�chā a wish, vā�ch to wish; also to Skr. van to like, to wish. �. See Winsome, Win, v. t., and cf. Wistful.]

senses.d: To desire; to long for; to hanker after; to have a mind or disposition toward.
q: I would not wish Any companion in the world but you.
I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper.

senses.d: To frame or express desires concerning; to invoke in favor of, or against, any one; to attribute, or cal down, in desire; to invoke; to imprecate.
q: I would not wish them to a fairer death.
I wish it may not prove some ominous foretoken of misfortune to have met with such a miser as I am.
Let them be driven backward, and put to shame, that wish me evil.

senses.d: To recommend; to seek confidence or favor in behalf of.
q: I would be glad to thrive, sir, And I was wished to your worship by a gentleman.

senses.d: Desire; eager desire; longing.
q: Behold, I am according to thy wish in God a stead.

senses.d: Expression of desire; request; petition; hence, invocation or imprecation.
q: Blistered be thy tongue for such a wish.

senses.d: A thing desired; an object of desire.
q: Will he, wise, let loose at once his ire . . . To give his enemies their wish!

senses.d: Knew.
To know; to learn.
q: Brethren, we do you to wit of the grace of God bestowed on the churches of Macedonia.
Thou wost full little what thou meanest.
We witen not what thing we prayen here.
When that the sooth in wist.

Wit.etym: [OE. witen, pres. ich wot, wat, I know (wot), imp. wiste, AS. witan, pres. wāt, imp. wiste, wisse; akin to OFries. wita, OS. witan, D. weten, G. wissen, OHG. wizzan, Icel. vita, Sw. veta, Dan. vide, Goth. witan to observe, wait I know, Russ. vidiete to see, L. videre, Gr. �, Skr. vid to know, learn;

senses.d: Mind; intellect; understanding; sense.
q: Who knew the wit of the Lord? or who was his counselor?
A prince most prudent, of an excellent And unmatched wit and judgment.
Will puts in practice what wit deviseth.
He wants not wit the dander to decline.

senses.d: A mental faculty, or power of the mind; — used in this sense chiefly in the plural, and in certain phrases; as, to lose one's wits; at one's wits' end, and the like.
q: I will stare him out of his wits.

senses.d: Felicitous association of objects not usually connected, so as to produce a pleasant surprise; also. the power of readily combining objects in such a manner.
q: The definition of wit is only this, that it is a propriety of thoughts and words; or, in other terms, thoughts and words elegantly adapted to the subject.
Wit which discovers partial likeness hidden in general diversity.
Wit lying most in the assemblage of ideas, and putting those together with quickness and variety wherein can be found any resemblance or congruity, thereby to make up pleasant pictures in the fancy.

senses.d: A person of eminent sense or knowledge; a man of genius, fancy, or humor; one distinguished for bright or amusing sayings, for repartee, and the like.
q: In Athens, where books and wits were ever busier than in any other part of Greece, I find but only two sorts of writings which the magistrate cared to take notice of; those either blasphemous and atheistical, or libelous.
Intemperate wits will spare neither friend nor foe.
A wit herself, Amelia weds a wit.
But my five wits nor my five senses can Dissuade one foolish heart from serving thee.

Wit.syn: Ingenuity; humor; satire; sarcasm; irony; burlesque.
Wit.etym: [AS. witt, wit; akin to OFries. wit, G. witz, OHG. wizzī, Icel. vit, Dan. vid, Sw. vett. √133. See Wit, v.]

senses.d: A cone of paper which is placed in a vessel of lard or other fat, and used as a taper.

One who practices the black art, or magic; one regarded as possessing supernatural or magical power by compact with an evil spirit, esp. with the Devil; a sorcerer or sorceress; — now applied chiefly or only to women, but formerly used of men as well.
q: There was a man in that city whose name was Simon, a witch.
He can not abide the old woman of Brentford; he swears she's a witch.

senses.d: An ugly old woman; a hag.
One who exercises more than common power of attraction; a charming or bewitching person; also, one given to mischief; — said especially of a woman or child.
A certain curve of the third order, described by Maria Agnesi under the name versiera.
The stormy petrel.

Witch.etym: [OE. wicche, AS. wicce, fem., wicca, masc.; perhaps the same word as AS. wītiga, wītga, a soothsayer (cf. Wiseacre); cf. Fries. wikke, a witch, LG. wikken to predict, Icel. vitki a wizard, vitka to bewitch.]

senses.d: To bewitch; to fascinate; to enchant.
q: witch sweet ladies with my words and looks.
Whether within us or without The spell of this illusion be That witches us to hear and see.

senses.d: The practices or art of witches; sorcery; enchantments; intercourse with evil spirits.
Power more than natural; irresistible influence.
q: He hath a witchcraft Over the king in 's tongue.

senses.d: With denotes or expresses some situation or relation of nearness, proximity, association, connection, or the like.
To denote a close or direct relation of opposition or hostility; — equivalent to against.
q: Thy servant will . . . fight with this Philistine.

senses.d: To denote association in respect of situation or environment; hence, among; in the company of.
q: I will buy with you, talk with you, walk with you, and so following; but I will not eat with you, drink with you, nor pray with you.
Pity your own, or pity our estate, Nor twist our fortunes with your sinking fate.
See where on earth the flowery glories lie; With her they flourished, and with her they die.
There is no living with thee nor without thee.
Such arguments had invincible force with those pagan philosophers.

senses.d: To denote a connection of friendship, support, alliance, assistance, countenance, etc.; hence, on the side of.
q: Fear not, for I am with thee, and will bless thee.

senses.d: To denote the accomplishment of cause, means, instrument, etc; — sometimes equivalent to by.
q: That with these fowls I be all to-rent.
Thou wilt be like a lover presently, And tire the hearer with a book of words.
entertained a coffeehouse with the following narrative.
With receiving your friends within and amusing them without, you lead a good, pleasant, bustling life of it.

senses.d: To denote association in thought, as for comparison or contrast.
q: Can blazing carbuncles with her compare.

senses.d: To denote simultaneous happening, or immediate succession or consequence.
q: With that she told me . . . that she would hide no truth from me.
With her they flourished, and with her they die.
With this he pointed to his face.

senses.d: To denote having as a possession or an appendage; as, the firmament with its stars; a bride with a large fortune.

With.etym: [OE. with, AS. wi� with, against; akin to AS. wi�er against, OFries. with, OS. wi�, wi�ar, D. weder, weêr (in comp.), G. wider against, wieder gain, OHG. widar again, against, Icel. vi� against, with, by, at, Sw. vid at, by, Dan. ved, Goth. wipra against, Skr. vi asunder. Cf. Withdraw, Withers, With

senses.d: With this; with that.
q: He will scarce be pleased withal.

senses.d: Together with this; likewise; at the same time; in addition; also.
q: Fy on possession But if a man be virtuous withal.
If you choose that, then I am yours withal.
How modest in exception, and withal How terrible in constant resolution.

senses.d: With; — put after its object, at the end of sentence or clause in which it stands.
q: This diamond he greets your wife withal.
Whatsoever uncleanness it be that a man shall be defiled withal.

senses.d: To take back or away, as what has been bestowed or enjoyed; to draw back; to cause to move away or retire; as, to withdraw aid, favor, capital, or the like.
q: Impossible it is that God should withdraw his presence from anything.

senses.d: To take back; to recall or retract; as, to withdraw false charges.
To retire; to retreat; to quit a company or place; to go away; as, he withdrew from the company.
A flexible, slender twig or branch used as a band; a willow or osier twig; a withy.
A band consisting of a twig twisted.
An iron attachment on one end of a mast or boom, with a ring, through which another mast or boom is rigged out and secured; a wythe.
A partition between flues in a chimney.
To bind or fasten with withes.
q: You shall see him withed, and haltered, and staked, and baited to death.

senses.d: To fade; to lose freshness; to become sapless; to become sapless; to dry or shrivel up.
q: Shall he hot pull up the roots thereof, and cut off the fruit thereof, that it wither?

senses.d: To lose or want animal moisture; to waste; to pin� away, as animal bodies.
q: This is man, old, wrinkled, faded, withered.
There was a man which had his hand withered.
Now warm in love, now with'ring in the grave.

senses.d: To lose vigor or power; to languish; to pass away.
q: States thrive or wither as moons wax and wane.

Wither.etym: [OE. wideren; probably the same word as wederen to weather (see Weather, v. & n.); or cf. G. verwittern to decay, to be weather-beaten, Lith. vysti to wither.]

senses.d: To cause to fade, and become dry.
q: The sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass, and the flower thereof falleth.

senses.d: To cause to shrink, wrinkle, or decay, for want of animal moisture.
q: Shot forth pernicious fire Among the accursed, that withered all their strength.

senses.d: To cause to languish, perish, or pass away; to blight; as, a reputation withered by calumny.
q: The passions and the cares that wither life.

senses.d: Faded; dried up; shriveled; wilted; wasted; wasted away.
To hold back; to restrain; to keep from action.
q: Withhold, O sovereign prince, your hasty hand From knitting league with him.

senses.d: To retain; to keep back; not to grant; as, to withhold assent to a proposition.
q: Forbid who will, none shall from me withhold Longer thy offered good.

senses.d: To keep; to maintain; to retain.
q: To withhold it the more easily in heart.

senses.d: In the inner or interior part of; inside of; not without; as, within doors.
q: O, unhappy youth! Come not within these doors; within this roof The enemy of all your graces lives.
Till this be cured by religion, it is as impossible for a man to be happy — that is, pleased and contented within himself — as it is for a sick man to be at ease.

senses.d: In the limits or compass of; not further in length than; as, within five miles; not longer in time than; as, within an hour; not exceeding in quantity; as, expenses kept within one's income.
q: Within these five hours lived Lord Hastings, Untainted, unexamined, free, at liberty.

senses.d: Hence, inside the limits, reach, or influence of; not going outside of; not beyond, overstepping, exceeding, or the like.
q: Both he and she are still within my power.
Within himself The danger lies, yet lies within his power.
Were every action concluded within itself, and drew no consequence after it, we should, undoubtedly, never err in our choice of good.

Within.etym: [OE. withinne, withinnen, AS. wiðinnan; wið with, against, toward + innan in, inwardly, within, from in in. See With, prep., In, prep.]

senses.d: In the inner part; inwardly; internally.
q: Ills from within thy reason must prevent.

senses.d: In the house; in doors; as, the master is within.
On or at the outside of; out of; not within; as, without doors.
q: Without the gate Some drive the cars, and some the coursers rein.

senses.d: Out of the limits of; out of reach of; beyond.
q: Eternity, before the world and after, is without our reach.

senses.d: Not with; otherwise than with; in absence of, separation from, or destitution of; not with use or employment of; independently of; exclusively of; with omission; as, without labor; without damage.
q: I wolde it do withouten negligence.
Wise men will do it without a law.
Without the separation of the two monarchies, the most advantageous terms . . . must end in our destruction.
There is no living with thee nor without thee.

Without.etym: [OE. withoute, withouten, AS. wið�tan; wið with, against, toward + �tan outside, fr. �t out. See With, prep., Out.]

senses.d: Unless; except; — introducing a clause.
q: You will never live to my age without you keep yourselves in breath with exercise, and in heart with joyfulness.

senses.d: On or art the outside; not on the inside; not within; outwardly; externally.
q: Without were fightings, within were fears.

senses.d: Outside of the house; out of doors.
q: The people came unto the house without.

senses.d: To stand against; to oppose; to resist, either with physical or moral force; as, to withstand an attack of troops; to withstand eloquence or arguments.
q: I withstood him to the face.
Some village Hampden, that, with dauntless breast. The little tyrant of his fields withstood.

Withstand.etym: [AS. wiðstandan. See With, prep., and Stand.]

senses.d: o� Withstand.
Attestation of a fact or an event; testimony.
q: May we with . . . the witness of a good conscience, pursue him with any further revenge?
If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true.

senses.d: That which furnishes evidence or proof.
q: Laban said to Jacob, . . . This heap be witness, and this pillar be witness.

senses.d: One who is cognizant; a person who beholds, or otherwise has personal knowledge of, anything; as, an eyewitness; an earwitness.
q: Upon my looking round, I was witness to appearances which filled me with melancholy and regret.

senses.d: One who testifies in a cause, or gives evidence before a judicial tribunal; as, the witness in court agreed in all essential facts.

Witness.etym: [AS. witness, gewitnes, from witan to know. √133. See Wit, v. i.]

senses.d: To see or know by personal presence; to have direct cognizance of.
q: This is but a faint sketch of the incalculable calamities and horrors we must expect, should we ever witness the triumphs of modern infidelity.
General Washington did not live to witness the restoration of peace.

senses.d: To give testimony to; to testify to; to attest.
q: Behold how many things they witness against thee.

senses.d: To see the execution of, as an instrument, and subscribe it for the purpose of establishing its authenticity; as, to witness a bond or a deed.
To bear testimony; to give evidence; to testify.
q: The men of Belial witnessed against him.
The witnessing of the truth was then so generally attended with this event that martyrdom now signifies not only to witness, but to witness to death.

senses.d: Knowingly; with knowledge; by design.
Possessed of wit; knowing; wise; skillful; judicious; clever; cunning.
Especially, possessing wit or humor; good at repartee; droll; facetious; sometimes, sarcastic; as, a witty remark, poem, and the like.

Witty.syn: Acute; smart; sharp; arch; keen; facetious; amusing; humorous; satirical; ironical; taunting.

senses.d: To marry, as a man; to take a wife.
q: Wherefore we pray you hastily to wive.

senses.d: To match to a wife; to provide with a wife.
To take for a wife; to marry.
q: I have wived his sister.

senses.d: pl. of Wife.
A wise man; a sage.
q: See how from far upon the eastern road The star-led wizards haste with odors sweet!

senses.d: One devoted to the black art; a magician; a conjurer; a sorcerer; an enchanter.
q: The wily wizard must be caught.

senses.d: Enchanting; charming.
Haunted by wizards.
q: Where Deva spreads her wizard stream.

senses.d: Grief; sorrow; misery; heavy calamity.
q: Thus saying, from her side the fatal key, Sad instrument of all our woe, she took.
weep each other's woe.

senses.d: A curse; a malediction.
q: Can there be a woe or curse in all the stores of vengeance equal to the malignity of such a practice?
O! woe were us alive .
Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker!
Woe worth the chase, woe worth the day, That costs thy life, my gallant gray!

Woe.etym: [OE. wo, wa, woo, AS. wā, interj.; akin to D. wee, OS. & OHG. wē, G. weh, Icel. vei, Dan. vee, Sw. ve, Goth. wai; cf. L. vae, Gr. �. √128. Cf. Wail.]

senses.d: Woeful; sorrowful.
q: His clerk was woe to do that deed.
Woe was this knight and sorrowfully he sighed.
And looking up he waxed wondrous woe.

senses.d: Full of woe; sorrowful; distressed with grief or calamity; afflicted; wretched; unhappy; sad.
q: How many woeful widows left to bow To sad disgrace!

senses.d: Bringing calamity, distress, or affliction; as, a woeful event; woeful want.
q: O woeful day! O day of woe!

senses.d: Wretched; paltry; miserable; poor.
q: What woeful stuff this madrigal would be!

senses.d: Any one of several species of wild and savage carnivores belonging to the genus Canis and closely allied to the common dog. The best-known and most destructive species are the European wolf (Canis lupus), the American gray, or timber, wolf (C. occidentalis), and the prairie wolf, or coyote. Wolves often hunt in packs, and may thus attack large animals and even man.
One of the destructive, and usually hairy, larvæ of several species of beetles and grain moths; as, the bee wolf.
Fig.: Any very ravenous, rapacious, or destructive person or thing; especially, want; starvation; as, they toiled hard to keep the wolf from the door.
A white worm, or maggot, which infests granaries.
An eating ulcer or sore. Cf. Lupus.
q: If God should send a cancer upon thy face, or a wolf into thy side.

senses.d: The harsh, howling sound of some of the chords on an organ or piano tuned by unequal temperament.
A willying machine.

Wolf.etym: [OE. wolf, wulf, AS. wulf; akin to OS. wulf, D. & G. wolf, Icel. ūlfr, Sw. ulf, Dan. ulv, Goth. wulfs, Lith. vilkas, Russ. volk', L. lupus, Gr. λύκοσ, Skr. vṛka; also to Gr. ἕλκειν to draw, drag, tear in pieces. √286. Cf. Lupine, a., Lyceum.]

senses.d: An adult female person; a grown-up female person, as distinguished from a man or a child; sometimes, any female person.
q: Women are soft, mild pitiful, and flexible.
And the rib, which the Lord God had taken from man, made he a woman.

I have observed among all nations that the women ornament themselves more than the men; that, wherever found, they are the same kind, civil, obliging, humane, tender beings, inclined to be gay and cheerful, timorous and modest.

senses.d: The female part of the human race; womankind.
q: Man is destined to be a prey to woman.

senses.d: A female attendant or servant.

Woman.etym: [OE. woman, womman, wumman, wimman, wifmon, AS. wīfmann, wīmmann; wīf woman, wife + mann a man. See Wife, and Man.]

senses.d: To act the part of a woman in; — with indefinite it.
To make effeminate or womanish.
To furnish with, or unite to, a woman.
The females of the human race; women, collectively.
q: A sanctuary into which womankind, with her tools of magic, the broom and mop, has very infrequent access.

senses.d: The belly; the abdomen.
q: And he coveted to fill his woman of the cods that the hogs eat, and no man gave him.
An I had but a belly of any indifferency, I were simply the most active fellow in Europe. My womb, my womb, my womb undoes me.

senses.d: The uterus. See Uterus.
The place where anything is generated or produced.
q: The womb of earth the genial seed receives.

senses.d: Any cavity containing and enveloping anything.
q: The center spike of gold Which burns deep in the bluebell's womb.

Womb.etym: [OE. wombe, wambe, AS. wamb, womb; akin to D. wam belly, OS. & OHG. wamba, G. wamme, wampe, Icel. vömb, Sw. våmb, Dan. vom, Goth. wamba.]

senses.d: To inclose in a womb, or as in a womb; to breed or hold in secret.
To dwell or abide.
q: This land where I have woned thus long.

senses.d: Dwelling; wone.

That emotion which is excited by novelty, or the presentation to the sight or mind of something new, unusual, strange, great, extraordinary, or not well understood; surprise; astonishment; admiration; amazement.
q: They were filled with wonder and amazement at that which had happened unto him.
Wonder is the effect of novelty upon ignorance.

senses.d: A cause of wonder; that which excites surprise; a strange thing; a prodigy; a miracle.
q: To try things oft, and never to give over, doth wonders.
I am as a wonder unto many.

Wonder.etym: [OE. wonder, wunder, AS. wundor; akin to D. wonder, OS. wundar, OHG. wuntar, G. wunder, Icel. undr, Sw. & Dan. under, and perhaps to Gr. � to gaze at.]

senses.d: To be affected with surprise or admiration; to be struck with astonishment; to be amazed; to marvel.
q: I could not sufficiently wonder at the intrepidity of these diminutive mortals.
We cease to wonder at what we understand.

senses.d: To feel doubt and curiosity; to wait with uncertain expectation; to query in the mind; as, he wondered why they came.
q: I wonder, in my soul, What you would ask me, that I should deny.

senses.d: Wonderful.
q: After that he said a wonder thing.

senses.d: Wonderfully.
Having performed wonders; able to perform wonderful things.
Adapted to excite wonder or admiration; surprising; strange; astonishing.
In a wonderful or surprising manner or degree; wonderfully.
q: For sylphs, yet mindful of their ancient race, Are, as when women, wondrous fond of place.
And now there came both mist and snow, And it grew wondrous cold.

Wondrous.etym: [OE. wonders, adv. (later also adj.). See Wonder, n., and cf. -wards.]

senses.d: Wonderful; astonishing; admirable; marvelous; such as excite surprise and astonishment; strange.
q: That I may . . . tell of all thy wondrous works.
Chloe complains, and wondrously's aggrieved.

senses.d: Using or doing customarily; accustomed; habituated; used.
q: If the ox were wont to push with his horn.

Wont.etym: [For woned, p. p. of won, wone, to dwell, AS. wunian; akin to D. wonen, OS. wun�n, OHG, won�n, G. wohnen, and AS. wund, gewuna, custom, habit; orig. probably, to take pleasure; cf. Icel. una to dwell, to enjoy, Goth. wunan to rejoice (in unwunands sad); and akin to Skr. van to like, to wish. ����. C

senses.d: Custom; habit; use; usage.
q: They are . . . to be called out to their military motions, under sky or covert, according to the season, as was the Roman wont.
From childly wont and ancient use.

senses.d: To be accustomed or habituated; to be used.
q: A yearly solemn feast she wont to make.

senses.d: To accustom; — used reflexively.
Mad; insane; possessed; rabid; furious; frantic.
q: Our hoste gan to swear as he were wood.

Wood.etym: [OE. wod, AS. w�d; akin to OHG. wuot, Icel. ��r, Goth. w�ds, D. woede madness, G. wuth, wut, also to AS. w�� song, Icel. ��r, L. vates a seer, a poet. Cf. Wednesday.]

senses.d: To grow mad; to act like a madman; to mad.
A large and thick collection of trees; a forest or grove; — frequently used in the plural.
q: Light thickens, and the crow Makes wing to the rooky wood.

senses.d: The substance of trees and the like; the hard fibrous substance which composes the body of a tree and its branches, and which is covered by the bark; timber.

The fibrous material which makes up the greater part of the stems and branches of trees and shrubby plants, and is found to a less extent in herbaceous stems. It consists of elongated tubular or needle-shaped cells of various kinds, usually interwoven with the shinning bands called silver grain.
Trees cut or sawed for the fire or other uses.

Wood.etym: [OE. wode, wude, AS. wudu, wiodu; akin to OHG. witu, Icel. vi�r, Dan. & Sw. ved wood, and probably to Ir. & Gael. fiodh, W. gwydd trees, shrubs.]

senses.d: To supply with wood, or get supplies of wood for; as, to wood a steamboat or a locomotive.
To take or get a supply of wood.
The threads that cross the warp in a woven fabric; the weft; the filling; the thread usually carried by the shuttle in weaving.
Texture; cloth; as, a pall of softest woof.

Woof.etym: [OE. oof, AS. ōwef, ōweb, āweb; on, an, on + wef, web, fr. wefan to weave. The initial w is due to the influence of E. weave. See On, Weave, and cf. Abb.]

senses.d: The soft and curled, or crisped, species of hair which grows on sheep and some other animals, and which in fineness sometimes approaches to fur; — chiefly applied to the fleecy coat of the sheep, which constitutes a most essential material of clothing in all cold and temperate climates.
Short, thick hair, especially when crisped or curled.
q: Wool of bat and tongue of dog.

senses.d: A sort of pubescence, or a clothing of dense, curling hairs on the surface of certain plants.

Wool.etym: [OE. wolle, wulle, AS. wull; akin to D. wol, OHG. wolla, G. wolle, Icel. & Sw. ull, Dan. uld, Goth, wulla, Lith. vilna, Russ. volna, L. vellus, Skr. ūrṇā wool, vṛ to cover. √146, 287. Cf. Flannel, Velvet.]

senses.d: The spoken sign of a conception or an idea; an articulate or vocal sound, or a combination of articulate and vocal sounds, uttered by the human voice, and by custom expressing an idea or ideas; a single component part of human speech or language; a constituent part of a sentence; a term; a vocable.
q: You cram these words into mine ears, against The stomach of my sense.
Amongst men who confound their ideas with words, there must be endless disputes.

senses.d: Hence, the written or printed character, or combination of characters, expressing such a term; as, the words on a page.
Talk; discourse; speech; language.
q: Why should calamity be full of words?
Be thy words severe; Sharp as he merits, but the sword forbear.

senses.d: Account; tidings; message; communication; information; — used only in the singular.
q: I pray you . . . bring me word thither How the world goes.

senses.d: Signal; order; command; direction.
q: Give the word through.

senses.d: Language considered as implying the faith or authority of the person who utters it; statement; affirmation; declaration; promise.
q: Obey thy parents; keep thy word justly.
I know you brave, and take you at your word.
I desire not the reader should take my word.

senses.d: Verbal contention; dispute.
q: Some words there grew 'twixt Somerset and me.

senses.d: A brief remark or observation; an expression; a phrase, clause, or short sentence.
q: All the law is fulfilled in one word, even in this; Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself.
She said; but at the happy word “he lives,” My father stooped, re-fathered, o'er my wound.
There is only one other point on which I offer a word of remark.

Word.etym: [AS. word; akin to OFries. & OS. word, D. woord, G. wort, Icel. orð, Sw. & Dan. ord, Goth. waúrd, OPruss. wirds, Lith. vardas a name, L. verbum a word; or perhaps to Gr. ρἥτωρ an orator. Cf. Verb.]

senses.d: To use words, as in discussion; to argue; to dispute.
To express in words; to phrase.
q: The apology for the king is the same, but worded with greater deference to that great prince.

senses.d: To ply with words; also, to cause to be by the use of a word or words.
To flatter with words; to cajole.
Exertion of strength or faculties; physical or intellectual effort directed to an end; industrial activity; toil; employment; sometimes, specifically, physically labor.
q: Man hath his daily work of body or mind Appointed.

senses.d: The matter on which one is at work; that upon which one spends labor; material for working upon; subject of exertion; the thing occupying one; business; duty; as, to take up one's work; to drop one's work.
q: Come on, Nerissa; I have work in hand That you yet know not of.
In every work that he began . . . he did it with all his heart, and prospered.

senses.d: That which is produced as the result of labor; anything accomplished by exertion or toil; product; performance; fabric; manufacture; in a more general sense, act, deed, service, effect, result, achievement, feat.
q: To leave no rubs or blotches in the work.
The work some praise, And some the architect.
Fancy . . . Wild work produces oft, and most in dreams.
The composition or dissolution of mixed bodies . . . is the chief work of elements.

senses.d: Specifically: (a) That which is produced by mental labor; a composition; a book; as, a work, or the works, of Addison. (b) Flowers, figures, or the like, wrought with the needle; embroidery.
q: I am glad I have found this napkin; . . . I'll have the work ta'en out, And give 't Iago.

senses.d: Structures in civil, military, or naval engineering, as docks, bridges, embankments, trenches, fortifications, and the like; also, the structures and grounds of a manufacturing establishment; as, iron works; locomotive works; gas works.
The moving parts of a mechanism; as, the works of a watch.
Manner of working; management; treatment; as, unskillful work spoiled the effect.

The causing of motion against a resisting force. The amount of work is proportioned to, and is measured by, the product of the force into the amount of motion along the direction of the force. See Conservation of energy, under Conservation, Unit of work, under Unit, also Foot pound, Horse power, Poundal, and Erg.
q: Energy is the capacity of doing work . . . Work is the transference of energy from one system to another.

senses.d: Ore before it is dressed.
Performance of moral duties; righteous conduct.
q: He shall reward every man according to his works.
Faith, if it hath not works, is dead.

Work.etym: [OE. work, werk, weork, AS. weorc, worc; akin to OFries. werk, wirk, OS., D., & G. werk, OHG. werc, werah, Icel. & Sw. verk, Dan. værk, Goth. gawaúrki, Gr. �, �, work, � to do, � an instrument, � secret rites, Zend verez to work. ����. Cf. Bulwark, Energy, Erg, Georgic, Liturgy, Metallurgy, Organ, S

senses.d: To exert one's self for a purpose; to put forth effort for the attainment of an object; to labor; to be engaged in the performance of a task, a duty, or the like.
q: O thou good Kent, how shall I live and work, To match thy goodness?
Go therefore now, and work; for there shall no straw be given you.
Whether we work or play, or sleep or wake, Our life doth pass.

senses.d: Hence, in a general sense, to operate; to act; to perform; as, a machine works well.
q: We bend to that the working of the heart.

senses.d: Hence, figuratively, to be effective; to have effect or influence; to conduce.
q: We know that all things work together for good to them that love God.
This so wrought upon the child, that afterwards he desired to be taught.
She marveled how she could ever have been wrought upon to marry him.

senses.d: To carry on business; to be engaged or employed customarily; to perform the part of a laborer; to labor; to toil.
q: They that work in fine flax . . . shall be confounded.

senses.d: To be in a state of severe exertion, or as if in such a state; to be tossed or agitated; to move heavily; to strain; to labor; as, a ship works in a heavy sea.
q: Confused with working sands and rolling waves.

senses.d: To make one's way slowly and with difficulty; to move or penetrate laboriously; to proceed with effort; — with a following preposition, as down, out, into, up, through, and the like; as, scheme works out by degrees; to work into the earth.
q: Till body up to spirit work, in bounds Proportioned to each kind.

senses.d: To ferment, as a liquid.
q: The working of beer when the barm is put in.

senses.d: To act or operate on the stomach and bowels, as a cathartic.
q: Purges . . . work best, that is, cause the blood so to do, . . . in warm weather or in a warm room.

Work.etym: [AS. wyrcean (imp. worthe, wrohte, p. p. geworht, gewroht); akin to OFries. werka, wirka, OS. wirkian, D. werken, G. wirken, Icel. verka, yrkja, orka, Goth. waúrkjan. √145. See Work, n.]

senses.d: To labor or operate upon; to give exertion and effort to; to prepare for use, or to utilize, by labor.
q: He could have told them of two or three gold mines, and a silver mine, and given the reason why they forbare to work them at that time.

senses.d: To produce or form by labor; to bring forth by exertion or toil; to accomplish; to originate; to effect; as, to work wood or iron into a form desired, or into a utensil; to work cotton or wool into cloth.
q: Each herb he knew, that works or good or ill.

senses.d: To produce by slow degrees, or as if laboriously; to bring gradually into any state by action or motion.
q: So the pure, limpid stream, when foul with stains Of rushing torrents and descending rains, Works itself clear, and as it runs, refines, Till by degrees the floating mirror shines.

senses.d: To influence by acting upon; to prevail upon; to manage; to lead.
To form with a needle and thread or yarn; especially, to embroider; as, to work muslin.
To set in motion or action; to direct the action of; to keep at work; to govern; to manage; as, to work a machine.
q: Knowledge in building and working ships.
Now, Marcus, thy virtue's the proof; Put forth thy utmost strength, work every nerve.
The mariners all 'gan work the ropes, Where they were wont to do.

senses.d: To cause to ferment, as liquor.
Break; twist.
The causing of motion against a resisting force, measured by the product of the force into the component of the motion resolved along the direction of the force.
q: Energy is the capacity of doing work. . . . Work is the transference of energy from one system to another.

senses.d: Ore before it is dressed.
One who, or that which, works; a laborer; a performer; as, a worker in brass.
q: Professors of holiness, but workers of iniquity.

senses.d: One of the neuter, or sterile, individuals of the social ants, bees, and white ants. The workers are generally females having the sexual organs imperfectly developed. See Ant, and White ant, under White.
One engaged in the same work with another; a companion in work.
A man employed in labor, whether in tillage or manufactures; a worker.
Hence, especially, a skillful artificer or laborer.
The art or skill of a workman; the execution or manner of making anything.
q: Due reward For her praiseworthy workmanship to yield.
Beauty is nature's brag, and must be shown . . . Where most may wonder at the workmanship.

senses.d: That which is effected, made, or produced; manufacture, something made by manual labor.
q: Not any skilled in workmanship embossed.
By how much Adam exceeded all men in perfection, by being the immediate workmanship of God.

senses.d: The earth and the surrounding heavens; the creation; the system of created things; existent creation; the universe.
q: The invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen.
With desire to know, What nearer might concern him, how this world Of heaven and earth conspicuous first began.

senses.d: Any planet or heavenly body, especially when considered as inhabited, and as the scene of interests analogous with human interests; as, a plurality of worlds.
q: Amongst innumerable stars, that shone Star distant, but high-hand seemed other worlds.
There may be other worlds, where the inhabitants have never violated their allegiance to their almighty Sovereign.

senses.d: The earth and its inhabitants, with their concerns; the sum of human affairs and interests.
q: That forbidden tree, whose mortal taste Brought death into the world, and all our woe.

senses.d: In a more restricted sense, that part of the earth and its concerns which is known to any one, or contemplated by any one; a division of the globe, or of its inhabitants; human affairs as seen from a certain position, or from a given point of view; also, state of existence; scene of life and action; as, the Old World; the New World; the religious world; the Catholic world; the upper world; the future world; the heathen world.
q: One of the greatest in the Christian world Shall be my surety.
Murmuring that now they must be put to make war beyond the world's end — for so they counted Britain.

senses.d: The customs, practices, and interests of men; general affairs of life; human society; public affairs and occupations; as, a knowledge of the world.
q: Happy is she that from the world retires.
If knowledge of the world makes man perfidious, May Juba ever live in ignorance.

senses.d: Individual experience of, or concern with, life; course of life; sum of the affairs which affect the individual; as, to begin the world with no property; to lose all, and begin the world anew.
The inhabitants of the earth; the human race; people in general; the public; mankind.
q: Since I do purpose to marry, I will think nothing to any purpose that the world can say against it.
Tell me, wench, how will the world repute me For undertaking so unstaid a journey?

senses.d: The earth and its affairs as distinguished from heaven; concerns of this life as distinguished from those of the life to come; the present existence and its interests; hence, secular affairs; engrossment or absorption in the affairs of this life; worldly corruption; the ungodly or wicked part of mankind.
q: I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine.

Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.

senses.d: As an emblem of immensity, a great multitude or quantity; a large number.
q: Nor doth this wood lack worlds of company.
A world of woes dispatched in little space.

World.etym: [OE. world, werld, weorld, weoreld, AS. weorold, worold; akin to OS. werold, D. wereld, OHG. weralt, worolt, werolt, werlt, G. welt, Icel. veröld, Sw. verld, Dan. verden; properly, the age of man, lifetime, humanity; AS. wer a man + a word akin to E. old; cf. AS. yld lifetime, age, ylde men, humanit

senses.d: Relating to the world; human; common; as, worldly maxims; worldly actions.
q: Many years it hath continued, standing by no other worldly mean but that one only hand which erected it.

senses.d: Pertaining to this world or life, in contradistinction from the life to come; secular; temporal; devoted to this life and its enjoyments; bent on gain; as, worldly pleasures, affections, honor, lusts, men.
q: With his soul fled all my worldly solace.

senses.d: Lay, as opposed to clerical.
With relation to this life; in a worldly manner.
q: Subverting worldly strong and worldly wise By simply meek.

senses.d: A creeping or a crawling animal of any kind or size, as a serpent, caterpillar, snail, or the like.
q: There came a viper out of the heat, and leapt on his hand. When the men of the country saw the worm hang on his hand, they said, This man must needs be a murderer.
'T is slander, Whose edge is sharper than the sword, whose tongue Outvenoms all the worms of Nile.
When Cerberus perceived us, the great worm, His mouth he opened and displayed his tusks.

senses.d: Any small creeping animal or reptile, either entirely without feet, or with very short ones, including a great variety of animals; as, an earthworm; the blindworm.
An internal tormentor; something that gnaws or afflicts one's mind with remorse.
q: The worm of conscience still begnaw thy soul!

senses.d: A being debased and despised.
q: I am a worm, and no man.

senses.d: Anything spiral, vermiculated, or resembling a worm
q: The threads of screws, when bigger than can be made in screw plates, are called worms.

senses.d: A spiral instrument or screw, often like a double corkscrew, used for drawing balls from firearms.
A certain muscular band in the tongue of some animals, as the dog; the lytta. See Lytta.
The condensing tube of a still, often curved and wound to economize space. See Illust. of Still.
A short revolving screw, the threads of which drive, or are driven by, a worm wheel by gearing into its teeth or cogs. See Illust. of Worm gearing, below.

Worm.etym: [OE. worm, wurm, AS. wyrm; akin to D. worm, OS. & G. wurm, Icel. ormr, Sw. & Dan. orm, Goth. waúrms, L. vermis, Gr. � a wood worm. Cf. Vermicelli, Vermilion, Vermin.]

senses.d: To work slowly, gradually, and secretly.
q: When debates and fretting jealousy Did worm and work within you more and more, Your color faded.

senses.d: To effect, remove, drive, draw, or the like, by slow and secret means; — often followed by out.
q: They find themselves wormed out of all power.
They . . . wormed things out of me that I had no desire to tell.

senses.d: To clean by means of a worm; to draw a wad or cartridge from, as a firearm. See Worm, n. 5 (b).
To cut the worm, or lytta, from under the tongue of, as a dog, for the purpose of checking a disposition to gnaw. The operation was formerly supposed to guard against canine madness.
q: The men assisted the laird in his sporting parties, wormed his dogs, and cut the ears of his terrier puppies.

senses.d: To wind rope, yarn, or other material, spirally round, between the strands of, as a cable; to wind with spun yarn, as a small rope.
q: Ropes . . . are generally wormed before they are served.

senses.d: A composite plant (Artemisia Absinthium), having a bitter and slightly aromatic taste, formerly used as a tonic and a vermifuge, and to protect woolen garments from moths. It gives the peculiar flavor to the cordial called absinthe. The volatile oil is a narcotic poison. The term is often extended to other species of the same genus.
Anything very bitter or grievous; bitterness.
q: Lest there should be among you a root that beareth gall and wormwood.

Wormwood.etym: [AS. werm�d, akin to OHG. wermuota, wormuota, G. wermuth, wermut; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: Bad, ill, evil, or corrupt, in a greater degree; more bad or evil; less good; specifically, in poorer health; more sick; — used both in a physical and moral sense.
q: Or worse, if men worse can devise.
was nothing bettered, but rather grew worse.
Evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse.
There are men who seem to believe they are not bad while another can be found worse.
“But I love him.” “Love him? Worse and worse.”

Worse.etym: [OE. werse, worse, wurse, AS. wiersa, wyrsa, a comparative with no corresponding positive; akin to OS. wirsa, OFries. wirra, OHG. wirsiro, Icel. verri, Sw. värre, Dan. värre, Goth. waírsiza, and probably to OHG. werran to bring into confusion, E. war, and L. verrere to sweep, sweep along. As bad has

senses.d: Loss; disadvantage; defeat.
That which is worse; something less good; as, think not the worse of him for his enterprise.
In a worse degree; in a manner more evil or bad.
q: Now will we deal worse with thee than with them.

Worse.etym: [AS. wiers, wyrs; akin to OS. & OHG. wirs, Icel. verr, Goth, waírs; a comparative adverb with no corresponding positive. See Worse, a.]

senses.d: To make worse; to put disadvantage; to discomfit; to worst. See Worst, v.
q: Weapons more violent, when next we meet, May serve to better us and worse our foes.

Worse.etym: [OE. wursien, AS. wyrsian to become worse.]

senses.d: Excellence of character; dignity; worth; worthiness.
q: A man of worship and honour.
Elfin, born of noble state, And muckle worship in his native land.

senses.d: Honor; respect; civil deference.
q: Of which great worth and worship may be won.
Then shalt thou have worship in the presence of them that sit at meat with thee.

senses.d: Hence, a title of honor, used in addresses to certain magistrates and others of rank or station.
q: My father desires your worships' company.

senses.d: The act of paying divine honors to the Supreme Being; religious reverence and homage; adoration, or acts of reverence, paid to God, or a being viewed as God.
q: The worship of God is an eminent part of religion, and prayer is a chief part of religious worship.

senses.d: Obsequious or submissive respect; extravagant admiration; adoration.
q: 'T is your inky brows, your black silk hair, Your bugle eyeballs, nor your cheek of cream, That can my spirits to your worship.

senses.d: An object of worship.
q: In attitude and aspect formed to be At once the artist's worship and despair.

Worship.etym: [OE. worshipe, wurðscipe, AS. weorðscipe; weorð worth + -scipe -ship. See Worth, a., and -ship.]

senses.d: To respect; to honor; to treat with civil reverence.
q: Our grave . . . shall have a tongueless mouth, Not worshiped with a waxen epitaph.
This holy image that is man God worshipeth.

senses.d: To pay divine honors to; to reverence with supreme respect and veneration; to perform religious exercises in honor of; to adore; to venerate.
q: But God is to be worshiped.
When all our fathers worshiped stocks and stones.

senses.d: To honor with extravagant love and extreme submission, as a lover; to adore; to idolize.
q: With bended knees I daily worship her.

Worship.syn: To adore; revere; reverence; bow to; honor.

senses.d: To perform acts of homage or adoration; esp., to perform religious service.
q: Our fathers worshiped in this mountain; and ye say that in Jerusalem is the place where men ought to worship.
Was it for this I have loved . . . and worshiped in silence?

senses.d: Bad, evil, or pernicious, in the highest degree, whether in a physical or moral sense. See Worse.
q: I have a wife, the worst that may be.
If thou hadst not been born the worst of men, Thou hadst been a knave and flatterer.

Worst.etym: [OE. werst, worste, wurste, AS. wyrst, wierst, wierrest. See Worse, a.]

senses.d: That which is most bad or evil; the most severe, pernicious, calamitous, or wicked state or degree.
q: The worst is not So long as we can say, This is the worst.
He is always sure of finding diversion when the worst comes to the worst.

senses.d: To gain advantage over, in contest or competition; to get the better of; to defeat; to overthrow; to discomfit.
q: The . . . Philistines were worsted by the captivated ark.

senses.d: To grow worse; to deteriorate.

To be; to become; to betide; — now used only in the phrases, woe worth the day, woe worth the man, etc., in which the verb is in the imperative, and the nouns day, man, etc., are in the dative. Woe be to the day, woe be to the man, etc., are equivalent phrases.
q: I counsel . . . to let the cat worthe.
He worth upon his steed gray.

Worth.etym: [OE. worthen, wurþen, to become, AS. weorðan; akin to OS. werðan, D. worden, G. werden, OHG. werdan, Icel. verða, Sw. varda, Goth. waírpan, L. vertere to turn, Skr. vṛt, v. i., to turn, to roll, to become. √143. Cf. Verse, -ward, Weird.]

senses.d: Valuable; of worthy; estimable; also, worth while.
q: It was not worth to make it wise.

senses.d: Equal in value to; furnishing an equivalent for; proper to be exchanged for.
q: A ring he hath of mine worth forty ducats.
All our doings without charity are nothing worth.
If your arguments produce no conviction, they are worth nothing to me.

senses.d: Deserving of; — in a good or bad sense, but chiefly in a good sense.
q: To reign is worth ambition, though in hell.
This is life indeed, life worth preserving.

senses.d: Having possessions equal to; having wealth or estate to the value of.
q: At Geneva are merchants reckoned worth twenty hundred crowns.

Worth.etym: [OE. worth, wurþ, AS. weorð, wurE; akin to OFries. werth, OS. werð, D. waard, OHG. werd, G. wert, werth, Icel. verðr, Sw. värd, Dan. værd, Goth. waírps, and perhaps to E. wary. Cf. Stalwart, Ware an article of merchandise, Worship.]

senses.d: That quality of a thing which renders it valuable or useful; sum of valuable qualities which render anything useful and sought; value; hence, often, value as expressed in a standard, as money; equivalent in exchange; price.
q: What 's worth in anything But so much money as 't will bring?

senses.d: Value in respect of moral or personal qualities; excellence; virtue; eminence; desert; merit; usefulness; as, a man or magistrate of great worth.
q: To be of worth, and worthy estimation.
As none but she, who in that court did dwell, Could know such worth, or worth describe so well.
To think how modest worth neglected lies.

Worth.etym: [OE. worth, wurþ, AS. weorð, wurð; weorð, wurð, adj. See Worth, a.]

senses.d: In a worthy manner; excellently; deservedly; according to merit; justly; suitably; becomingly.
q: You worthily succeed not only to the honors of your ancestors, but also to their virtues.
Some may very worthily deserve to be hated.

senses.d: Having worth or excellence; possessing merit; valuable; deserving; estimable; excellent; virtuous.
q: Full worthy was he in his lordes war.
These banished men that I have kept withal Are men endued with worthy qualities.
Happier thou mayst be, worthier canst not be.
This worthy mind should worthy things embrace.

senses.d: Having suitable, adapted, or equivalent qualities or value; — usually with of before the thing compared or the object; more rarely, with a following infinitive instead of of, or with that; as, worthy of, equal in excellence, value, or dignity to; entitled to; meriting; — usually in a good sense, but sometimes in a bad one.
q: No, Warwick, thou art worthy of the sway.
The merciless Macdonwald, Worthy to be a rebel.
Whose shoes I am not worthy to bear.
And thou art worthy that thou shouldst not know More happiness.
The lodging is well worthy of the guest.

senses.d: Of high station; of high social position.
q: Worthy women of the town.

Worthy.etym: [OE. worthi, wurþi, from worth, wurþ, n.; cf. Icel. verðugr, D. waardig, G. würdig, OHG. wirdīg. See Worth, n.]

senses.d: A man of eminent worth or value; one distinguished for useful and estimable qualities; a person of conspicuous desert; — much used in the plural; as, the worthies of the church; political worthies; military worthies.
q: The blood of ancient worthies in his veins.

senses.d: To render worthy; to exalt into a hero.
Commonly used as an auxiliary verb, either in the past tense or in the conditional or optative present. See 2d & 3d Will.
q: Right as our Lord hath would.

Would.etym: [OE. & AS. wolde. See Will, v. t.]

senses.d: A hurt or injury caused by violence; specifically, a breach of the skin and flesh of an animal, or in the substance of any creature or living thing; a cut, stab, rent, or the like.
q: Showers of blood Rained from the wounds of slaughtered Englishmen.

senses.d: Fig.: An injury, hurt, damage, detriment, or the like, to feeling, faculty, reputation, etc.
An injury to the person by which the skin is divided, or its continuity broken; a lesion of the body, involving some solution of continuity.

Wound.etym: [OE. wounde, wunde, AS. wund; akin to OFries. wunde, OS. wunda, D. wonde, OHG. wunta, G. wunde, Icel. und, and to AS., OS., & G. wund sore, wounded, OHG. wunt, Goth. wunds, and perhaps also to Goth. winnan to suffer, E. win. √140. Cf. Zounds.]

senses.d: To hurt by violence; to produce a breach, or separation of parts, in, as by a cut, stab, blow, or the like.
q: The archers hit him; and he was sore wounded of the archers.

senses.d: To hurt the feelings of; to pain by disrespect, ingratitude, or the like; to cause injury to.
q: When ye sin so against the brethren, and wound their weak conscience, ye sin against Christ.

senses.d: To snatch up; transport; — chiefly used in the p. p. wrapt.
q: Lo! where the stripling, wrapt in wonder, roves.

senses.d: To wind or fold together; to arrange in folds.
q: Then cometh Simon Peter, . . . and seeth . . . the napkin that was about his head, not lying with the linen clothes, but wrapped together in a place by itself.
Like one that wraps the drapery of his couch About him, and lies down to pleasant dreams.

senses.d: To cover by winding or folding; to envelop completely; to involve; to infold; — often with up.
q: I . . . wrapt in mist Of midnight vapor, glide obscure.

senses.d: To conceal by enveloping or infolding; to hide; hence, to involve, as an effect or consequence; to be followed by.
q: Wise poets that wrap truth in tales.
Leontine's young wife, in whom all his happiness was wrapped up, died in a few days after the death of her daughter.
Things reflected on in gross and transiently . . . are thought to be wrapped up in impenetrable obscurity.

Wrap.etym: [OE. wrappen, probably akin to E. warp. √144. Cf. Warp.]

senses.d: A wrapper; — often used in the plural for blankets, furs, shawls, etc., used in riding or traveling.
Violent anger; vehement exasperation; indignation; rage; fury; ire.
q: Wrath is a fire, and jealousy a weed.
When the wrath of king Ahasuerus was appeased.
Now smoking and frothing Its tumult and wrath in.

senses.d: The effects of anger or indignation; the just punishment of an offense or a crime.

Wrath.syn: Anger; fury; rage; ire; vengeance; indignation; resentment; passion. See Anger.
Wrath.etym: [OE. wrathe, wraþþe, wrethe, wræððe, AS. wrǣððo, fr. wrāð wroth; akin to Icel. reiði wrath. See Wroth, a.]

senses.d: To anger; to enrage; — also used impersonally.
q: If him wratheth, be ywar and his way shun.

senses.d: Full of wrath; very angry; greatly incensed; ireful; passionate; as, a wrathful man.
Springing from, or expressing, wrath; as, a wrathful countenance.
Something twisted, intertwined, or curled; as, a wreath of smoke; a wreath of flowers.
q: of his tortuous train Curled many a wanton wreath.

senses.d: A garland; a chaplet, esp. one given to a victor.
q: Conquest doth grant He dear wreath to the Grecian combatant.
Far back in the ages, The plow with wreaths was crowned.

senses.d: An appendage to the shield, placed above it, and supporting the crest (see Illust. of Crest). It generally represents a twist of two cords of silk, one tinctured like the principal metal, the other like the principal color in the arms.

Wreath.etym: [OE. wrethe, AS. wrǣð a twisted band, fr. wrīðan to twist. See Writhe.]

senses.d: To cause to revolve or writhe; to twist about; to turn.
q: And from so heavy sight his head did wreathe.

senses.d: To twist; to convolve; to wind one about another; to entwine.
q: The nods and smiles of recognition into which this singular physiognomy was wreathed.
From his slack hand the garland wreathed for Eve Down dropped.

senses.d: To surround with anything twisted or convolved; to encircle; to infold.
q: Each wreathed in the other's arms.
Dusk faces with withe silken turbants wreathed.
And with thy winding ivy wreathes her lance.

senses.d: To twine or twist about; to surround; to encircle.
q: In the flowers that wreathe the sparkling bowl, Fell adders hiss.

senses.d: To be intewoven or entwined; to twine together; as, a bower of wreathing trees.
Twisted; made into a wreath.
To turn; to twist; esp., to twist or extort by violence; to pull of force away by, or as if by, violent wringing or twisting.
q: Our country's cause, That drew our swords, now secret wrests them from our hand.
They instantly wrested the government out of the hands of Hastings.

senses.d: To turn from truth; to twist from its natural or proper use or meaning by violence; to pervert; to distort.
q: Wrest once the law to your authority.
Thou shalt not wrest the judgment of thy poor.
Their arts of wresting, corrupting, and false interpreting the holy text.

senses.d: To tune with a wrest, or key.

Wrest.etym: [OE. wresten, AS. wr�stan; akin to wr�� a twisted band, and wrī�n to twist. See Writhe.]

senses.d: The act of wresting; a wrench; a violent twist; hence, distortion; perversion.
Active or moving power.
A key to tune a stringed instrument of music.
q: The minstrel . . . wore round his neck a silver chain, by which hung the wrest, or key, with which he tuned his harp.

senses.d: A partition in a water wheel, by which the form of the buckets is determined.
To contend, by grappling with, and striving to trip or throw down, an opponent; as, they wrestled skillfully.
q: To-morrow, sir, I wrestle for my credit, and he that escapes me without some broken limb shall acquit him well.
Another, by a fall in wrestling, started the end of the clavicle from the sternum.

senses.d: Hence, to struggle; to strive earnestly; to contend.
q: Come, wrestle with thy affections.
We wrestle not against flesh and blood.
Difficulties with which he had himself wrestled.

Wrestle.etym: [OE. wrestlen, wrastlen, AS. wr�stlian, freq. of wr�stan to wrest; akin to OD. wrastelen to wrestle. See Wrest, v. t.]

senses.d: To wrestle with; to seek to throw down as in wrestling.
A struggle between two persons to see which will throw the other down; a bout at wrestling; a wrestling match; a struggle.
q: Whom in a wrestle the giant catching aloft, with a terrible hug broke three of his ribs.

senses.d: A miserable person; one profoundly unhappy.
q: Hovered thy spirit o'er thy sorrowing son, Wretch even then, life's journey just begun?

senses.d: One sunk in vice or degradation; a base, despicable person; a vile knave; as, a profligate wretch.

Wretch.etym: [OE. wrecche, AS. wrecca, wræcca, an exile, a wretch, fr. wrecan to drive out, punish; properly, an exile, one driven out, akin to AS. wræc an exile, OS. wrekkio a stranger, OHG. reccheo an exile. See Wreak, v. t.]

senses.d: Very miserable; sunk in, or accompanied by, deep affliction or distress, as from want, anxiety, or grief; calamitous; woeful; very afflicting.
q: O cruel! Death! to those you are more kind Than to the wretched mortals left behind.

senses.d: Worthless; paltry; very poor or mean; miserable; as, a wretched poem; a wretched cabin.
Hatefully contemptible; despicable; wicked.
q: Nero reigned after this Claudius, of all men wretchedest, ready to all manner vices.

senses.d: The quality or state of being wretched; utter misery.
A wretched object; anything despicably.
q: Eat worms and such wretchedness.

senses.d: To twist and compress; to turn and strain with violence; to writhe; to squeeze hard; to pinch; as, to wring clothes in washing.
q: so sweat that men might him wring.
The king began to find where his shoe did wring him.
The priest shall bring it unto the altar, and wring off his head.

senses.d: Hence, to pain; to distress; to torment; to torture.
q: Too much grieved and wrung by an uneasy and strait fortune.
Didst thou taste but half the griefs That wring my soul, thou couldst not talk thus coldly.

senses.d: To distort; to pervert; to wrest.
q: How dare men thus wring the Scriptures?

senses.d: To extract or obtain by twisting and compressing; to squeeze or press (out); hence, to extort; to draw forth by violence, or against resistance or repugnance; — usually with out or form.
q: Your overkindness doth wring tears from me.
He rose up early on the morrow, and thrust the fleece together, and wringed the dew out of the fleece.

senses.d: To subject to extortion; to afflict, or oppress, in order to enforce compliance.
q: To wring the widow from her 'customed right.
The merchant adventures have been often wronged and wringed to the quick.

senses.d: To bend or strain out of its position; as, to wring a mast.

Wring.etym: [OE. wringen, AS. wringan; akin to LG. & D. wringen, OHG. ringan to struggle, G. ringen, Sw. vränga to distort, Dan. vringle to twist. Cf. Wrangle, Wrench, Wrong.]

senses.d: To writhe; to twist, as with anguish.
q: 'T is all men's office to speak patience To those that wring under the load of sorrow.
Look where the sister of the king of France Sits wringing of her hands, and beats her breast.

senses.d: A writhing, as in anguish; a twisting; a griping.
A winkle.
A small ridge, prominence, or furrow formed by the shrinking or contraction of any smooth substance; a corrugation; a crease; a slight fold; as, wrinkle in the skin; a wrinkle in cloth.
q: Within I do not find wrinkles and used heart, but unspent youth.

senses.d: hence, any roughness; unevenness.
q: Not the least wrinkle to deform the sky.

senses.d: A notion or fancy; a whim; as, to have a new wrinkle.

Wrinkle.etym: [OE. wrinkil, AS. wrincle; akin to OD. wrinckel, and prob. to Dan. rynke, Sw. rynka, Icel. hrukka, OHG. runza, G. runzel, L. ruga. ����.]

senses.d: To contract into furrows and prominences; to make a wrinkle or wrinkles in; to corrugate; as, wrinkle the skin or the brow.
q: Her wrinkled form in black and white arrayed.

senses.d: Hence, to make rough or uneven in any way.
q: A keen north wind that, blowing dry, Wrinkled the face of deluge, as decayed.
Then danced we on the wrinkled sand.

senses.d: To shrink into furrows and ridges.
That which is written; writing; scripture; — applied especially to the Scriptures, or the books of the Old and New testaments; as, sacred writ.
q: Then to his hands that writ he did betake, Which he disclosing read, thus as the paper spake.
Babylon, so much spoken of in Holy Writ.

senses.d: An instrument in writing, under seal, in an epistolary form, issued from the proper authority, commanding the performance or nonperformance of some act by the person to whom it is directed; as, a writ of entry, of error, of execution, of injunction, of mandamus, of return, of summons, and the like.
To set down, as legible characters; to form the conveyance of meaning; to inscribe on any material by a suitable instrument; as, to write the characters called letters; to write figures.

To set down for reading; to express in legible or intelligible characters; to inscribe; as, to write a deed; to write a bill of divorcement; hence, specifically, to set down in an epistle; to communicate by letter.
q: Last night she enjoined me to write some lines to one she loves.
I chose to write the thing I durst not speak To her I loved.

senses.d: Hence, to compose or produce, as an author.
q: I purpose to write the history of England from the accession of King James the Second down to a time within the memory of men still living.

senses.d: To impress durably; to imprint; to engrave; as, truth written on the heart.
To make known by writing; to record; to prove by one's own written testimony; — often used reflexively.
q: He who writes himself by his own inscription is like an ill painter, who, by writing on a shapeless picture which he hath drawn, is fain to tell passengers what shape it is, which else no man could imagine.

Write.etym: [OE. writen, AS. wrītan; originally, to scratch, to score; akin to OS. wrītan to write, to tear, to wound, D. rijten to tear, to rend, G. reissen, OHG. rīzan, Icel. rīta to write, Goth. writs a stroke, dash, letter. Cf. Race tribe, lineage.]

senses.d: To form characters, letters, or figures, as representative of sounds or ideas; to express words and sentences by written signs.
q: So it stead you, I will write, Please you command.

senses.d: To be regularly employed or occupied in writing, copying, or accounting; to act as clerk or amanuensis; as, he writes in one of the public offices.
To frame or combine ideas, and express them in written words; to play the author; to recite or relate in books; to compose.
q: They can write up to the dignity and character of the authors.

senses.d: To compose or send letters.
q: He wrote for all the Jews that went out of his realm up into Jewry concerning their freedom.

senses.d: One who writes, or has written; a scribe; a clerk.
q: They that handle the pen of the writer.
My tongue is the pen of a ready writer.

senses.d: One who is engaged in literary composition as a profession; an author; as, a writer of novels.
q: This pitch, as ancient writers do report, doth defile.

senses.d: A clerk of a certain rank in the service of the late East India Company, who, after serving a certain number of years, became a factor.

The act or art of forming letters and characters on paper, wood, stone, or other material, for the purpose of recording the ideas which characters and words express, or of communicating them to others by visible signs.
Anything written or printed; anything expressed in characters or letters
q: And Pilate wrote a title . . . And the writing was, Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.

senses.d: Handwriting; chirography.
Twisted; wry; as, a wrong nose.

Not according to the laws of good morals, whether divine or human; not suitable to the highest and best end; not morally right; deviating from rectitude or duty; not just or equitable; not true; not legal; as, a wrong practice; wrong ideas; wrong inclinations and desires.

Not fit or suitable to an end or object; not appropriate for an intended use; not according to rule; unsuitable; improper; incorrect; as, to hold a book with the wrong end uppermost; to take the wrong way.
q: I have deceived you both; I have directed you to wrong places.

senses.d: Not according to truth; not conforming to fact or intent; not right; mistaken; erroneous; as, a wrong statement.
Designed to be worn or placed inward; as, the wrong side of a garment or of a piece of cloth.

Wrong.syn: Injurious; unjust; faulty; detrimental; incorrect; erroneous; unfit; unsuitable.
Wrong.etym: [OE. wrong, wrang, a. & n., AS. wrang, n.; originally, awry, wrung, fr. wringan to wring; akin to D. wrang bitter, Dan. vrang wrong, Sw. vrång, Icel. rangr awry, wrong. See Wring.]

senses.d: In a wrong manner; not rightly; amiss; morally ill; erroneously; wrongly.
q: Ten censure wrong for one that writes amiss.

senses.d: That which is not right.
Nonconformity or disobedience to lawful authority, divine or human; deviation from duty; — the opposite of moral right.
q: When I had wrong and she the right.
One spake much of right and wrong.

senses.d: Deviation or departure from truth or fact; state of falsity; error; as, to be in the wrong.

Whatever deviates from moral rectitude; usually, an act that involves evil consequences, as one which inflicts injury on a person; any injury done to, or received from; another; a trespass; a violation of right.
q: Friend, I do thee no wrong.
As the king of England can do no wrong, so neither can he do right but in his courts and by his courts.
The obligation to redress a wrong is at least as binding as that of paying a debt.

senses.d: To treat with injustice; to deprive of some right, or to withhold some act of justice from; to do undeserved harm to; to deal unjustly with; to injure.
q: He that sinneth . . . wrongeth his own soul.

senses.d: To impute evil to unjustly; as, if you suppose me capable of a base act, you wrong me.
q: I rather choose To wrong the dead, to wrong myself and you, Than I will wrong such honorable men.

senses.d: Full of wrong; injurious; unjust; unfair; as, a wrongful taking of property; wrongful dealing.
To root with the snout. See 1st Root.
Full of wrath; angry; incensed; much exasperated; wrathful.
q: Revel and truth as in a low degree, They be full wroth [i.e., at enmity] all day.
Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell.

Wroth.etym: [OE. wroth, wrap, AS. wrāð wroth, crooked, bad; akin to wrīðan to writhe, and to OS. wrēðangry, D. wreed cruel, OHG. reid twisted, Icel. reiðr angry, Dan. & Sw. vred. See Writhe, and cf. Wrath.]

senses.d: Worked; elaborated; not rough or crude.
Act of one who wrestles; specif., the sport consisting of the hand-to-hand combat between two unarmed contestants who seek to throw each other.
